Immunohistochemistry may support diagnosis7; pleomorphic adenoma gene 1 (PLAG1) staining is often positive and serves as a surrogate marker for underlyingPLAG1fusion (chromosome 8q12), the most prevalent genetic alteration found in PA.8In this case, a triphasic mixture was observed (Figure 2), and PLAG1 demonstrated nuclear positivity in each component, with strongest expression in cells surrounding ductal structures, consistent with the characteristic staining pattern of PA.8,9 Complete surgical excision is the standard of care for PAs.10Definitive treatment of airway PA would typically involve a segmental tracheal resection with end-to-end anastomosis.2,3Endoscopic resection or repeated debulking may be considered in selected cases, although the risk of recurrence and malignant transformation remains a concern. Given this patient’s young age, a segmental tracheal resection was performed without tracheostomy. Long-term surveillance, including endoscopic and radiologic evaluations, is recommended, although standardized follow-up protocols have not been established. Although PA is a familiar diagnosis in head and neck pathology, this case illustrates the importance of including PA in the differential diagnosis when evaluating airway lesions, as these common tumors may present in highly unusual locations.

caption: A, Direct laryngoscopy visualizing a laryngeal mass causing globus, muffled voice, and acute hemoptysis. B, Contrasted computed tomography (CT) image of the laryngeal mass.
scenario: A 76-year-old Armenian man presented to the emergency department with a 6-week history of globus sensation and muffled voice and acute onset frank hemoptysis. He denied odynophagia, dysphagia, or dyspnea. He had a medical history of coronary artery disease with recent drug-eluting stent placement requiring use of clopidogrel and aspirin as well as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease treated with fluticasone propionate/salmeterol inhaler for more than 20 years. The patient had no prior history of immunosuppression or organ transplant, and results of his HIV test were negative. He had no significant history of tobacco or alcohol use. Head and neck examination findings were notable for a small, purple, and painless nodule behind the left pinna. Laryngoscopy revealed a large mobile, multilobulated, broadly pedunculated mass that was friable and oozing on the lingual surface of the epiglottis (Figure 1A). Contrasted computed tomography of the neck and chest demonstrated a large lobulated enhancing soft tissue mass on the epiglottis measuring 3.5 × 2.3 × 1.6 cm without any suspicious lymphadenopathy, lung nodules, or any other masses (Figure 1B). There were no other abnormalities in the oropharynx, hypopharynx, or larynx. Operative direct laryngoscopy and debulking biopsies were performed. Bleeding was controlled with oxymetazoline and selective cauterization.
explanation: Kaposi sarcoma (KS) is a vascular neoplasm originating from endothelial cells of blood and lymphatic vessels infected with human herpes virus type 8 (HHV-8). The exact mechanism of HHV-8–mediated oncogenesis is not fully understood.1KS lesions usually appear as cutaneous painless violaceous macules that progress into indurated plaques and nodules with possible mucosal and visceral involvement. There are 4 variants of KS: classic (Mediterranean), endemic (African), iatrogenic (immunosuppressed/transplant related), and epidemic (HIV/AIDS associated). Classic KS is traditionally indolent, presenting in the lower extremities of elderly men of Mediterranean or eastern European descent. Classic KS may also be a sign of a secondary malignant neoplasm.2Lesions may appear in the head and neck, especially the oropharynx and lymph nodes. Although an uncommon cause of laryngeal mass, KS poses a life-threatening risk of airway obstruction if not identified and managed promptly3and thus should be considered in the differential diagnosis of a patient with hemoptysis and a laryngeal mass. Diagnostic features include a violaceous pedunculated mass on laryngoscopy with narrow-band imaging confirming high vascularity. Imaging findings are nonspecific, often describing an enhancing mass affecting 1 or more laryngeal subsites. Tissue biopsy is diagnostic with hallmark features of slitlike vascular spaces formed by spindled cells and immunohistochemistry positive for HHV-8, CD34, and CD31.2There is currently no guideline in the management of KS in the larynx, but a recent systematic review suggests its management and prognosis depend on the variant, depth of invasion, and involvement of surrounding structures.3Classic KS is treated with larynx-sparing surgical excision or radiotherapy with complete resolution of disease, whereas epidemic KS was typically treated with chemotherapy and had poor outcomes. In this case, the patient most likely has classic KS. A shared decision was made to perform urgent operative direct laryngoscopy and excisional biopsies. The patient was easily mask ventilated but was difficult to intubate due to poor visualization from the large mobile and oozing tumor, and thus a Dedo laryngoscope was used to intubate. A Lindholm laryngoscopy was used to examine the airway followed by debulking biopsies of the entire lingual epiglottic mass off the cartilage itself using a combination of straight and up-biting cups and alligator forceps. Histopathology revealed spindle-shaped cells arranged in a slitlike pattern and positive immunohistochemical staining for CD34 and HHV-8 consistent with KS (Figure 2). The patient elected for watchful waiting given localized disease. After 3 months, he returned with reported increased cutaneous lesions affecting his ear, lower extremities and trunk as well as globus sensation. Laryngoscopy showed many lesions on his larynx, including a 1.5-cm pedunculated mass on the left arytenoid that partially obstructs airflow with inspiration and smaller lesions on the right posterior arytenoid, right ventricle, and right laryngeal surface of the epiglottis. Excisional biopsy of the left arytenoid mass confirmed KS. He did well after 8 cycles of doxorubicin but relapsed 2 years later with cutaneous lesions but none involving the larynx on laryngoscopy. Doxorubicin was restarted with good success. This case demonstrated laryngoscopy and immunohistopathology findings of KS, an uncommon cause for a supraglottic and laryngeal mass.

scenario: A large oral mass was noted at time of delivery in a female neonate at gestational age of 39 weeks. Primary symptom was difficulty feeding without notable respiratory distress. Prenatal history included maternal herpes simplex virus, well controlled with valacyclovir. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the neck with and without contrast was obtained showing a 3-cm heterogeneously enhancing mass arising from the posterior aspect of the tongue, abutting the inferior surface of the uvula with mild T1 hypointensity. On examination, a tan lobulated-appearing mass was noted occupying nearly all of the oral cavity and was adherent to the tongue posteriorly. No connection was noted to soft or hard palate, buccal mucosa, tonsillar fossae, or alveolar ridges. Surgical excision was performed on day 6 of life. The mass was noted to be attached just anteriorly to the dorsal lingual papillae with a wide base and was excised from the underlying tongue using cautery along with a cuff of lingual tissue (Figure 1). Direct laryngoscopy after removal of the mass revealed a grade I view with no other lesions present. Primary suture closure was accomplished without difficulty. The final specimen measured 3.5 cm anterior to posterior, 2.3 cm medial to lateral, and 1.1 cm in average thickness. The internal tissue was yellow-tan, fatty, and interdigitating with the underlying musculature.
explanation: On microscopic evaluation, the specimen consisted of glioneuronal tissue showing both neurons positive for NeuN1 and glial cells positive for glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) in a fibrotic background. CD57 was previously well utilized for glial heterotopia, but GFAP has replaced this stain in most institutions. The neuronal component showed focal forms with eosinophilic cytoplasm and a peripherally positioned, flattened nucleus. The specimen had 2 mitotic figures per 10 high-powered fields, structures consistent with choroid plexus, and negative HMB45 staining. HMB45 is useful to rule out melanotic neuroectodermal tumor of infancy, as other melanoma markers are typically negative. The pigmented macrophages are highlighted by CD68, and a second stain is needed to rule out melanotic neuroectodermal tumor of infancy. While rare, it is found in the oral cavity. CD68 staining showed marked increase in macrophages. Granular cell tumor is a mimic of glial heterotopia; this neuroectodermal tumor is differentiated by CD68, which draws attention to cytoplasmic lysosomal granules, negative in this tumor. Ki-67 index was high at 15% to 20%. This was consistent with diagnosis of glial heterotopia (Figure 2). Glial heterotopia is a congenital, nonhereditary malformation of infants that represents benign cerebral tissue of extracranial sites. It most frequently occurs in the nasal area but rarely can present at other sites of the head and neck, including oral cavity, middle ear, tonsillar fossa, and orbit.1,2It is considered benign, although rare cases of malignant transformation have been reported. It is estimated to occur in 20 000 to 40 000 live births; more frequently in males at an approximate 3:2 ratio. Most cases are diagnosed by age 3 years.3 Glial cells are normally located in the central nervous system and serve as neuronal support cells. The development of glial heterotopia is embryologically similar to encephaloceles or dermoid cysts.4There are many proposed mechanisms, including encephalocele that loses intracranial connection, displacement of neuroectodermal cells during early embryogenesis, or glial cell migration from the olfactory bulb. Glial heterotopia lesions consist of mature astrocytes and glial fibers embedded in a fibrovascular stroma, often with elements of ependymal lined structures including choroid plexus, as in the present case.5,6 Workup for these lesions should include imaging such as ultrasonography, computed tomography, or MRI to rule out intracranial extent or skull base defects prior to intervention.3,7MRI and computed tomography cannot distinguish a glial heterotopic lesion from other common midline masses of the head and neck, including thyroglossal duct cyst, teratoma, and lymphatic malformations.6Biopsy can be considered after ruling out intracranial extent, especially in older patients to rule out malignancy.4Surgical resection is generally recommended, especially in the setting of functional complications including airway distress, dysphagia, or failure to thrive.4,5Early surgical intervention is recommended in the case of rapid growth. Recurrence is not uncommon, at a reported rate of 4% to 15%. This is more common in the first few weeks after surgical resection.4Complete resection with histologically clear margins and a follow-up period of at least 12 months is recommended. Repeat MRI can be considered in cases of uncertain recurrence.4There is an overall lack of long-term outcome data for these patients.4 Congenital epulis is another rare congenital phenomenon of the oral cavity, generally located on the alveolar ridge but can rarely present on the tongue. Management for these lesions includes surgical excision, and diagnosis is made on pathological examination showing large sheets of typical polygonal granular cells without nuclear atypia and no particular cellular arrangement.8Lymphatic malformations show anastomosing lymphatic and venous channels on histology.9Lingual thyroid has similar histologic features to normal thyroid tissue, and generally arises at the foramen cecum.10

scenario: A 20-year-old Chinese male competitive swimmer presented with bilateral conductive hearing loss. Evaluation of the right ear revealed a hypotympanic cholesteatoma with a large tympanic membrane perforation and absent incus and stapes suprastructure. In the left ear, an absence of the stapes suprastructure was noted. A single-stage surgery on the right ear was performed, involving cholesteatoma removal via a canal-wall-up mastoidectomy and ossicular chain reconstruction. Postoperative computed tomography (CT) scans revealed an unusual finding (Figure 1). Nevertheless, the patient maintained stable hearing with an average air conduction threshold of 30 dB over a 9-year follow-up period.

options.A: Absent incus due to previous surgery and disease
options.B: Repositioned incus with an ossicular bone graft from previous surgery
options.C: Stapedotomy surgery with a titanium implant from previous surgery
options.D: Middle ear bone graft with evidence of stapedotomy from previous surgery

answer: Middle ear bone graft with evidence of stapedotomy from previous surgery
distractors: Absent incus due to previous surgery and disease
Repositioned incus with an ossicular bone graft from previous surgery
Stapedotomy surgery with a titanium implant from previous surgery
explanation: D. Middle ear bone graft with evidence of stapedotomy from previous surgery CT axial and coronal cuts of the right middle ear reveal a middle ear ossicular bone graft instead of an absent incus (Figure 2). The graft’s almost vertical limb connects the malleus handle to the stapes footplate, differing in shape from a refashioned incus and lacking the signal properties of a titanium implant. The graft has also penetrated the vestibule, creating a stapedotomylike appearance. Cholesteatoma as a cause for middle ear disease has become increasingly rare due to improved treatment of childhood otitis. Much less encountered are complications arising from complete erosion of the middle ear ossicles resulting in maximal conductive hearing loss. In this case, it was difficult to determine whether the patient’s ossicular absence was congenital or as a consequence of the hypotympanic cholesteatoma itself. Congenital cholesteatoma is a rare disease that most commonly presents with an intact tympanic membrane in the anterosuperior quadrant of the mesotympanum,1with only 2 cases of hypotympanic congenital cholesteatomas reported in the literature thus far.2,3While acquired cholesteatomas usually present in the attic and posterosuperior quadrant,4the patient’s excellent speech clarity and presence of a large inferior tympanic membrane perforation suggest an acquired origin. Currently, no consensus has been reached regarding which prosthesis material or surgical technique yields the best clinical outcome in ossicular reconstruction.5,6Factors affecting the outcome of ossiculoplasty include composition and design of prosthesis used, eustachian tube function, status of residual ossicular chain, and degree of preoperative hearing loss.7Recent studies have found no significant differences in hearing outcomes between autogenous and alloplastic prostheses for both partial and total ossicular replacement prostheses.8,9In this case, a 1.5 × 0.5-cm rectangular graft was harvested from the temporal bone by drilling a well around it and carefully chiseling it off. After meticulous cholesteatoma removal, the cortical bone graft was refashioned into a7shape using a 1-mm diamond burr and used for ossicular chain reconstruction. Considerations for graft selection included risk of cartilage resorption over time and the extensive infection control measures required for allograft storage but was ultimately based on the surgeon’s preference. Despite challenges in harvesting, fashioning, and reconstructing the graft as well as an extended surgical time, cortical bone was chosen as a biocompatible and cost-effective alternative to synthetic prosthesis. To minimize the risk of recurrent cholesteatoma, the autograft was harvested from the temporal region, outside the surgical field of disease. The surgery successfully restored hearing and maintained long-term stability with no clinical evidence of cholesteatoma recurrence; hence, yearly observation was offered over more invasive investigations. Repeated CT scans confirmed complete cholesteatoma extirpation. Notably, postoperative imaging revealed graft penetration into the vestibule, where the patient’s active involvement in competitive water polo may have contributed to this spontaneous stapedotomylike outcome. To our knowledge, this is the first reported case of autograft migration without complications, such as perilymphatic fistula development, over 9 years of follow-up. We speculate that this may have even facilitated stable auditory function by creating a more efficient direct sound transmission pathway. The patient’s unilateral hearing satisfaction also led him to decline treatment for his left congenital hearing loss. In conclusion, all surgical options for ossicular chain reconstruction are associated with risks of extrusion, infection, and sensorineural hearing loss, requiring a case-by-case approach to managing cholesteatoma with conductive hearing loss. This case demonstrates that autologous cortical bone grafting can yield good and sustained hearing results, which presents a durable and a viable alternative to the more costly option of active middle ear implants and bypasses the need for second-stage surgery.

scenario: A 64-year-old woman was referred to our clinic for continued management of long-standing chronic rhinosinusitis without nasal polyps. Medical history included type 2 diabetes, congestive heart failure, coronary artery disease, chronic kidney disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, hypertension, obstructive sleep apnea, a 42–pack-year smoking history, and chronic rhinosinusitis for which she underwent endoscopic sinus surgery 23 years prior. Despite surgery, she had persistent, thick postnasal drip with mucopurulent drainage and was treated with saline and gentamicin rinses 10 years prior to presentation with symptomatic improvement. Imaging available from this period did not demonstrate obstructive sinus disease. The patient continued using the irrigations for the next 8 years until stopping 2 years prior to presentation. On history, the patient continued to report ongoing headaches and discolored nasal drainage bilaterally. A computed tomographic scan obtained 2 months prior to presentation for facial trauma workup demonstrated right posterior maxillary wall and ethmoid sinus changes (Figure 1). Nasal endoscopic results revealed yellow-green mucopurulent debris in the right maxillary sinus, which was sent for culture. The culture subsequently identifiedPseudomonas aeruginosa.As a result, the patient was again treated with gentamicin and budesonide nasal irrigations. Clearance of the mucopurulent debris provided an unobstructed view of the nasal mucosa during repeat endoscopy, revealing multiple outgrowths with a cobblestone appearance on the posterior walls of the maxillary sinus.
explanation: Often seen in “surfer’s ear,” exostoses are benign bony growths commonly found in the external auditory canal (EAC).1While the exact mechanism of exostosis formation has yet to be fully elucidated, it is typically observed in patients who frequently engage in surfing or aquatic activities.1,2Literature dating back to 1938 demonstrates a relationship between prolonged and repeated water exposure, particularly cold water, and the formation of exostoses in the EAC. Kroon et al3demonstrated that each year spent surfing was associated with a 12% increased risk of developing exostosis, as well as a 10% increased risk of exostosis progression. As the periosteum of the EAC lacks the insulating protection of subcutaneous fat, it is hypothesized that cold water entering the EAC causes a periosteal insult, triggering a hyperplastic response that leads to the formation of new bone layers as a protective mechanism.4Histologically, these lesions are identified by concentric layers of lamellar bone, which likely result from repeated stimulation of the periosteum from cold temperatures.5Clinically, EAC exostoses present with a range of symptoms depending on degree of obstruction; ear fullness, trapped water, otitis externa, conductive hearing loss, and tinnitus are known complications.2Although rare, several cases of paranasal sinus exostoses (PSE) have been reported.4,6-8Similar to the EAC, the lining of the paranasal sinuses is thin and lacks an insulating layer of subcutaneous adipose tissue. Thus, it is suggested that paranasal sinus bone is similarly susceptible to temperature fluctuations and resulting periosteal reactivity.4 PSE have been described in dentistry,9,10radiology,8and otolaryngology4,6,7literature. On review of reports where otolaryngologists have been involved in the evaluation and management of PSE,4,6-8diagnosis was based on a combination of endoscopic and radiographic findings. Endoscopic examination of PSE demonstrates multiple small, oval, cystic-appearing protuberant outgrowths arranged in cobblestone patterns that are firm to instrument palpation (Figure 2). Radiographically, PSE appears as rounded, compact, radio-dense, multifocal bony outgrowths on the luminal surfaces and septa of the paranasal sinuses, without intracranial or infraorbital extension. PSE has been described in the maxillary, ethmoid, and sphenoid sinuses.4,6-8History typically reveals prior sinus surgery and the use of cold nasal irrigations, including saline or antimicrobial rinses. No cases of PSE have been reported in stenotic or obstructed sinuses, nor in association with overlying mucosal edema or inflammatory processes. Biopsies of PSE by Ramakrishnan et al4demonstrated histopathological similarities between PSE and EAC exostoses, while Haffey et al reported “benign-appearing fragments of bone, with no evidence of malignancy.”6(p1894)In all cases, no symptoms were directly attributed to PSE.4,6-8PSE were not demonstrated to further grow or develop once cold irrigations were stopped.6,7 This case demonstrated an uncommon paranasal sinus lesion in a common rhinologic clinical scenario, diagnosed through endoscopy, computed tomographic imaging, and patient history. The patient experienced resolution of her chronic rhinosinusitis symptoms with gentamicin rinses, without recurrence following the transition to saline irrigations. She was counseled on the use of warm or room temperature rinses to mitigate the risk of exostosis progression. Given the location of the exostosis, we did not believe it contributed to her history of recurrent sinusitis or posed a risk of obstructive sinus disease; therefore, surgical intervention was not indicated. Paranasal exostoses should be considered in the differential diagnosis of maxillary and ethmoid sinus lesions, and management includes cessation of cold-water irrigations and clinical monitoring.

caption: A, Low-powered hematoxylin-eosin stain of polypoidal mucosa with edematous stroma and numerous ectatic vascular channels (original magnification ×200). B, Coronal postcontrast T1 fat-saturated image acquired in a 3-T magnet.
scenario: A 16-year-old male with a history of mild seasonal allergies presented with right-sided congestion, thick discolored nasal drainage, facial pain/pressure, anosmia, and intermittent epistaxis for approximately 1 year. Nasal endoscopy revealed moderate global deviation of the septum to the left. On the right, thick mucus and crusting anterior to the middle turbinate was seen, completely occluding the nasal cavity. Physical examination was otherwise normal. Magnetic resonance imaging showed a heterogeneous, expansile mass measuring 6 (anteroposterior) × 3.1 (transverse) × 5 (craniocaudal) cm within the right nasal cavity extending to the nasopharynx, with obliteration of the nasopharyngeal airway and anteroinferior displacement of the soft palate (Figure, B). The adjacent sinuses had drainage obstruction. Biopsy results showed fragments of necrotic and fibrinous debris with acute inflammatory exudate and bacterial colonies. Findings during surgery included a fibrous expansile mass filling the right nasal cavity and bowing the septum to the left. It crossed the midline to fill the nasopharynx and extended inferiorly toward the oropharynx. The mass was noted to originate at the posterior wall of the maxillary sinus. Pathologic evaluation showed fragments of polypoidal mucosa with edematous stroma, numerous ectatic vascular channels, and a sprinkling of inflammatory cells (Figure, A). The surface epithelium was largely ulcerated, covered with fibrinous and inflammatory debris and bacterial colonies. Immunostaining showed CD31 and CD34 positivity. Stromal cells did not have β-catenin present. Elastic stain results showed scant elastic fibers in the vascular proliferation.
explanation: Of the 5 histological subtypes of sinonasal polyps (edematous, glandular, fibrous, cystic, and angiomatous or angiectatic), angiomatous nasal polyps (ANPs) make up about 4% to 5% of these sinonasal lesions.1Sinonasal polyps may present with nasal obstruction, facial pain or pressure, snoring, anosmia, epistaxis, and nasal drainage.2Some reports of ANPs describe a foul odor associated with the lesions, raising concern for bacterial, fungal, or malignant processes.3These presenting symptoms, however, are nonspecific, and additional workup must be completed to assess for other causes, such as inverted papilloma (IP), sinonasal tract angiofibroma (STA), and lobular capillary hemangioma (LCH). On computed tomography, ANPs typically present as a heterogenous density with minimal enhancement at the lesion’s edges and accompanying bony changes.4When visualized on magnetic resonance imaging, ANPs display heterogeneous isointense signal intensity on T1-weighted images and a hypointense peripheral rim on T2-weighted images.5IPs may have similar imaging appearance and display hypointense T1 signal with isointense or hypointense signal on T2-weighted image; contrast enhancement is in a convoluted cerebriform pattern.6Imaging of LCHs often show bone destruction and evidence of phleboliths.7STAs typically demonstrate heterogenous signal intensity on T1-weighted images and may be either high intensity or isointensity predominant on T2-weighted images.8Internal flow voids and intense enhancement are also seen in the majority of STAs, as well as LCHs.7In STAs, involvement of the sphenopalatine foramen/pterygopalatine fossa is often present,8which is not seen in ANPs. Location of origin is another factor that may differentiate these tumors. ANPs typically originate from the maxillary sinus and may spread to the choana.4LCHs most commonly originate from the anterior nasal septum, while STAs originate from the sphenopalatine foramen region along the posterior nasal cavity.7Alternatively, IPs usually arise from the lateral nasal wall or the paranasal sinuses. Imaging findings for this patient reflect ANP, with a large heterogeneous expansile mass extending from the right nasal cavity to the nasopharynx and into the posterior aspect of the maxillary sinus, with mass effect and mild resorption of the surrounding bones. When examined via light microscopy, ANPs often have an ulcerated roof and areas lined by respiratory epithelium, which may show squamous metaplasia.2ANPs also show scattered atypical pleomorphic spindle cells in the stroma, a paucity of inflammatory infiltrate, and abundant amorphous, Congo red–negative material.1ANPs are characterized by a high degree of vascular proliferation and ectasia; as such, these blood vessels may be subject to compression leading to infarction.3Given the highly vascularized and potentially necrotic nature of ANPs, it is understandable that these polyps may present with diagnostic difficulty due to potential confusion with other vascular tumors. Fully developed LCHs typically display lobules of back-to-back capillaries, with endothelial cells divided by fibrous or myxoid septa.9STAs, on the other hand, demonstrate a dense stromal component with numerous fibroblasts and have varying levels of vessel density. Immunohistochemical stains are also helpful in differentiating STAs from other tumors and will be positive for β-catenin, androgen receptor, estrogen receptor β, and prostate-specific antigen.7IPs are characterized histologically by an inverted appearance due to thickened epithelium enclosed by basement membrane, along with transmigrating intraepithelial neutrophilic inflammation.6The pathology and immunohistochemistry findings, as outlined in this case, align with ANP. The standard treatment for ANPs is resection via endoscopic approach. This treatment allows for symptom relief and a definitive pathologic characterization. Removal of the site of origin of these polyps is crucial for preventing recurrence. The present patient underwent successful endoscopic resection and followed up regularly outpatient after surgery. The patient’s presenting symptoms have resolved, and there was no evidence of recurrence at 6 months.

caption: A, Diffuse, ulcerative thickening of the nasal sills bilaterally, with the right side being more severe than the left. B, Noncontrast sinus computed tomography showed nasal septal perforation with heterogeneous opacification in the nasal vestibules, along with patchy opacification of the inferior and middle meatus.
scenario: A 40-year-old male patient presented to a primary care clinic with a 2-month history of a pruritic, nontender irritation at the nasal sills bilaterally after minor trauma that involved scratching his nose after getting fiberglass particles in his nostrils while installing lights in his attic. He was a tobacco smoker but was otherwise healthy, with no known allergies. The primary care physician and consulting dermatologist initially diagnosed cellulitis and allergic rhinitis, and the patient was administered a 5-day course of an antibiotic ointment and, as needed, oral antihistamines. Two months later, the patient was referred to the otolaryngology department, as the nasal irritation progressed into a diffuse, destructive process. On physical examination, there was diffuse, ulcerative thickening of the nasal sills bilaterally, with the right side being more severe than the left (Figure 1A). Noncontrast sinus computed tomography showed nasal septal perforation with heterogeneous opacification in the nasal vestibules, along with patchy opacification of the inferior and middle meatus (Figure 1B). Cultures were negative for 1,3 β-d-glucan, aspergillus, cryptococcus, and syphilis. The patient’s erythrocyte sedimentation rate was within normal limits, and autoimmune serology results (antinuclear antibody, myeloperoxidase, proteinase 3, and angiotensin-converting enzyme) were negative. Urine toxicology screening yielded negative results.
explanation: A. Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA) is a chronic necrotizing granulomatous vasculitis that is characterized by eosinophilic infiltration of small and medium blood vessels. EGPA is classically associated with asthma, chronic rhinosinusitis with or without polyposis, peripheral eosinophilia, and positive antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA).1Although the association of EGPA with ANCA is well recognized, clinically only approximately one-third of patients with EGPA have positive test results.2Skin manifestations occur in two-thirds of patients with EGPA with a range of findings, such as palpable purpura, hemorrhagic bullae, urticaria, and dermal or subcutaneous papules and nodules.3 This patient exhibited an atypical presentation of EGPA. He presented with nasal sill irritation and subsequent crusting following minor trauma but was otherwise asymptomatic. An infectious process was initially suspected; however, the lack of response to multiple courses of antibiotics and progressively worsening nasal mucosal, septal, and skin findings suggested the presence of a more concerning underlying condition. The patient’s lack of history of lung involvement, asthma, and rhinosinusitis, coupled with his normal erythrocyte sedimentation rate and negative autoimmune serologies (antinuclear antibody, myeloperoxidase, proteinase 3, and angiotensin-converting enzyme) erroneously eliminated EGPA and other autoimmune pathologies from the running differential diagnosis. With sinus computed tomography showing evidence of nasal septal perforation and opacification in the nasal vestibule and inferior and middle meatus, concern shifted toward the possibility of an extranodal nasal natural killer/T-cell lymphoma (ENKTL). This rare type of non-Hodgkin lymphoma is associated with Epstein-Barr virus infection and characterized by ulceration or necrosis of the nasal cavity and aggressive destruction of nasal structures, such as the palate, nasal fossa, and septum.4,5ENKTL has a poor prognosis and requires immediate treatment with radiotherapy and chemotherapy.6 Further investigation was conducted by an ear, nose, and throat specialist. An endoscopic biopsy and debridement of the right nasal sill, nasal septum, left nasopharynx, left nasal floor, and skin was performed and additional laboratory tests and antibodies were ordered. On nasal endoscopy, subtotal septal perforation with necrosis along the bilateral inferior turbinates and exposed bone along the septum was appreciated (Figure 2A). On pathology, the biopsy specimens showed foci suspicious for vasculitis (Figure 2B) and ulceration with eosinophilic inflammation (Figure 2C). Stains were negative for Epstein-Barr virus. The laboratory results showed elevated eosinophil counts (2300 cells/μL [to convert to ×109/L, multiply by 0.001]; 17%), and an indirect immunofluorescent antibody test was positive for perinuclear ANCA (1:320 titer). With these new findings, there was enough pathological and clinical evidence to rule out ENKTL and, according to the American College of Rheumatology and European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology 2022 Classification Criteria, to diagnose EGPA.7 In this case study, we report a rare presentation of EGPA. As evident in this patient, the absence of lung involvement, asthma, rhinosinusitis, and an initial unremarkable autoimmune serology were not enough to rule out EGPA. Dermatological manifestations of EGPA are also variable, with this case to our knowledge being the first description of a nasal sill irritation that progressed into an ulceration and eventually led to destructive perforation of the nasal septum. For future clinicians faced with a persistent rash or ulceration that is unresponsive to multiple courses of antibiotics, it may be beneficial to order a routine complete blood cell count with differential, undergo a subsequent biopsy if eosinophil counts are elevated, and not completely rule out autoimmune pathologies if initial inflammatory markers and autoimmune antibodies are negative.

caption: Computed tomography (CT) imaging showing heterotopic ossification within the external auditory canals (yellow arrowheads) and opacification (asterisks) extending to the mineralized tympanic membranes (blue arrowheads).
scenario: An 11-year-old boy with a history of cleft palate repair, placement of multiple sets of pressure-equalizing tubes, and suspected ectodermal dysplasia (not confirmed with genetic testing) was referred from a general ear, nose, and throat physician. The patient had presented with a chief concern of a 1-year history of hearing loss. He had no otorrhea or otalgia during this time. Otoscopic examination of the ear showed bilateral dead-end ear canals with smooth hypervascular fibrosis extending medially from the bony cartilaginous junction. There were no granulation tissue, pit, or tract. Computed tomography (CT) imaging showed bilateral severe external auditory canal (EAC) stenosis due to heterotopic ossification in the medial aspects of each EAC and nonossified opacification extending to the tympanic membrane (Figure). The middle and inner ears were otherwise normal. Noncontrast magnetic resonance imaging showed bilateral EAC stenosis with soft tissue, and on diffusion-weighted imaging the material within the EAC did not show decreased diffusivity. Behavioral pure-tone audiometry revealed bilateral moderately severe mixed hearing loss. Speech perception was greater than 95% bilaterally, and tympanometry was flat bilaterally. The patient’s mother indicated that she has had a similar set of symptoms for much of her life. She reported maximum conductive hearing loss for which she had not had hearing rehabilitation nor further workup. Otoscopic examination of the mother’s ears showed identical findings to the patient.
explanation: The ectodermal dysplasia syndromes are a group of rare genetic diseases that occur when there is a congenital defect in at least 2 ectodermal derivatives, one of which involves the hair, teeth, nails, or sweat glands. The inheritance pattern is variable (typically X-linked recessive or autosomal dominant) depending on the specific syndrome, and the estimated incidence is 0.7 to 1 per 100 000 live births.1,2Patients with ectodermal dysplasia typically have ear-, nose-, and throat-related disease manifestations, such as nasal obstruction/dryness, otitis media, and hearing loss.2 Conductive hearing loss is relatively common and can result from obstruction of the EACs; however, all listed possible diagnoses represent rare etiologies of conductive hearing loss.3,4The physical examination finding of dead-end ear canals could be caused by any of the diagnoses, although aural atresia is a congenital condition that would have been present throughout the life of the patient and prevented prior ear tube placement; furthermore, aural atresia is often accompanied by microtia of the pinna. The presence of bilateral disease makes ear canal cholesteatoma less likely, as does the young age of the patient.4Diagnostic features in this case also include CT findings showing ear canals filled with debris of mineralized/ossified material, but without EAC enlargement/erosion, as expected in keratosis obturans. Ear canal cholesteatoma typically occurs in older children or adults and results in asymmetric bone erosion with drainage. Noncontrast magnetic resonance imaging with diffusion-weighted imaging can also be used to help exclude alternative diagnoses, including cholesteatoma, which classically demonstrates decreased diffusivity. Diagnosis was made for this patient from his examination and imaging findings in the setting of ectodermal dysplasia. The presence of the same finding in the patient’s mother supports a hereditary origin rather than a spontaneous genetic mutation or other sporadic cause. Ectoderm plays a critical role in normal ear development, including external, middle, and inner ear structures, and otologic manifestations of ectodermal dysplasia, reported in small case series, include varied manifestations of disease, such as chronic otitis media, sensorineural hearing loss, cerumen impaction, and pinna abnormalities.1,5-7There have been few reported cases of external ear canal stenosis due to ectodermal dysplasia, and there are no descriptions of physical examination findings.1,7,8One patient with EAC stenosis due recurrent otitis externa underwent CT, which showed bilateral soft tissue opacification filling the EACs.8 Management of ectodermal dysplasia requires a multidisciplinary team, and treatment is typically aimed toward symptom management. It is recommended that patients with ectodermal dysplasia of any age undergo hearing tests if hearing loss is suspected. Treatment of common otologic manifestations includes placement of ear tubes for recurrent acute or chronic serous otitis media, use of hearing aids for sensorineural hearing loss, and lubricant ear drops to help soften ear wax. In this case, canaloplasty and bone-conduction hearing aid devices were discussed with the patient and his family. Due to concerns that the ear canal fibrosis would recur given his underlying condition, it was recommended that the patient pursue a bone-anchored hearing aid. The patient started with a trial of a soft-band bone conduction device and ultimately underwent surgery for placement of a transcutaneous active bone conduction implant. Due to his ectodermal dysplasia, placement of a percutaneous device was not recommended. The patient’s mother expressed interest in understanding her options for treatment as well. To our knowledge, this case demonstrates the first reported description of otoscopic findings in a family with ear canal stenosis due to ectodermal dysplasia and describes characteristic CT findings. Ectodermal dysplasia can cause EAC stenosis that manifests in childhood, and all patients with ectodermal dysplasia should undergo otologic and audiologic assessment.

caption: Computed tomography (CT) images of 2 brothers with bilateral lesions in the olfactory clefts. A, Cone-beam CT in the 69-year-old brother demonstrated significant widening of the olfactory clefts and right-sided bony thinning. B, Reformatted conventional CT scan in the 76-year-old brother showed similar findings.
scenario: Two brothers, aged 69 and 76 years, were independently referred to our center in the same week for evaluation of a right olfactory cleft tumor that had been progressively developing over several years. The brothers had not been in contact with each other for many years. Neither had a history of chronic rhinosinusitis. The 69-year-old patient had a medical history of benign prostatic hypertrophy and prior septoplasty. The 76-year-old brother had no relevant medical or surgical history. Both brothers reported an ipsilateral nasal obstruction, with no other significant symptoms. Clinical examination on both patients revealed a lesion originating from the right olfactory cleft. Imaging studies were performed to further characterize the findings. A computed tomography scan demonstrated bilateral masses causing widening of the olfactory clefts, with the right-sided lesion being larger than the left and causing nasal bone thinning in both patients (Figure 1). Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a smooth, larger, right-sided lesion in the olfactory clefts with heterogeneous T2 signal and heterogenous contrast enhancement, along with a smaller lesion on the left side.
explanation: After initial evaluation and imaging, both patients underwent surgical resection of the tumor in the right olfactory cleft to improve their nasal breathing and for pathological examination. A biopsy of the lesion located in the left olfactory cleft for both patients was also performed. Pathological examination revealed a similar finding in both brothers: a polypoid formation with dystrophic respiratory glands, sometimes with intestinal metaplasia and sometimes with ciliated lining, anarchically distributed within the chorion, without adenomatous or atypical character. This histopathological presentation strongly supports the diagnosis of respiratory epithelial adenomatoid hamartoma (REAH), despite the absence of genetic analysis.1,2 Olfactory cleft hamartomas are benign tumors that may be isolated or associated with chronic rhinosinusitis. They typically appear as a smooth polypoid mass in the anterior part of the nasal cavity. These lesions predominantly affect men, with a male to female ratio of 7:2.2The olfactory cleft is the most common site for hamartoma, followed by the posterior region of the septum. Both nasal cavities are involved in most cases (53%).3On imaging, hamartomas are usually seen as exophytic polypoid homogeneous lesions with smooth expansion of the olfactory cleft without bony erosion and exhibiting a characteristic crescentic half-moon appearance on the sagittal views when the lesion is situated along the olfactory cleft.4 The 5th World Health Organization Classification identifies 3 types of hamartomas: REAH, seromucinous hamartoma, and nasal chondromesenchymal hamartoma (CMH). Pathological examination and molecular analysis are essential for differentiation, as REAH and seromucinous hamartoma cannot be distinguished based on imaging alone. CMHs are usually found in infants and contain mixed mesenchymal elements, including cartilage. CMH can be associated with aDICER1(tumor-suppressor gene) variant.4,5 There is currently no cause identified for isolated REAH, but research is limited. Some evidence suggests that hamartomas may arise secondary to inflammatory processes, such as chronic rhinosinusitis.3A congenital cause is also suspected, but no genetic basis has been identified yet. It is quite rare to see similar isolated REAH in 2 brothers without any associated inflammatory conditions. This clinical case raises the possibility of an unknown underlying genetic mechanism. Treatment is symptom dependent. Surgical removal is often performed in cases of nasal obstruction or to restore olfactory function, with a high success rate and a low risk of recurrence.1,3While surgery is not always necessary, a biopsy is recommended when imaging findings are inconclusive to rule out other potential diagnoses. Differentials diagnosis include Schneiderian papilloma, sinonasal adenocarcinoma, or olfactory neuroblastoma. Imaging often helps to differentiate REAH from other diagnoses. In chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps, nasal polyps typically originate from the ethmoid sinuses, whereas the imaging here clearly shows a lesion widening the olfactory cleft (Figure 2). Schneiderian papillomas are rarely bilateral and typically exhibit a more irregular or lobulated appearance on T2-weighted imaging, often accompanied by bone remodeling at the attachment point or bone erosion—features that are absent in this case. Malignant tumors, such as ethmoid sinus adenocarcinoma, typically demonstrate aggressive characteristics, including bone destruction, heterogeneous enhancement, and invasion of adjacent structures, none of which were observed here. Finally, encephaloceles are characterized by herniation of intracranial contents into the nasal cavity and are commonly associated with skull base defects, which are not identified in these images.

caption: A, Transaxial positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT) image showing intense bilateral symmetric tonsillar hypermetabolism and bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy hypermetabolism. B, Low-powered (original magnification ×40) and high-powered (inset; original magnification ×400) hematoxylin-eosin stain after tonsillectomy showing lymphoid follicular hyperplasia with a polymorphic inflammatory infiltrate.
scenario: A previously healthy 67-year-old man was referred to the otolaryngology department due to a progressively worsening sore throat over several weeks that was associated with an unintentional 5-kg weight loss and night sweats. The patient did not report recent travel, nor autoimmune conditions, and reported only heterosexual intercourse. A physical examination revealed a mobile, nontender left-sided jugular lymph node. Dentition and oropharyngeal examinations were unremarkable. Results of flexible laryngoscopy were normal. Routine blood work findings showed an elevated C-reactive protein level and a polyclonal elevation of gamma globulins. Complete blood cell count, kidney markers, and liver enzymes were normal. Computed tomographic (CT) angiography of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis was unremarkable. Due to substantial worsening of the patient’s symptoms during the next weeks, positron emission tomography/CT was performed, with results showing intense bilateral tonsillar hypermetabolism and abnormal lymph node hypermetabolism above and below the diaphragm (Figure 1A). The patient underwent unilateral tonsillectomy followed by a course of antibiotics and prednisone. On pathologic examination, the tonsils showed lymphoid follicular hyperplasia associated with a polymorphic inflammatory infiltrate without abnormal lymphoid cells and plasmocytes (Figure 1B). Further exploration of the patient’s history revealed that 1 year before the otolaryngology evaluation, he developed a cutaneous eruption on the trunk.

options.B: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma of the tonsil

distractors: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma of the tonsil
explanation: Almost 1 year after initial presentation, a pathology review of the tonsils found strong positive immunostaining of antitreponemal antibody (Figure 2) associated with a rapid plasma reagin (RPR) blood titer of 1:4. Treponemal antibody test (chemiluminescent immunoassay) confirmed the syphilis diagnosis. The patient received intramuscular injections of 2.4 million units of benzathine penicillin G once a week for 3 weeks, with rapid and complete regression of his symptoms. Syphilis is a sexually transmitted infection with increased incidence in high-income countries over the past several decades,1with the majority of cases found in men who have sex with men. Acquired syphilis is divided into early syphilis (primary, secondary, and early latent syphilis [ie, acquired within 1 year]) and late syphilis (late latent and tertiary syphilis [ie, acquired after 1 or more years or unknown duration]). Primary syphilis typically begins with a painless ulcer at the site of infection, which can be overlooked when located in the oropharynx, vagina, or rectum. Consequently, many individuals consult clinicians during the secondary stage, which can have various presentations, the most common being a generalized, nonitchy, erythematous maculopapular rash affecting the palms of the hands and soles of the feet. Herein, retrospective analysis of the cutaneous eruption 1 year before otolaryngologist referral could suggest secondary syphilis, although RPR and treponemal antibody tests were not performed at that time. Secondary syphilis comprises other symptoms, such as lymphadenopathy, fever, and asthenia. After untreated infection, tertiary syphilis can develop, leading to severe neurological and cardiac complications. Syphilis of the tonsils rarely presents as a symptom of secondary syphilis. At this stage, the condition presents as bilateral tonsillitis rather than unilateral tonsillitis, as in primary syphilis.2Although tonsils usually exhibit redness, swelling, and a gray exudate, often with a diffuse pharyngitis, initial clinical examination can be normal, and tonsillitis is only revealed by positron emission tomography/CT.3,4It is predominantly associated with cervical or generalized lymphadenopathy. Diagnosis is often delayed and performed using a histopathological analysis (tonsil or lymph node) and fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption. Confirmation with treponemal antibody test is required because of high false positivity rate of RPR, up to 15%, and treponemal immunohistochemical stain is not specific ofTreponema pallidumand can cross-react with commensal spirochetes of the gastrointestinal tract. Because syphilis cases are increased among men who have sex with men, thorough sexual history might also orientate laboratory workup.5 Regarding differential diagnoses, Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease is a benign evolving necrotizing histiocytic lymphadenitis mainly described in Asia. It occurs in young women in the context of an infectious or autoimmune condition. It typically presents with painful persistent cervical lymphadenopathy associated with fever and leukopenia.6Excisional biopsy of a lymph node is essential for the diagnosis, showing paracortical areas of fibrinoid necrosis, abundant karyorrhexis, and mononuclear cell infiltration.7 Tonsils are a frequent site of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma of the Waldeyer ring.8It is a rare subtype of extranodal non-Hodgkin lymphoma occurring predominantly in older men and presenting as odynophagia with cervical lymphadenopathy. Histopathological analysis shows proliferation of large-sized tumor cells with pleomorphic nuclei and immunohistochemistry stains positive for B-cell antigens with a high Ki67 proliferation index.9 Primary tonsillar tuberculosis represents a rare presentation of extrapulmonary tuberculosis. Patients present with recurrent or chronic tonsillitis associated with cervical lymphadenopathy and coexisting pulmonary disease. Diagnosis is based on histopathological examination of the tonsil showing epithelioid granulomas and areas of caseous necrosis. Coloration of Ziehl-Neelsen is frequently positive in this location, showing acid-fast bacilli.10 Syphilis has diverse presentations and is referred to as the “great masquerader.” Given this and the increasing incidence of syphilis, a nontreponemal blood test could be included in the diagnosis approach when facing persistent sore throat and lymphadenopathy.

caption: This computed tomography image of the paranasal sinuses in the coronal plane was taken to determine disease severity and treatment course.
scenario: A 41-year-old male patient presented with symptoms of chronic rhinosinusitis lasting several years. Endoscopic evaluation of the nasal cavity revealed edematous mucosa without discrete mass. A computed tomography (CT) scan of the paranasal sinuses was performed to evaluate the extent of disease and for surgical planning (Figure 1). Based on the CT results, the patient opted not to pursue surgery.
explanation: Nasal turbinates are critical for air filtration, humidification, and airflow regulation. Although the typical nasal anatomy includes the superior, middle, and inferior turbinates, variations can occur, resulting in additional structures such as secondary or accessory turbinates. These variations are often incidental findings in radiologic imaging, but they may carry clinical implications, particularly in surgical planning. The secondary middle turbinate (SMT) is a distinct anatomic structure arising from the lateral wall of the ethmoid bulla just beneath the basal lamella (Figure 2).1,2SMT arises posterosuperior to the infundibulum and is most often described as projecting medially and then turning superiorly within the meatus; however, cases do exist demonstrating inferomedial projection.1,3SMT is differentiated from accessory middle turbinate (AMT), described as a medially bent uncinate process. If the uncinate process is bent medially and folded anteriorly, it may give the impression that 2 middle turbinates are present.1 The incidence of SMT has been reported between 0.8% and 6.8%.1,2,4,5How anatomic variants, such as SMT and AMT, contribute to nasal symptoms is not fully understood. When evaluated, no obstruction of the osteomeatal complex from SMT or AMT was detected.4,5There is no consensus guideline for the management of SMT. However, a 2011 study demonstrated that endoscopic surgery eliminating the lateral nasal wall contact points in patients with SMT or AMT on CT imaging resulted in significant symptom improvement of both headaches and the sensation of nasal obstruction based on patient-reported symptom scores compared to patients that did not undergo endoscopic removal.5 An understanding of the embryology of nasal turbinates helps differentiate SMT and AMT. The ethmoidal turbinates originate from ridges (termedethmoturbinals) in the lateral nasal wall of the fetus. Six ridges separated by furrows initially form; however, not all develop into permanent turbinates.6,7The first ethmoturbinal does not develop into a permanent turbinate; however, it does form the uncinate process. The segment between the first and second ethmoturbinal becomes the ethmoidal infundibulum. The second ethmoturbinal develops into the permanent middle turbinate.1,7Variations in the second ethmoturbinal may cause anomalies associated with the middle turbinate, such as SMT, whereas variations in the first ethmoturbinal may lead to anomalies of the uncinate process, such as AMT.6 AMT may resemble SMT. Normally, the uncinate process is a thin sickle-shaped structure with the distance between its free posterior edge and the lamina papyracea between 1.5 mm and 5 mm.1,7If the uncinate process is bent medially to greater than 5 mm and folded anteriorly, it may give the impression that 2 middle turbinates are present. SMT can be distinguished from AMT’s medially deviated uncinate process because SMT is located posterosuperior to the infundibulum.1Case reports do exist of SMT coexisting with AMT.6Additionally, SMT may be mistaken for a polyp or osteoma on endoscopic examination.1,2,8On CT imaging, osteomas appear as round, highly radiodense lesions.9Lastly, concha bullosa refers to the pneumatization of the middle turbinate, which appears as an air-filled space.10 In conclusion, SMT is a distinct anatomic variant arising from the lateral wall of the ethmoid bulla just beneath the basal lamella. It can be differentiated from a medially bent uncinate process (ie, AMT) by its origin and location posterosuperior to the infundibulum. Failure to recognize these anatomic variants could lead to inadvertent damage to the orbital lamina papyracea during surgery, endangering the globe. The recognition of this variation is also important as it may predispose to inflammatory sinus disease; however, the mechanism is poorly understood due to a lack of osteomeatal narrowing.5,8

caption: Axial (A) and coronal (B) T2-weighted constructive interference in steady state magnetic resonance imaging demonstrating hyperintensity in the bilateral labyrinthine Fallopian canal and mild hyperintensity in right mastoid air cells.
scenario: A 39-year-old female with a history of idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH) medically managed with topiramate and furosemide, eustachian tube dysfunction with tympanostomy tube placement in adulthood, allergic rhinitis, and obstructive sleep apnea presented for evaluation of right aural fullness, pulsatile tinnitus, and conductive hearing loss. On physical examination, a retracted bilateral tympanic membrane with right serous middle ear effusion was noted. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the internal auditory canal was obtained, with hyperintensity on T2-weighted images indicating bilateral perigeniculate expansile lesions contiguous with the Fallopian canal (Figure 1). Computed tomography (CT) of the temporal bone showed smooth expansion of the lesions with no destructive bony changes. The patient had no other signs of active cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) leak (clear rhinorrhea). Tympanostomy tubes were placed, with resolution of middle ear effusion and improvement in conductive hearing loss and no operative findings of active CSF leak. The patient inquired further regarding the diagnosis and management of the perigeniculate lesions.
explanation: Meningoceles are herniations of the meninges through a defect in the skull or spinal column. Skull base meningoceles are commonly associated with increased intracranial pressure (ICP) leading to meningeal herniation through congenital or acquired skull base defects.1Conditions that elevate ICP, such as intracranial trauma, tumors, or IIH, are known risk factors for developing meningoceles.2,3Meningoceles is estimated to occur in 11% of patients with IIH and is caused by chronically elevated ICP resulting in bony erosion and remodeling with subsequent herniation of the meninges through the weakened defects.3Additionally, meninges may herniate through the Fallopian canal into the perigeniculate area.1 The clinical presentation of geniculate meningoceles may vary depending on size and the route of expansion. Involvement of the ossicles or middle ear space may cause hearing loss, tinnitus, and aural fullness, while mass effect directly on the facial nerve can lead to facial palsy. Cerebrospinal fluid leaks may also manifest as clear rhinorrhea or otorrhea with a salty or metallic taste, often accompanied by headaches that can be worsened in an upright position and improve when lying flat.3,4 Computed tomography and MRI are useful tools in distinguishing meningoceles from other potential pathologies. High-resolution CT of the temporal bone reveals bony defects with well-demarcated edges and, in the setting of a CSF leak, opacification of the middle ear or mastoid air cells, but ultimately cannot distinguish between fluid and soft tissue pathologies (Figure 2). Thus, MRI particularly with T2-weighted sequences is valuable for identifying fluid accumulation suggestive of a CSF-filled meningocele. This is in contrast to gadolinium contrast-enhancing lesions, such as a schwannoma or hemangioma.1,5,6Arachnoid granulations, although similar in appearance as lesions with hyperintensity on T2-weighted sequences, can be distinguished from geniculate meningoceles by their location, as they typically arise adjacent to cerebral sinuses and often extend into adjacent venous structures on MRI.7Lastly, the presence of bilateral disease also makes geniculate encephalocele a more likely diagnosis compared with other pathologies, as there is a global intracranial pathology impacting the bilateral internal auditory canal and Fallopian canal. Management of geniculate meningoceles depends on symptom severity. Asymptomatic or mildly symptomatic cases without CSF leaks can be managed with observation and medical treatment of the underlying conditions—most commonly IIH. More symptomatic patients or those with CSF leaks may require surgical intervention with a transmastoid or middle fossa approach to repair bony defects, restore skull base integrity, and prevent recurrent CSF leaks or meningitis. In patients with IIH, a shunt may also be required to normalize ICP and prevent further development of skull base defects.4 While the presence of middle ear effusion with imaging findings demonstrating meningoceles raises suspicions for CSF otorrhea, the fluid characteristics on MRI (Figure 1) was notably different between the geniculate meningocele and the middle ear effusion, making CSF otorrhea unlikely. The patient underwent bilateral tympanostomy tube placement, with resolution of middle ear effusion and conductive hearing loss. The geniculate meningoceles were successfully managed conservatively with medical management given the incidental nature of this finding. Geniculate meningoceles are rare pathologies associated with increased ICP. While ruling out an associated CSF leak is a critical step in management of patients with geniculate meningoceles, it is prudent for clinicians to consider imaging characteristics that reduce the likelihood of CSF leak and differentiate it from similar-appearing lesions or other pathologies that may occur in the region. Ultimately, many incidentally discovered or asymptomatic geniculate meningoceles may be managed medically with control of ICP.

caption: A, Large, rounded submucosal lesion of the anterior maxilla facial and apical to tooth number 9. B, Low-power histomicrograph shows a nodule of fibrous connective tissue surfaced by keratinized stratified squamous epithelium (original magnification ×5). The bulk of the specimen consists of densely to loosely arranged collagen bundles with scattered fibroblasts. Centrally, there is a focal proliferation of odontogenic epithelium (pink arrowhead). The inset shows a higher-power image with a proliferation of odontogenic epithelium composed of hyperchromatic ovoid cells that are arranged into pseudoductal structures (blue arrowheads; original magnification ×20). Small basophilic calcifications also are identified within the epithelial proliferation (black arrowhead).
scenario: A 12-year-old boy with no relevant medical history presented with a left maxillary gingival swelling of 4 years’ duration associated with palatal tipping of the left maxillary central incisor. The lesion reportedly grew over a 2-year period but remained unchanged over the past 2 years. The patient denied pain, bleeding, or neurosensory disturbances associated with the lesion or dentition. Intraoral examination was notable for a firm, 1 × 1-cm, pink, dome-shaped gingival mass extending onto the facial surface of tooth number 9, coalescing with a broader, pale-appearing, soft to firm gingival enlargement apical to the tooth (Figure, A). No edema, erythema, or signs of infection were appreciated, and the adjacent teeth demonstrated no mobility with normal periodontal probing depths and vitality. Extraoral examination was unremarkable. Radiographic examination showed no endodontic involvement or intralesional calcifications; however, cone-beam computed tomography imaging revealed saucerization of the facial bone near tooth number 9. Excisional biopsy of the lesion was performed, and microscopic examination of multiple sections revealed a nodule of keratinized superficial stratified squamous epithelium overlying fibrous connective tissue (Figure, B). The surface epithelium demonstrated a normal maturational pattern. The underlying fibrous connective tissue was composed of densely to loosely arranged collagen bundles interspersed with fibroblasts, blood vessels, and scattered chronic inflammatory cells. Notably, within the central portions of the fibrous nodule on deeper levels, there was a proliferation of odontogenic epithelium composed of mildly hyperchromatic ovoid cells arranged into pseudoducts (Figure, B). Small basophilic spherical calcifications were intermixed with the odontogenic epithelium.
explanation: C. Peripheral adenomatoid odontogenic tumor Adenomatoid odontogenic tumor (AOT) is a noninvasive odontogenic tumor with approximately two-thirds associated with impacted canine teeth in the anterior maxilla and a female:male predilection of 1.9:1; as such, it is often referred to as thetwo-thirds tumor. Typically occurring in the second decade of life, an AOT originates from remnants of the dental lamina or enamel organ and is associated with mutations in theKRASgene (mitogen-activated protein kinase pathway; p.G12V and p.G12R loci) in 70% of AOTs according to recent genetic data published in the fifth edition of the World Health Organization’s classification of odontogenic and maxillofacial bone tumors.1,2While 97.7% of all AOTs fall into either the follicular (71%) or extrafollicular (29%) subtypes of the central variant, a peripheral AOT (PAOT) is rare but possible, with 2.3% of all AOTs solely involving the gingival tissue overlying the alveolar ridge.3The PAOT also demonstrates a much higher female predilection, with a reported female:male ratio of 6.3:1.4The pathogenesis of a PAOT involves proliferation of epithelial remnants within the gingival tissue following tooth eruption in response to an unknown stimulus. Radiographically, follicular and extrafollicular AOTs appear as well-defined, circumscribed, and unilocular radiolucencies associated with unerupted teeth with varying degrees of calcification. As a PAOT occurs in soft tissue, there are no pathognomonic radiographic findings; however, erosion of the labial plate and displacement of teeth, as seen in this case, as well as deep periodontal pockets are not uncommon.5Histologically, both central AOTs and PAOTs demonstrate ductlike structures arising from the cuboidal epithelial cell component of the lesion, with spindle-shaped epithelial cells interspersed with cementumlike calcifications or amyloidlike homogeneous eosinophilic material. Typically, AOTs are well encapsulated with connective tissue and, as such, are easily separated from adjacent anatomic structures; however, this encapsulation is usually not present in PAOTs.6-8Due to their similar pathogenesis and cellular origin, many reactive proliferation lesions, including peripheral ossifying fibroma, peripheral giant cell granuloma, and pyogenic granuloma, as well as many peripheral odontogenic cysts or tumors, including peripheral ameloblastoma, odontogenic fibroma, gingival cyst, peripheral ameloblastic fibroma, peripheral odontoma, peripheral odontogenic keratocyst, and peripheral calcifying odontogenic cyst, can demonstrate similar gingival enlargement as seen with PAOTs.6-8As a result of multiple lesions appearing similar clinically, definitive diagnosis is made only after histopathological examination. Treatment for a PAOT typically involves conservative surgical removal via enucleation and curettage of the lesion down to bone, resulting in very rare instances of recurrence of the tumor, with excellent prognosis.6,9The present patient was followed up at 1 month at the Department of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery at the University of Illinois Chicago College of Dentistry, and subsequently at 6 months at the patient’s initial referring dentist, with no evidence of lesion recurrence. While no appreciable spontaneous buccal movement of the malpositioned left maxillary lateral incisor was observed at 1-month follow-up, the patient was cleared to initiate orthodontic intervention. This case highlights the unique nature of odontogenic lesions to occur throughout the oral cavity and consideration of a broad differential diagnosis, because even benign-appearing lesions could potentially represent devastating diseases. Additionally, early diagnosis and intervention helped in limiting underlying bone loss and further displacement of tooth number 9, demonstrating that early detection and biopsy play important roles in therapeutic success.

caption: A, An axial view shows a mass lesion completely occupying left nasal cavity. B, Incisional biopsy demonstrated a malignant squamous epithelial proliferation with bulky papillary and endophytic architecture (hematoxylin and eosin, original magnification, ×4). C, Image demonstrates cytologic atypia and several mitotic figures (hematoxylin and eosin, original magnification, ×20).
scenario: A 59-year-old male patient presented with many months of progressively worsening left nasal obstruction. He also endorsed associated occasional left occipital pain, as well as substantial unintentional weight loss. He denied any epistaxis and had no significant history of alcohol or tobacco use. Physical examination revealed a papillomatous-appearing mass completely occupying the left nasal cavity. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the maxillofacial region demonstrated a large, heterogeneously enhancing lesion occupying the left nasal cavity, left orbit, and bilateral pterygopalatine fossae (Figure 1A). The mass crossed the midline into the right nasal cavity and nasopharynx, with thin and subtle left frontal dural enhancement, suggesting early intracranial extension. A biopsy of the left nasal cavity lesion was performed in the clinic. Gross examination of the incisional specimen revealed irregular, polypoid fragments of soft tissue, measuring up to 1.5 cm in greatest dimension. Histologic examination demonstrated an epithelial proliferation with squamous differentiation and papillary and blunt bulbous architecture (Figure 1B). Cytologic atypia and increased mitotic figures were observed (Figure 1C). Conventional invasion was not identified in the biopsy material, nor was lymphovascular or perineural invasion. Ancillary testing was performed, and the tumor cell results were negative for p16, CD99, and high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV) RNA in situ hybridization. They demonstrated focal positivity for low-risk HPV RNA in situ hybridization.
explanation: A. Papillary squamous cell carcinoma Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) is the most common  cancer of the sinonasal tract (SNT), representing 65% to 70% of carcinomas diagnosed at this site.1SCC is a malignant squamous epithelial neoplasm defined by atypical cytologic and architectural features. There is a male predilection, and SCC usually occurs in patients in their 50s or 60s.2The nasal cavity is the second-most commonly affected sinonasal anatomical site.2Patients present with nonspecific symptoms like unilateral nasal obstruction, sinusitis, and/or epistaxis. Symptoms become more severe over time and may involve proptosis, vision impairment, facial swelling, paresthesia, or pain.1Imaging by computed tomography or MRI is essential, and they reveal a space-occupying mass, often demonstrating soft tissue infiltration and destruction of surrounding bone.3 Histologically, SCC of the SNT may be broadly categorized into keratinizing and nonkeratinizing types.2Keratinizing SCC is characterized by tumor cells with overt keratinization and hyperchromatic nuclei that are linked by identifiable intercellular bridges. Dyskeratotic cells and squamous pearls may be seen.4Nonkeratinizing SCC (NKSCC) grows in a more ribbonlike or nested pattern, often with papillary and/or inverted architecture.2Tumor cells have large round to elongated nuclei with loss of polarity. Sinonasal NKSCCs are diverse in etiopathogenesis. Smoking increases one’s risk of developing NKSCC by 2 to 3 times.5Approximately half of patients with NKSCC also have high-risk HPV,6and infection with Epstein-Barr virus occurs in a few cases.7Recently, recurrent molecular signatures, such asDEK::AFF2fusions, have been described in sinonasal tumors with NKSCC morphologic characteristics.8The presence of low-risk HPV in this patient was interesting. The patient was taken to the operating room for endoscopic resection. The excisional specimen showed a bland papillary epithelial proliferation (closely associated with the papillary SCC;Figure 2). Identification of the benign papillary component, combined with the presence of low-risk HPV, supported a final diagnosis of papillary SCC ex–sinonasal papilloma (ex-SP). The margins were negative, and the patient is currently being assessed for postoperative radiation therapy. SCC is the most common malignant neoplasm that arises in conjunction with sinonasal papilloma (SP), a benign squamous epithelial proliferation. This occurrence is rare, affecting 2% to 4% of patients with SP. Low-risk HPV has been reported in patients with both exophytic and inverted SPs.2,9Papillary SCC is a curious NKSCC subtype defined by complex and bulky exophytic and/or endophytic architecture, combined with cytologic features of malignant neoplasia.2,6Papillary SCC may arise de novo, or it may be identified in association with conventional SCC. Quite rarely, it may be associated with SP.2High-risk HPV is identified in 80% of patients with papillary SCC.1Conventional stromal invasion is not required to make this diagnosis.1,9This represents a diagnostic pitfall, especially when evaluating incisional biopsies. In this patient, low-risk HPV was present in both the SP and malignant components, consistent with previously reported cases.9Patients diagnosed with SCC ex-SP are treated with surgical excision and postoperative radiotherapy. Long-term radiological and clinical monitoring for recurrence is necessary.10

caption: Axial sections of contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) of the neck showing multiple peripherally enhanced cystic lesions involving deep spaces of the neck, including the retropharyngeal space.
scenario: A 65-year-old woman presented with a 2-week history of worsening, painful, right-sided neck swelling with dysphagia, odynophagia, and fever. The neck swelling started with a small lump at the upper neck, which progressively increased in size. There were no symptoms of airway obstruction or aspiration, and the patient denied any constitutional symptoms. She had no history of tuberculous contact, irradiation, preceding trauma, or alleged foreign body impaction in the throat. Examination of the neck showed multiple palpable firm to fluctuant areas of neck swelling over bilateral cervical nodal levels II, III, and V. There was also similar swelling located over the anterior neck, which was fixed and immobile. Flexible nasopharyngolaryngoscopy showed bulging of the right posterior pharyngeal wall at the level of nasopharynx and velopharynx, with pooling of saliva at the pyriform fossae and vallecullae. The vocal folds were normal and mobile. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) scan of the neck showed multiple peripherally enhancing, centrally hypoattenuating lymph nodes; an irregular thyroid mass; and a retropharyngeal fluid collection (Figure 1).
explanation: Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma (ATC) is the most aggressive thyroid carcinoma, with an estimated median survival of 5 to 6 months.1It represents 1% to 2% of all thyroid carcinomas, with an annual incidence of 1.2 in 1 000 000.2Due to the rapidity of its progression, up to 63% of patients with ATC present with nodal metastasis in their first presentation, and up to 91% may develop extrathyroidal extension.3Diagnosis of ATC requires tissue-based histopathological assessment either via fine-needle aspiration cytology or tissue biopsy, aided with immunohistochemistry staining.4In the present case, fine-needle aspiration of multiple sites of neck swelling was initially performed because tuberculous infection was originally suspected as a possible cause, as previously reported in Malaysia.5Testing of the aspirated mucoid fluid revealed only atypical cells with microbiological cultures, and mycobacterium tests showed no evidence of infection. Subsequent incisional biopsy of the thyroid gland and level II lymph node showed pleomorphic cells with hyperchromatic nuclei and abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm with abnormal mitosis. Immunohistochemistry staining showed strong positivity toward cytokeratin AE1 and AE3, PAX8, p53 with negative thyroid transcription factor-1, and thyroglobulin. Cross-sectional imaging such as a CT scan is invaluable in cases of ATC. Local and regional extent of the tumor with involvement of other critical structures in the neck may be assessed with a high-quality CT scan.3ATC is also commonly associated with extrathyroidal extension, poorly defined margins, and invasion of surrounding cervical structures. Regional lymph node involvement has shown nodal necrosis in most cases of ATC.6This contrasts with lymphadenopathy in differentiated thyroid carcinoma, which has shown a more homogenous feature of a cystic or solid mass, with the nodes being rarely necrotic.3The CT features of the cystic lesions within the different spaces of the neck, including the retropharyngeal space, are also similar to tuberculous infection and disseminated neck abscess. Our literature review revealed a case previously reported in which CT features of ATC mimicked thyroid abscess.5Thyroid lymphoma may present similarly, including in the present patient who had a rapidly enlarging neck mass and obstructive symptoms. However, the CT features of thyroid lymphoma normally show lesions that are homogenous without calcification or necrosis, in contrast to the case presented herein (Figure 2).7 Management of ATC involves a multidisciplinary approach with the aim of either curative or palliative outcome. Surgical intervention may be considered for several reasons, including relief of aerodigestive obstruction (with or without tracheostomy) or tumor resection. Other options of treatment include radiotherapy with systemic and targeted molecular therapy.4Most patients with ATC, especially those with unresectable tumors, have shown only a 10% survival rate 1 year after diagnosis.8 In the case of this patient, the acute progression of lymphatic involvement, especially of the retropharyngeal lymph nodes, presented a diagnostic conundrum. CT features of hypodense lesions with peripheral enhancement of the lymph nodes and thyroid gland initially pointed toward an infective cause. With a negative microorganism culture and atypical cytology, results from tissue biopsy were invaluable in achieving the diagnosis of ATC. Despite the diagnosis and planning made to manage her condition, the patient died due to complications of hospitalization and tumor progression.

caption: A, Computed tomography (CT) image of the nasal mass displayed an irregular rim-enhancing fluid collection in the soft tissues along the anterior nasal bones (arrowhead).
