B, Hematoxylin-eosin (original magnification ×10) of the nasal mass showed aggregates of amorphous to fibrillary, pale eosinophilic material, surrounded by palisading histiocytes and multinucleated giant cells.
scenario: A male patient in their mid-30s presented with a 4-week history of progressively increasing pain and swelling involving the bridge of their nose. Physical examination revealed a bulbous subcutaneous mass involving the upper nasal dorsum, with erythema of the overlying skin. They denied fever, chills, sweats, or recent local trauma. Computed tomography scan revealed an irregular rim-enhancing fluid collection in the soft tissues along the anterior margin of the nasal bones measuring approximately 2.1 × 2.1 × 1.4 cm, which appeared to abut the right and left nasal bones with marginal erosion (Figure 1A). Incision and drainage were performed, revealing a white cottage cheese–like discharge. An antibiotic regimen was prescribed, and the patient was discharged. At follow-up, the patient revealed that the erythema and tenderness had initially improved but then had worsened over the last few days. The patient was taken for surgical excision and debridement of the presumed nasal abscess. During the operation, the surgeons noted that the lesion possessed a capsule and was adherent to the bony/cartilaginous junction with significant scarring and bony remodeling, and a white cottage cheese–like material was expressed upon dissection of the lesion. Histological sections from the lesion showed ulcerated squamous epithelium with acute and chronic inflammation. The underlying soft tissue and bone contained numerous collections of pale eosinophilic, amorphous to fibrillary material which was surrounded by palisading histiocytes and multinucleated giant cells (Figure 1B).
explanation: Gout is the most common form of microcrystalline arthropathy.1It is triggered by either an excessive production of uric acid or a decrease in its renal excretion.2Sustained elevation in uric acid levels leads to accumulation of mono-sodium urate crystals in various tissues and organs.2These crystals incite inflammation when ingested by neutrophils, triggering recurrent bouts of gouty arthritis, and potentially progressing to tophaceous gout over time.3 Tophus formation commonly occurs within or near joints, bursae, and tendon sheaths, often eroding bone and leading to distinctive lytic lesions.4In the head and neck region, tophi are most commonly found in the helix of the outer ear but can also rarely occur in other areas such as the middle ear, nasal bridge, nasal cavity, and larynx, leading to diverse symptoms from hearing loss to stridor.4Gouty involvement of the cricoarytenoid, temporomandibular, and sternoclavicular joints has also been documented.4 The diagnosis of gout relies on identifying negatively birefringent urate crystals in joint fluid or gouty tophus samples under a polarized light microscope (Figure 2).2Important differential diagnoses include conditions like pseudo-gout, rheumatoid nodule, and immune-mediated systemic diseases like granulomatosis with polyangiitis as they may exhibit similar otolaryngological manifestations, such as nasal bridge collapse, inflammation of the parasinus and sinuses, mucosal ulceration, among others.5 Topheous pseudogout may have remarkably similar histological findings to gout but will show rhomboid-shaped crystals with weakly positive birefringence under polarized light microscopy.6Rheumatoid nodule manifests as palisading granulomas surrounding areas of fibrinoid necrosis,7and granulomatosis with polyangiitis will present with necrotizing granulomatous inflammation without birefringent crystals. When a patient lacks a clinical history of gout or arthritic symptoms, as in the present case, the diagnosis can be particularly challenging. Typically, chronic tophaceous gout emerges following a decade or more of recurrent polyarticular gout; development of tophi without prior episodes of gouty arthritis is uncommon.8In this case, the patient did not initially disclose a history of gout, but upon further questioning during his postsurgical follow-up visit, he did report having intermittent arthritic symptoms in the past involving his fingers and toes. Surgical removal of the nasal mass was the preferred approach for this case and similar cases in the literature.2-9American College of Rheumatology guidelines also recommend that all patients diagnosed with tophaceous gout should undergo urate-lowering therapy together with a 6-month course of anti-inflammatory prophylaxis.10 The final diagnosis in this case was of a common inflammatory process that presented in an unexpected location. Tophaceous gout can be recognized or at least suspected on frozen section or routine histologic examination, but confirmatory diagnosis relies on the detection of mono-sodium urate crystals under polarized light microscopy. The clinical history of gout may be helpful but is not always readily available to the pathologist, who must maintain a high index of suspicion when confronted with an inflammatory mass-forming lesion in the head and neck.

caption: Computed tomography image of the sinuses showing the coronal (A) and axial (B) view. Note the small volume and complete opacification of maxillary sinuses (blue arrowheads), lateralization of uncinate processes (yellow arrowheads), and inferior bowing of the orbital floor (pink arrowheads) associated with enophthalmos.
scenario: A 13-year-old female was referred to pediatric otolaryngology by the oral surgery clinic for chronic facial pain and abnormal computed tomography (CT) scan findings. Relevant medical history included developmental delay, atrial septal defect, cerebral palsy, and pulmonary artery sling. The patient’s mother reported recurrent sinus infections with associated headaches, facial pain, nasal congestion, facial swelling, and nasal drainage. She had no history of sinus surgery or facial trauma. On physical examination, the patient had an elongated and narrow face, left-sided nasal septal deviation, as well as bilateral enophthalmos. The patient was previously evaluated by oral surgery for multiple impacted teeth; cone-beam CT showed opacified maxillary sinuses and a left-sided molar within the maxillary sinus. Follow-up CT of the sinuses showed bilateral small volume maxillary sinuses with associated opacification, lateralized nasal cavity walls, and inferior bowing of bilateral orbital floors (Figure 1). She subsequently underwent endoscopic sinus surgery. During surgery, bilateral uncinate processes, maxillary ostia, and ethmoid bullae were easily identified. Sinus mucosa was thickened without polyp formation. The retained molar was removed from the left maxillary sinus endoscopically.

options.D: Cystic fibrosis with sinonasal polyposis and hypoplasia

distractors: Cystic fibrosis with sinonasal polyposis and hypoplasia
explanation: A. Bilateral silent sinus syndrome Silent sinus syndrome (SSS) is a condition of maxillary sinus wall collapse with resulting enophthalmos from orbital floor collapse.1The cause is believed to be an obstructive process of the natural maxillary sinus ostium that induces a negative pressure within the sinus leading to collapse of all maxillary sinus walls.2Patients with SSS generally lack a significant history of infection, trauma, congenital anomaly, or sinus surgery. The literature suggests, however, that most patients can present with associated acute or chronic sinonasal symptoms.3Additionally, SSS can present with facial asymmetry and multiple ophthalmologic complications including enophthalmos, hypoglobus, and diplopia. The systematic literature review by Rosso et al2revealed the most common and consistent diagnostic criteria for SSS is the presence of enophthalmos and maxillary atelectasis, which is defined as persistent reduction in maxillary sinus volume due to inward bowing of antral walls. The criterion standard treatment for SSS involves reestablishing the integrity of the maxillary sinus via functional endoscopic sinus surgery with possible orbital floor reconstruction when indicated.2Unilateral SSS is rare in and of itself, but the presence of SSS bilaterally has only been documented a handful of times in the literature. Additionally, documentation of SSS in the pediatric population is uncommon.4The presence of bilateral enophthalmos due to SSS is extremely rare but nonetheless plausible in this case. While both SSS and maxillary sinus hypoplasia involve the maxillary sinus, they represent different clinical entities. Maxillary sinus aplasia and hypoplasia involve a congenital or developmental absence or reduction in the size of the maxillary sinus, whereas in SSS, the sinus was initially normal, but later collapsed. The maxillary sinuses normally develop beginning in the third gestational month and progress through the individual’s eighth year of life. Sinonasal complications can present following interruption or arrest of normal development. The incidence of maxillary sinus hypoplasia ranges between 1.5% and 10% and can present asymptomatically or with associated facial pain and pressure, headaches, nasal congestion, nasal drainage, and voice changes. Additionally, maxillary sinus hypoplasia is typically associated with hypoplastic or absent uncinate process.5CT imaging is the criterion standard for identifying this pathology and distinguishing it from similar conditions.6Key distinguishing radiographic findings in maxillary sinus hypoplasia include a small, underdeveloped sinus with intact orbital floor and nasal wall. In SSS, a degree of collapse of all maxillary sinus walls would be expected. Cystic fibrosis (CF) is a genetic disorder associated with the production of thick mucosal secretions that can obstruct airways and cause an array of respiratory symptoms. It is caused by variants in theCFTRgene. CF with sinonasal polyposis is a condition that presents with benign growths (polyps) in the nasal passages. These can obstruct the airway and exacerbate respiratory symptoms leading to recurrent sinus infections and increased trouble with breathing. Additionally, these can present with persistent nasal congestion and drainage, facial pain and pressure, and alterations in sense of smell. In contrast to SSS, patients with CF can present with evidence of widespread sinus changes, obstruction, and opacification due to polyposis and mucus plugging. Additionally, inferior displacement of the orbital floor would be unexpected. It has been reported that chronic infection and inflammation resulting from complications from CF can alter the growth and development of sinuses, leading to hypoplasia.7 A 2020 publication by Albadr et al8noted that diagnosis of SSS relies on a review of imaging that reveals reduction in size of the maxillary sinus antrum and inward bowing of most or all maxillary sinus walls. Additionally, the presence of a large middle meatus and laterally deviated uncinate is included among the most common findings in patients with SSS. Additionally, the presence of a large middle meatus and laterally deviated uncinate is included among the most common findings in patients with SSS. This can also be seen endoscopically (Figure 2).

caption: Anterior-posterior digital subtraction angiography showing the maxillary artery (pink arrowheads) and superficial temporal artery (blue arrowheads). A, The image from the left external carotid artery vasodilation before intervention demonstrates feeders from the occipital artery (1), posterior auricular artery (2), and middle meningeal artery (3), as well as early anterograde filling of the left sigmoid sinus. B, After intervention, there are no arterial feeders visible; however, coil occlusion of the left transverse sinus (4), and receiver-stimulator of the cochlear implant (5) can be seen.
scenario: A 67-year-old patient presented with persistent vertigo and pulsatile tinnitus in the left ear for the past 3 months. The initial magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) depicted arterial flow signal in the left transverse sinus. Results of digital subtraction angiography (Figure 1) revealed a complex dural arteriovenous fistula with multiple arterial feeders with anterograde filling of the left transverse sinus (Cognard type 1). Branches of the left external carotid artery (occipital artery, posterior auricular artery, and middle meningeal artery) provided the main supply to the fistula. Small feeding arteries also emerged from the left internal carotid artery (meningohypophyseal and inferior lateral trunk). The fistula point was in the distal transverse sinus below the inflow of the vein of Labbé. Due to the patient’s persistent symptoms, endovascular therapy was indicated. In another hospital, the fistula was only partially occluded transarterially, and the patient asked for a second opinion at our clinic. We performed treatment with transvenous coil occlusion of the left transverse sinus. The pulsatile tinnitus disappeared directly after the intervention, and the patient was free of symptoms. The patient received therapeutic doses of heparin and reported subjective well-being for 5 days. On the evening of the fifth day posttreatment, he experienced acute hearing loss of the left ear and vertigo.

options.A: Subacute infarction in the Heschl convolutions
options.D: Glue embolism in the tympanic cavity

distractors: Subacute infarction in the Heschl convolutions
Glue embolism in the tympanic cavity
explanation: MRI revealed an intracochlear as well as intralabyrinthine hemorrhage as a rare complication of sinus occlusion (Figure 2). In adults, only a few cases with sudden hearing loss can be found in literature,1in which 1 case reported bilateral bleeding.2 Venous congestion following cerebral vein or sinus thrombosis can cause ischemia and inadequate blood supply to the inner ear canal. Conductive hearing loss has been described as a rare complication of dural arteriovenous fistulas.3It is common for vascular pathologies to produce pulsatile tinnitus and/or vertigo.4Endovascular and/or neurosurgical treatment is usually the treatment of choice depending on the degree of the fistula and the patient’s age, symptoms, and likelihood of bleeding. Continued surveillance is also an alternative, though if the fistula increases in size and recruits cortical veins, the procedure may become more difficult. A case of an cochlear ischemia (but not of hemorrhage) after endovascular therapy of the sigmoid sinus was reported by Li et al.5In a larger study, Baltsavias et al6detected no identifiable cause on MRI for acute hearing loss following endovascular therapy for 2 of 52 patients. Finding the correct radiologic diagnosis of an inner-ear hemorrhage is not trivial.7In the present patient, we could detect the subacute cochlear hemorrhage in T1-weighted sequences. This was mainly due to the timing of the MRI being performed 2 days after the onset of symptoms, when subacute hemorrhage is more conspicuous on MRI. Labyrinthitis is a differential diagnosis, with fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) and T1-weighted hyperintense signal abnormalities in the inner ear as well. High-resolution T1-weighted, T2-weighted, and FLAIR sequences have highly variable sensitivities and specificities depending on age of the hemorrhage and resolution; 3-dimensional FLAIR demonstrated the highest sensitivity in children followed by T1-weighted and T2-weighted sequences.8Hemorrhagic lesions have been detected in the vestibule, cochlea, and posterior and lateral semicircular canals.9The prognosis of such a cochlear hemorrhage is generally poor10; thus, we opted for a cochlear implant. Placement of this implant likely preserved the patient’s hearing. Unfortunately, the vertigo persisted and had to be treated conservatively. We were unable to resolve the question of whether the cause of the bleeding was secondary hemorrhagic ischemia or direct bleeding into the cochlea due to the altered drainage conditions and venous congestion.

caption: A, A reddish, elevated scarlike plaque with an eccentric orifice containing mucouslike exudate at the left sternoclavicular joint. B, Sagittal T2-weighted, fat-suppressed magnetic resonance image (MRI) showed an irregular hyperintense tract (arrowhead) extending toward the left sternoclavicular joint (circle).
scenario: A 32-year-old female patient presented with chronic discharging sinus with recurrent infection at the left sternoclavicular joint (SCJ). A skin dimple with a little mucouslike secretion had been noticed since birth. Local painful swelling and abscess formation of the cutaneous pit began at age 4 years and subsided after intravenous antibiotics and incision. Thereafter, 5 similar infection episodes occurred in the last 20 years. There was no family history of similar disorders. Physical examination showed a 2.8 × 2.5-cm, reddish, elevated scarlike plaque with a 6-mm sinus orifice containing mucouslike exudate at the left SCJ (Figure 1A). Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a 23 × 14-mm irregular subcutaneous tract with low T1-weighted and high T2-weighted signal intensity extending toward the left SCJ (Figure 1B). The distance between the tract bottom and sternal end of the left clavicle was approximately 1.5 mm. Intraoperative laryngoscopy found no pyriform fistula. The sinus with adjacent scar tissue was completely excised under general anesthesia after sinus staining with methylene blue. The sinus terminated at the fascia of the clavicular head of the left sternocleidomastoid muscle. Postoperative histopathology uncovered that the sinus was lined by keratinizing squamous epithelium with pilosebaceous glands and intraluminal keratinous materials.
explanation: Sternoclavicular sinus (SCS), or sinus sternoclavicularis, is a relatively uncommon congenital sinus near the SCJ.1It is also named as congenital sternoclavicular dermoid sinus and congenital dermoid fistula/sinus of the anterior chest region due to its similar characteristics of dermoid cysts.1,2To date, approximately 389 cases have been reported, of which 56.6% are females and 85.3% are left sided.3-5Its embryological origin is still debatable. First, SCS may be analogue to dermoid cysts resulting from entrapment of epithelial elements in the deeper tissues along embryonic fusion lines.1Second, SCS could originate from a disorderly fusion between the upper sternum and proximal clavicle.3However, both would explain the blind ending near the SCJ but does not account for the left-sided predominance and occasionally endodermal origin of ciliated epithelium and salivary glands.1,6Third, considering that its sinus occurring predominantly in the left side and locating at the sternoclavicular end of the sternocleidomastoid muscle correspond to the anatomical position of the fourth branchial cleft, some authors propose that SCS may represent the cutaneous remnant of fourth branchial cleft.1,3,4,7 SCS typically manifests as a cutaneous pit, sinus, or infected mass near the SCJ with a left-sided predominance. Despite its presentation at birth, it often becomes apparent only after infection.2,4Recurrent infections and abscesses are common, while the pyriform sinus and thyroid gland are unaffected. The sinus tract is relatively short and ends blindly at the deep surface of the platysma muscle or the superficial surface of the clavicular head of the sternocleidomastoid muscle.3,4Histopathologically, the sinus tract is predominantly lined with squamous epithelium with adnexal structures including pilosebaceous and sweat glands, and occasionally with ciliated epithelium (Figure 2).4,6 Clinical diagnosis of SCS is usually straightforward based on medical history and clinical presentations. A skin streak sign, a pale skin streak extending superiorly from the sinus orifice toward the ipsilateral thyroid gland, may be diagnostic.4Imaging examinations are useful for identifying the sinus tract’s length and path. Ultrasonography is preferable for initial evaluation, whereas computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging are helpful to demystify the extent of SCS, especially if there are other anatomical anomalies.4-6 Main differential diagnoses comprise epidermoid cysts, dermoid cysts, and branchial cleft anomalies.2,4Epidermoid and dermoid cysts develop from entrapment of epithelial structures during closure of the branchial arches and often locate along the midline,8and their cystic walls are lined by keratinized squamous epithelium with or without adnexal structures in dermoid or epidermoid cysts, respectively.2,4Branchial cleft anomalies result from a failure to obliterate the embryonic branchial apparatus, and their cyst/sinus walls are composed of either squamous or ciliated epithelium. Second branchial sinus/fistula is the most common subtype, with its external orifice locating above the SCJ and along the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle, and its course running in a cranial direction. Third and fourth branchial anomalies often possess an internal opening in the lateral wall of the pyriform sinus, and present with recurrent neck abscess and acute suppurative thyroiditis.2,4,9 Because of the risk of infection and abscess formation, complete resection of the sinus tract from skin orifice to the blind end during quiescent inflammation phase is recommended.1-5Intrasinus cannulation and methylene blue stain can facilitate en bloc resection of sinus tract.5,9This patient underwent complete excision of the entire sinus tract with surrounding scar tissue using methylene blue stain, with no complications and relapse at 2-month follow-up.

caption: Clinical examination (A) and computed tomography (CT) scan with axial, sagittal, and coronal views (B).
scenario: A 60-year-old female patient presented with odynophagia and dysphagia for approximately 1.5 months. Her medical history included dwarfism, scoliosis, hypothyroidism, and dyslipidemia. The primary care physician initially diagnosed a left tonsillitis, and the patient underwent a monthlong antibiotic treatment with multiple courses of antibiotics. She did not experience any fever. Due to the lack of improvement of odynophagia, she was referred to an ear, nose, and throat specialist. On clinical examination, a left-sided erythematous oropharyngeal bulging was observed (Figure 1A). A puncture was performed using an 18-gauge syringe, revealing dark bloody fluid. A contrast-enhanced cervical computed tomography (CT) scan was conducted (Figure 1B).
explanation: C. Bilateral internal carotid artery aneurysm On CT scan, a structure measuring 35 mm in its long axis was observed in the left parapharyngeal space. The structure showed arterial opacification beginning in the cervical internal carotid artery and extending into the carotid canal in the petrous temporal bone. This appearance suggests an aneurysm of the internal carotid artery with anterior thrombus, leading to a right shift of the oropharyngeal tract (Figure 1B). A similar structure with a long axis of 19 mm was also identified on the right side (Figure 1B). Clinical signs of peritonsillar abscess include odynophagia, dysphagia, ipsilateral swelling of the soft palate, trismus, and voice change or hoarseness. The patient exhibited 2 of these clinical signs but no clinical inflammatory syndrome. The CT scan, prompted by the discovery of dark bloody fluid during a puncture and a strong suspicion of peritonsillar abscess, revealed the aneurysm. Careful inspection and palpation could reveal pulsation, emphasizing the importance of keen physical examination in peritonsillar abscess suspicion cases.1However, in this case, the anterior portion consisted of a thrombus and pulsation could not be felt. The diagnosis of bacterial tonsillitis could have been considered in the presence of symptoms resembling those of a peritonsillar abscess, along with hypertrophic and erythematous tonsils, possibly accompanied by a radiologic finding of an abscess within the tonsils. Regarding the diagnosis of necrotic nodes, clinically they may resemble a peritonsillar or parapharyngeal abscess. However, the localization in the oropharynx is atypical. In both cases, arterial opacification helped rule out these diagnoses. Carotid aneurysms predominantly affect the internal and common carotid artery, with the external carotid artery less frequently involved morphologically. Internal carotid artery aneurysms are rare, accounting for less than 1% of all carotid pathologies.2The most common site for extracranial carotid artery aneurysms is the carotid bifurcation. The main causes include atherosclerosis, iatrogenic factors from prior procedures such as carotid endarterectomy or angiography, trauma, infection, fibromuscular dysplasia, Marfan syndrome, congenital factors, and postirradiation in head and neck malignancy.3-6Presentation may include a pulsatile neck mass in the oropharynx, ischemic stroke, and cranial nerves deficit or oropharyngeal bulge, without clinical inflammatory syndrome. Carotid aneurysms have a high mortality rate often caused by substantial neurological or hemorrhagic disorders.7Ultrasonography can differentiate between abscess and vascular swelling, while Doppler provides information on flow dynamics. CT angiography (Figure 2) offers details on origin, flow, extent, and lesion site, with a sensitivity and specificity of 70% and 90%, respectively, replacing classic angiography.8 In cases of unilateral oropharyngeal bulge, a thorough clinical examination is essential. The absence of an inflammatory clinical picture should raise suspicion of an oropharyngeal or deep lobe tumor of the parotid or vascular abnormalities, such as an aneurysm of the internal carotid artery. CT scan would be a ideal before a blind puncture of the tonsillar fossa to potentially avoid disastrous complications.

caption: Coronal reconstruction of computed tomography (CT) image of bone window showing expansion of the left mandibular ramus (A). Axial bone window image (B) showing underlying bone sclerosis (arrowhead) and overlying lamellated periosteal reaction (asterisk).
scenario: A 9-year-old male presented with a 2-year history of left-sided jaw swelling with insidious onset. It was not associated with pain, fever, or functional debilitation. The patient’s parent reported that the swelling had resolved with an unidentified oral over-the-counter medication and then recurred 5 times during the 2 years. The patient was afebrile. Physical examination revealed a palpable hard mass, approximately 5 × 4 cm in size, at the left ramus of the mandible. A contrast-enhanced computed tomography scan of the patient’s neck revealed an expansile lesion involving the left ramus of the mandible with ground glass matrix, thickened overlying cortex, and lamellated periosteal reaction (Figure 1). The left masseter was diffusely swollen with ill-defined hypodensities within it. A technetium-99m bone scan showed uptake within the mandibular lesion. Fine-needle aspiration cytology results showed the presence of macrophages, lymphocytes, and a few polymorphs, but no atypical cells. Given that the mass was clinically suggestive of a malignant neoplasm, an ultrasonography-guided biopsy procedure of the mass was performed. Histopathologic examination of the specimen showed chronic inflammatory infiltrate without any evidence of a malignant tumor.
explanation: After radiopathologic correlation, the final diagnosis was chronic Garré sclerosing osteomyelitis (GSO).1This is a rare and specific form of chronic osteomyelitis with proliferative periostitis, characterized by periosteal reaction in the form of cortical thickening and a related loss of the bony medullary canal (Figure 2). When first described in 1893,1it presented some initial confusion regarding the existence of suppuration or sequestration. GSO commonly affects males in childhood or early adulthood,2with the mandible being most commonly involved.3 Poor oral hygiene and secondary periodontal issues, such as odontogenic infections or moderate periodontitis, may be associated with the cause of GSO. Dental extraction has been described as a potential risk factor.4Symptoms are gradual and appear over several months as recurrent, nonprogressive, and episodic pains without any substantial functional loss of the involved bone.5The disease usually presents with no active signs of infection.2Larger lesions may develop swelling and asymmetry.3Notably, the duration of GSO is variable among patients and may even occur over several years. Most patients are relatively healthy between clinical episodes.6Although the disease has a low risk of mortality, it has been associated with a high degree of morbidity in some cases. The causes of GSO are unclear but they are thought to involve a low-virulence bacterial species. Even after treatment, infection can persist and perpetuate the chronic process. There are no specific diagnostic criteria for GSO, and diagnosis is usually based on imaging findings in combination with a clinical history of a prolonged disease course. Laboratory test results may occasionally show elevated inflammatory markers, such as C-reactive protein and erythrocyte sedimentation rate. Radiography findings demonstrate cortical thickening with medullary sclerosis.3Computed tomography imaging may be more sensitive in demonstrating the bony expansion and may also reveal redundant periosteal layering of the cortex (onionskin appearance).6The imaging features in GSM are attributed to repeated irritation and inflammation of the periosteum, secondary to the low-grade chronic infection. Results of isotope scans may also show increased uptake at the site of involvement.2Although imaging results indicative of Ewing sarcoma may be similar, distinguishing characteristics of GSO are the acuity of the swelling along with local site discomfort and tenderness.7Cortical thickening and periosteal reaction may be seen in a primary bone lymphoma (PBL); however, PBL is uncommon in children younger than 10 years and it is usually accompanied by localized pain and B symptoms (ie, associated with lymphoma).8Bony expansion and sclerosis may be seen in fibrous dysplasia; however, there will be absence of overlying periosteal reaction, unless there is a pathologic fracture.9 Histopathologic findings for GSO are inconclusive and may show chronic nonspecific inflammation.10Although low-virulence bacteria are the culprits in most cases, results of cultures are usually negative.5Polymerase chain reaction testing can be requested for diagnosing the causative organism when clinical suspicion is high.6Occurrence of a lesion of this nature in a pediatric patient demands an aggressive workup—without proper clinical context, imaging may mimic a more sinister lesion such as Ewing sarcoma. Other pathologies with a similar presentation include osteoid osteoma, eosinophilic granuloma, and osteosarcoma.2Ultimately, in this patient we diagnosed GSO based on the findings of the physical examination, normal laboratory test results, nonspecific histologic results, and typical radiographic abnormalities in this patient. Treatment of GSO usually involves symptomatic management and administration of broad-spectrum antibiotics.2Surgical interventions are only considered for individuals who do not respond to standard treatments because the necrotic-sclerotic bone and its associated blood supply may prevent antibiotics from reaching the infected tissues.3,6Furthermore, the use of endodontic therapy may be an alternative or substitute treatment4given that it does hold promise; however, further studies are needed to compare it with other treatment modalities.

caption: A, Clinical image of an 18-year-old male presenting with a pedunculated papule perpendicular to the nasal mucosa. B, Hematoxylin-eosin–stained biopsy of the nasal papule (original magnification ×40).
scenario: An 18-year-old male with no significant medical history presented for evaluation of a nasal papule. He reported that the papule had been present for 1 year. The lesion was asymptomatic without any associated pain, pruritus, or bleeding. He did not report any trauma to the area, and it was not causing nasal obstruction. It had not grown or changed over the past year. He had never had a similar lesion. On physical examination there was a flesh-colored, well-circumscribed papule perpendicular to the nasal mucosa, protruding into the nasal cavity (Figure, A). Focused examination of the face additionally revealed a flesh-colored papule on the left tragus, clinically consistent with an accessory tragus. The nasal papule was biopsied at the base under local anesthesia with iris scissors and sent for histopathologic examination. Grossly, the lesion was a 2 × 1 × 1 mm tan papule. Microscopically the lesion was a small and well-circumscribed proliferation of spindled cells arranged as fascicles with intervening clefts (Figure, B). Some foci showed palisading of nuclei around anuclear zones (ie, Verocay bodies).
explanation: Palisaded encapsulated neuroma (PEN), also known as solitary circumscribed neuroma (SCN), was originally reported in 1972 by Reed et al1as a benign hyperplasia of axons and sheath cells derived from Schwann cell origin. Clinically, most PENs will present in middle-aged adults as an asymptomatic, slow growing, flesh-colored papule on the face or neck.1-3However, rare cases have been reported on other sites including the oral mucosa, eyelid, and glans penis.4-6In addition, there has been a singular report from 1998 of a PEN arising from the nasal mucosa.7It is relatively rare for a patient to have a PEN protruding into the nasal cavity. Clinically, a PEN is often indistinguishable from a neurofibroma, fibrous papule, nonmelanoma skin cancer, or benign appendageal tumors.8Thus, biopsy is often indicated, as in the case of this patient. The pathologic differential diagnosis of PEN includes schwannoma, neurofibroma, and traumatic neuroma.4Most cases can be differentiated with hematoxylin-eosin staining alone, without the need for additional stains. PEN prototypically demonstrates a well-circumscribed, dermal nodule with spindle cells grouped in fascicles and separated by clefts.2,9Prominent palisading, akin to Verocay body formation, can be seen (as with schwannoma).2Axons are typically seen throughout the proliferation. In diagnostically challenging cases, immunohistochemical stains can be used. Because the lesion comprises mostly Schwann cells, S100 will stain positively in PENs. Epithelial membrane antigen will typically highlight the perineurial layer surrounding the fascicles. Neurofilament will highlight the interfascicular axons. In addition, glial fibrillary acidic protein will show negative results in PEN, but typically shows positive results in schwannomas, neurofibromas, and traumatic neuromas.4Traumatic neuromas are a result of mechanical injury, and similar to PENs, will also demonstrate smaller grouped fascicles and clefts; however, they will be situated in a fibrous scar.2 It is critical to differentiate PEN from schwannoma and neurofibroma because PEN has no underlying association with systemic or malignant disease.6Schwannomas are usually anatomically deeper, and contain densely cellular and fascicular Antoni A regions separated by Verocay bodies, and less cellular Antoni B regions with loose arrangement of tissue.4,8Cutaneous schwannomas, particularly plexiform schwannomas, have been associated with neurofibromatosis type 2, an autosomal dominant disorder with a variant in theNF2gene.10Early identification of cutaneous plexiform schwannomas can aid in this diagnosis, which is associated with other tumors such as meningiomas and ependymomas.10Neurofibromas are nonencapsulated tumors of spindle cells with wavy nuclei and numerous mast cells.2,4Cutaneous neurofibromas can be seen with neurofibromatosis type 1 and mucosal neurofibromas with multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2B.3Neurofibromatosis type 1 is an autosomal dominant variant ofNF1and presents with several cutaneous findings including neurofibromas, café au lait macules, and axillary freckling. Patients with multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2B characteristically can have marfinoid habitus and have multiple small mucosal nodules on the lips or distal anterior tongue and are at increased risk of medullary thyroid carcinoma and pheochromocytoma.7 Patients with PEN can be reassured with observation or conservative removal, with minimal likelihood of recurrence and no indication for further systemic workup.3,9

caption: Laryngeal stenosis with infracordal edema marked by the asterisk (A) and resultant subglottic mass indicated by the red arrowhead (B).
scenario: A man in his 70s was referred to the otolaryngology clinic with a right-sided submandibular mass that had gradually increased to approximately 5 cm in size during 8 months; it had an uneven surface, hard texture, and poor mobility. The patient had begun to experience hoarseness at 2 months; this was followed by breathing difficulty at rest by 5 months but no cough, blood in sputum, or dysphagia were present. The patient’s medical history was important for hypertension, diabetes, and atrial flutter accompanied by irregular atrioventricular conduction. Endoscopy imaging revealed laryngeal stenosis (Figure 1A) and resultant subglottic mass (Figure 1B) with normal vocal fold movement. Magnetic resonance imaging of the larynx revealed a T2 hyperintense, enhancing lesion with thickening of the right laryngeal wall at the glottic and subglottic levels producing laryngeal stenosis. Swelling of the right submandibular gland and adjacent space was also seen. A tracheostomy procedure was performed to relieve breathing difficulty. After adjustment of the cardiac function, a biopsy procedure of the subglottic and submandibular masses was conducted under general anesthesia. The immunohistochemical results showed the specimen was positive for myeloperoxidase, CD99, CD43; and negative for CD20, PAX5, CD138, κ, λ, cyclin D1, CD3, CD4, CD123, and TdT. The Ki-67 proliferation index was approximately 80%, and the bone marrow aspiration and biopsy specimen were negative for evidence of myeloid leukemia.
explanation: Granulocytic sarcoma (GS) can be an isolated mass or an extramedullary spread of acute or chronic myeloid leukemia, which may occur before, during, or as a presentation of relapse of myeloid leukemia.1Primary GS has been identified in every anatomic location, including skin, soft tissue, bone, and lymph nodes.2It has been reported that the head and neck regions compose approximately 12% of all GS cases.3Nevertheless, it rarely shows laryngeal involvement. The exact incidence of GS of the larynx is yet unknown, with limited published cases due to its rarity. GS is more common in children than adults, with no sex predilection.4 The differential diagnosis of subglottic laryngeal masses includes benign lesions (amyloidosis, sarcoidosis, and tuberculosis infection), and malignant tumors (squamous cell carcinoma, inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor, lymphomas, and sarcomas). Primary subglottic malignant neoplasm is rare. Myeloid leukemias tend to infiltrate the glottis more than the supraglottis.1To our knowledge, no subglottic GS involvement has been reported prior to this case. Radiologic findings do not show specific signs for GS.5Given its lack of pathognomonic macroscopic features, GS is often confused with other malignant tumors (eg, lymphomas or sarcomas); therefore, histopathologic evaluation is required for diagnosis of GS.1In this case report, myeloid leukemia accompanying GS was not detected at the time of diagnosis. Therefore, a diagnosis of primary GS with metastasis of submandibular gland was considered. Then the patient was admitted to the hematology department, and subsequently started receiving chemotherapy. The endoscopic images revealed tumor remission 3 months after the chemotherapy completion (Figure 2). The patient reported improvement in hoarseness and breathing. Tracheocutaneous fistula closure surgery was then performed. GS prognosis is poor and somewhat similar to that of acute myeloid leukemia. If left untreated, 88% of GS cases may progress to acute myeloid leukemia within an average of 11 months. Chemotherapy may prolong nonleukemic periods to approximately 2 years.6The role of supplementary surgical removal and radiation therapy remains to be elucidated.7

caption: Swallowing dynamic computed tomography (SD-CT) imaging at rest (A) and during swallowing (B) with anterior cervical tissue (white arrow) not observed at rest and anterolateral displacement of the sternocleidomastoid muscle (white arrowheads). SD-CT was performed with tube voltage, 120 kV; tube current, 50 mA; exposure time, 3.3 sec; total exposure dose, 2.59 mSv.
scenario: A 28-year-old man presented to our hospital complaining of a bulge on the left side of his neck and severe stabbing pain during swallowing. The patient reported having experienced a left-side neck contusion 1 year prior with subsequent persistent pain, which the next day, developed into swelling and subcutaneous bleeding. These gradually improved over time; however, 2 weeks after the injury, he started experiencing a left cervical bulge and intense stabbing pain during swallowing. Despite having undergone various pharmacologic interventions at multiple medical facilities, these symptoms remained entirely unchanged. When the patient presented to our hospital, his vital signs were within normal ranges and blood tests revealed no abnormal findings. Symptomatically quiescent at rest, he reported substantial pain and swelling localized to the left sternocleidomastoid (SCM) and omohyoid (OH) muscles only during swallowing, accompanied by intense pain. Neck ultrasonography imaging was performed, which identified abnormal movement of the left OH toward the anterointernal direction during swallowing. Laryngoscopy and barium swallow testing showed no abnormalities. These findings were suggestive of posttraumatic scarring or neuritis; therefore, the patient was treated with ultrasonography-guided local triamcinolone injections around the bulging area and neuropathic pain medications; however, no improvement was noted. Hence, we performed swallowing dynamic computed tomography (SD-CT) to assess the dynamic structural changes during swallowing. SD-CT can reveal moving structures during swallowing by creating a dynamic-volume dataset.1,2The findings of SD-CT imaging at rest and during swallowing are shown inFigure 1and theVideo, A.
explanation: Given the findings of the reconstructed SD-CT imaging showing that the position of the intermediate tendon of the OH moved from a deep to a superficial position during swallowing and that it pushed the SCM up from below (Figure 2;Video), we diagnosed the patient with omohyoid muscle syndrome (OMS). Fifteen units of botulinum toxin type A (BTX) were injected into the OH for abnormal muscle contraction. After 1 week, the neck bulge and pain on swallowing were markedly improved; however, 3 months later, the bulging of the left side of the neck during swallowing and its associated symptoms reappeared. Injections of 20 units of BTX are currently being administered to the patient, as needed, for symptom management. OMS is a rare condition characterized by a lateral neck bulge that appears during swallowing and disappears at rest. Patients with OMS are asymptomatic at rest, and the symptoms, such as tenderness, discomfort, and limited cervical extension in the lateral neck, appear only during swallowing. The mechanisms of OMS include abnormal motion due to injury or loosening of the OH intermediate tendon and muscle fiber degeneration.1,2OMS is diagnosed on the basis of clinical presentation and diagnostic tests. Real-time ultrasonography imaging is a key diagnostic tool because it can demonstrate anterolateral displacement of the SCM by a thickened omohyoid muscle during swallowing.3,4Treatments for OMS include local injections of BTX or surgical treatment (OH resection by endoscopic or external approaches), with no symptom recurrence after surgery.5,6 The differential diagnoses for OMS include cervical chyloma, pseudoaneurysm, and traumatic cervical cystic hygroma. Cervical chyloma is an infrequent pseudocystic structure, which arises from the thoracic duct or its tributaries after a neck trauma or surgery, especially on the left side. CT scans and ultrasonography findings can confirm the cystic structure.7Pseudoaneurysms in the neck can occur due to various reasons, including trauma, iatrogenic injury during surgery, or radiation therapy, that can be associated with various symptoms, such as pain, dysphagia, hoarseness, or neurological deficits. A combination of imaging studies, including ultrasonography and CT angiography, is useful in its diagnosis.8Traumatic cervical cystic hygroma is a rare condition characterized by benign, painless, and soft swelling associated with lymphatic system malformations. It commonly presents in children 2 years or younger but can occur in older adults (60 years and older) in association with infection or trauma.9These conditions differ somewhat from OMS in terms of imaging findings and symptoms. In the present case, SD-CT revealed abnormal lateral movement of the OH during swallowing, suggesting some impairment of the intermediate tendon of the OH. Traumatic injury to the intermediate tendon can cause OH contraction during swallowing, which pushes up and compresses the SCM from the inside, forming a left cervical bulge. SD-CT was very useful in the diagnosis of OMS because it enabled us to observe the contraction of the entire OH, including the intermediate tendon, during swallowing. Four-dimensional evaluation by ultrasonography has been applied in the fetus and the heart,10but is currently not suitable for evaluation of neck musculature in terms of resolution and image evaluation range. Although pain is not common in OMS, the pain in this patient is likely associated with abnormal posttraumatic nerve regeneration. The patient reported less pain after the BTX injection; thus, BTX may be contributing to relief of pain and neck swelling during swallowing, likely by inhibiting OH movement during swallowing. Additional BTX treatment will be considered as needed; however, dosage and administration intervals should be adjusted according to the patient’s condition. Surgical treatment, such as partial left OH resection, is another option.

caption: Clinical photographs showing generalized maxillary alveolar hyperplasia. The arrowhead depicts maxillary alveolar hypertrophy.
scenario: An 87-year-old woman was admitted due to sudden-onset worsening right facial swelling and pain persisting for 1 day. Additionally, she reported a decade-long history of a slow-growing cheek swelling. She denied any recent dental procedures, and there was no pain on mastication. On examination, she had a fever, and her right cheek exhibited gross swelling and erythema with mild induration. Intraorally, foul-smelling pus was observed with poor dental hygiene, as well as caries with pus expressed from the right second and third maxillary molars. Additionally, there was generalized maxillary alveolar hyperplasia noted, as depicted inFigure 1. She had full eye range of motion and no eye symptoms. Computed tomography (CT) results revealed a marked expansion of the maxilla with mixed sclerotic lytic areas. There were areas of cortical erosions seen with diffuse soft tissue thickening with inflammatory stranding. Dehiscence of the right maxillary sinus floor with complete opacification of the right maxillary sinus was noted. What is the most likely diagnosis in this patient with a superimposed odontogenic and sinus infection?
explanation: Figure 2depicts the CT of the face, which revealed marked expansion of the maxilla with mixed sclerotic lytic areas. There were areas of cortical erosions that were seen with diffuse soft tissue thickening with inflammatory stranding. Dehiscence of the right maxillary sinus floor with complete opacification of the right maxillary sinus was noted. She received a diagnosis of right sinusitis and facial cellulitis secondary to an odontogenic infection on a background of newly diagnosed Paget disease of the skull. She underwent an endoscopic drainage of the right maxillary sinusitis and dental extractions, as well as a course of intravenous antibiotics. She was discharged in good health and remained healthy at her follow-up review. Radionuclide bone scintigraphy performed showed increased tracer accumulation at the frontal, skull base, occipital, maxillary, and mandibular regions in the blood pool phase. In the delayed imaging, all these sites showed intense tracer uptake and appeared expanded. Paget disease, also known as osteitis deformans, is a chronic bone disorder characterized by the disruption of the usual cycle of bone remodeling that causes erratic bone resorption and formation. Various studies have suggested a potential connection between viruses, particularly paramyxoviruses and measles virus, and the disease’s pathogenesis; however, conclusive evidence is lacking.1There is a strong genetic component, and 15% to 20% of those affected have a first-degree relative with the disease.2Paget disease is most prevalent among elderly individuals and frequently observed in individuals older than 55 years. It exhibits a higher incidence in male individuals, with a sex ratio of 1.8:1. Geographical variations are notable; occurrence of the disease is rare in Asia, Scandinavia, and Africa.3 Paget disease exhibits diverse clinical presentations that primarily depend on the affected bones. Commonly involved areas include the pelvis, lumbosacral spine, skull, femur, or tibia. The condition can manifest locally in 1 or a few bones or extend widely throughout the skeleton, usually in the form of pain or increased bone size. Numerous authors have emphasized that bones affected by Paget disease are particularly prone to infection on exposure to oral flora.4This was apparent in this case, in which the patient presented with progressive cheek swelling with a superimposed dental infection. In some cases, Paget disease is asymptomatic and is incidentally discovered through radiological investigations or an increase in serum alkaline phosphatase activity. Diagnosis of Paget disease is primarily through radiological investigations. In relation to this case, there are classical features that may be seen on the skull radiography and CT. In the initial stage,Osteoporosis circumscriptamanifests as large and well-defined lytic lesions that involve the inner aspect of the outer table of the skull. The inner table remains preserved at this stage. The skull may exhibit a cotton wool appearance as the disease progresses. This refers to the presence of mixed lytic and sclerotic lesions that create a distinctive pattern on the skull. Advanced manifestation involves diploic widening in which the inner and outer calvarial tables are affected. A pathognomonic appearance associated with advanced Paget disease in the skull is termed theTam o’ Shanter sign, which is characterized by platybasia and basilar invagination, resulting in the skull seeming to fall over the facial bones.5While radiological features are typically distinctive, occasional cases may make it difficult to distinguish between sclerotic or lytic metastases. For a thorough diagnostic evaluation, it is recommended to incorporate an isotope bone scan. This offers a comprehensive view of the entire skeleton, enabling precise assessment of the extent of the disease. The typical appearances on the scan, which are affected by skeletal metabolic activity reflected in tracer uptake, provide early insight into changes in disease activity.6 There are varied complications of Paget disease. Pagetic bone pain only occurs in a minority of patients. Deformities, such as femur or tibia bowing, may be asymptomatic or associated with mechanical pain. The predominant neurological complication in Paget disease is hearing impairment, typically originating from the affected petrous temporal bone. The deafness may exhibit conductive characteristics that result from middle-ear ossicle involvement, sensorineural features caused by compression of the auditory nerve, or cochlear engagement. Management of Paget disease centers around symptom control and reducing complications. Bisphosphonates, such as alendronate, play a crucial role in normalizing the aberrant bone remodeling process. Pain management and ensuring adequate calcium and vitamin D intake are integral components of the treatment approach.7 In essence, Paget disease presents a nuanced challenge in the realm of bone disorders. Management requires a comprehensive approach to diagnosis and treatment to mitigate its effect on bone health and overall well-being.

caption: Contrast-enhanced computed tomographic imaging demonstrates a low-density mass in the left neck.
scenario: A 23-year-old male patient sought evaluation at the vascular thyroid surgery clinic for a large neck tumor that appeared abruptly 10 days prior. The patient reported experiencing tightness and discomfort in the left side of the neck but denied experiencing any pain. He denied any recent incidents of neck trauma or impact. Furthermore, his medical history did not reveal any previous hematological disorders. The ultrasonography examination detected the presence of a well-defined, solid mass located in the left lobe of the thyroid gland. The mass exhibited regular shape, distinct boundaries, heterogeneous echogenicity, and observable blood flow signals. Computed tomography (CT) of the neck detected heterogeneous density mass shadows within the soft tissue region near the left lobe of the thyroid, exhibiting distinct boundaries measuring 53 × 41 × 88 mm. Subsequent enhanced CT did not reveal notable enhancement of the cystic components of the mass (Figure 1). Due to persistent symptoms, the patient expressed a desire for surgical resection. Consequently, the patient underwent open surgery to remove the mass, aiming to establish a definitive diagnosis and provide appropriate treatment.
explanation: During the surgical procedure, a sizable tumor displaying consistent morphology was identified in close proximity to the vagus nerve within the cervical sheath. Subsequent histopathologic assessment substantiated the existence of a distinctly demarcated mass, while intraoperative pathology suggested the presence of a spindle cell tumor, specifically identified as a schwannoma. Additionally, the diagnosis was reinforced by immunohistochemical observations, which revealed positive outcomes for S100 and SOX10, as well as a negative result for p53, alongside a Ki-67 proliferation index of 3%. These findings collectively provided further confirmation that the tumor in question was indeed a vagal schwannoma. A schwannoma, which is alternatively referred to as neuroschwannoma, neurilemmoma, or neurinoma of Verocay, is a nonmalignant neoplasm that arises from Schwann cells located in the cranial, peripheral, and autonomic perineural regions.1Schwannomas have the potential to develop along any cranial, peripheral, or autonomic nerve within the human body, with the exception of the olfactory and optic nerves due to the absence of Schwann cells.2Research indicates that approximately 25% to 45% of schwannomas are located in the extracranial head and neck region, predominantly in the lateral aspect of the neck.3The vagal schwannoma is a solitary, asymptomatic, indolent benign tumor located in the neck. Presently, clinical reports do not provide any epidemiological characteristics associated with cervical vagal nerve schwannomas; however, a previous study has indicated that vagal nerve schwannomas do not show a sex-specific predisposition and can affect individuals of all age groups, with a higher occurrence observed between the ages of 30 and 50 years.1Although the transformation of a benign schwannoma into a malignant form is uncommon, it has been documented. Schwannomas exhibit a gradual progression as neoplasms, typically growing at an annual rate of 3 mm.4In this particular case, the patient presented with a sudden, unexpectedly large tumor, which had previously been overlooked as schwannoma before surgery. Normally, vagal schwannomas need only surgical treatment, and there have been no recurrences in this patient. The literature commonly suggests using ultrasonography, CT, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) as diagnostic investigations for schwannomas.5,6Nevertheless, it is worth noting that FNAC often poses challenges in accurately characterizing schwannomas, and some authors have found it to be of limited assistance in the diagnostic process. In this particular case, the patient forwent MRI and FNAC before surgery. MRI, being the most sensitive and specific preoperative method, enables a more precise determination of the originating nerve. Our apprehension regarding FNAC stemmed from the potential risk of considerable hemorrhaging associated with the mass. In this particular instance, the use of surgical resection accompanied by microscopic tissue examination proved indispensable in establishing the diagnosis of schwannoma. Furthermore, the diagnosis was additionally supported by immunohistochemical findings, including positive results for S100, SOX10 (Figure 2), PGP9.5, and H3K27Me3, while displaying negative results for NF, SMA, p53, and CKpan and a Ki-67 proliferation index of 3%. In this case, the presence of S100 and SOX10 proteins was observed through immunohistochemistry, which serves as a valuable marker for Schwann cells.7Previous research has indicated that a majority of malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumors (MPNSTs) exhibit immunoreactivity for Ki-67 in 5% to 65% of tumor cell nuclei, while benign peripheral nerve sheath tumors display nuclear staining not exceeding 5%.8Furthermore, a sizable proportion of MPNSTs demonstrate nuclear staining for p53 ranging from 5% to 100%, whereas no benign peripheral nerve sheath tumors exhibit nuclear staining exceeding 1%.8In this case, the p53 antigen exhibited a negative result, while the Ki-67 proliferation index was determined to be 3% through the application of immunohistochemistry. These assessments were conducted to exclude the possibility of a MPNST.

caption: Image from flexible fiber-optic nasolaryngoscopy (A). Histopathologic image with hematoxylin-eosin stain (B).
scenario: A male in his 60s presented with a hoarse and weak voice. He has a history of follicular lymphoma with multiple relapses treated with an allogeneic stem cell transplant complicated by graft-vs-host disease and was treated with sirolimus and steroids. Flexible fiber-optic nasolaryngoscopy demonstrated symmetric nodular projections with edema along the whole length of both true vocal folds (Figure 1A). The patient underwent microdirect laryngoscopy and biopsy of the vocal fold lesions. The histopathologic image is shown inFigure 1B.
explanation: Rhabdomyoma is a rare skeletal or cardiac muscle benign tumor and the first rhabdomyoma was reported in 1864 by Zenker.1Cardiac origin is more common and typically occurs in young children with tuberous sclerosis complex. Extracardiac rhabdomyoma is rare and is subdivided into 3 types based on histology: adult rhabdomyoma (ARM), fetal rhabdomyoma (FRM), and genital types. The ARM and FRM have a predilection for the head and neck region of elderly and pediatric individuals, respectively. The genital type affects the genital tract, more common in adult female individuals.2Among the extracardiac rhabdomyoma subtypes, the ARM is the most common.3ARM represents less than 2% of all muscle tumors and is mostly reported in elderly men.4In contrast, FRM affects young male children and is rare with only a small number of cases reported in the literature.5FRM in adults is exceedingly rare with less than 30 cases reported to date and to our knowledge.5 The pathogenesis of cardiac rhabdomyoma in children with tuberous sclerosis involves variants in theTSC1andTSC2genes, affecting downstream mammalian target of rapamycin signaling pathway.6The pathogenesis of extracardiac rhabdomyoma is largely unknown. Rhabdomyoma typically presents as a solitary mass with symptoms related to the mass effect. Patients with extracardiac rhabdomyoma in the head and neck may present with hoarseness, dysphagia, or dyspnea. Extracardiac rhabdomyomas are histologically classified based on the degree of tumor cell differentiation. ARM is composed of large polygonal or round cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm and small round nuclei with prominent nucleoli. FRM shows bland, elongated spindle cells in abundant myxoid matrix and immature skeletal muscle fibers.3Immunohistochemical studies showed expression of muscle-specific actin, desmin, myogenin (scattered), and PAX7 (rare scattered). Although no malignant transformation has been documented, embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma has to be considered as a differential diagnosis. Of the 2 possibilities, FRM may be confused for an embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma in limited biopsies. Features that may favor FRM over rhabdomyosarcoma include (1) superficial location, (2) circumscription and lack of infiltrative margins, (3) lack of cellular atypia, (4) absence of cambium layer, and (5) paucity of mitotic figures.7Additionally, the histological feature may resemble other lesions such as granular cell tumor, hibernoma, oncocytoma, paraganglioma, and immunohistochemical staining is required for diagnosis.8One case report showed an erroneous diagnosis of squamous cell carcinoma with microinvasion due to the severe degree of pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia with inflammatory reaction, resulting in a total laryngectomy for a localized laryngeal rhabdomyoma.9 Treatment consists of surgical resection, with the most common type of resection being limited to local endoscopic excision.8Extralaryngeal extension requiring open hemilaryngectomy has also been reported.8Sirolimus, a mammalian target of rapamycin inhibitor, has been reported to be effective in treating cardiac rhabdomyomas associated with tuberous sclerosis and is well tolerated.10The present patient started taking sirolimus for graft-vs-host disease 10 weeks before the biopsy. During the biopsy, there was improvement in the vocal fold lesions, and a limited biopsy was performed. During follow-up after the biopsy, there were no lesions seen on the vocal folds (Figure 2). This raises the question of whether sirolimus plays a beneficial role in the treatment of rhabdomyoma, regardless of subtype. If sirolimus proves to be effective, there are several potential avenues for its application. First, it can be considered an adjunctive treatment in large tumors with extralaryngeal extension. This will potentially avoid serious complications from major surgical excision. Additionally, as rhabdomyoma is a benign tumor with no malignant potential, sirolimus could be considered as an alternative treatment option in patients who are averse to surgery. More studies into the role of sirolimus in rhabdomyoma treatment will be beneficial in expanding treatment options.

caption: Axial noncontrast computed tomography scan of the neck.
scenario: A 58-year-old woman presented with a several-week history of a painless right-sided swelling on her anterior neck. She denied trauma, recent illnesses, respiratory symptoms, dysphagia, oral lesions, hemoptysis, fever, fatigue, weight loss, and night sweats. She had an unremarkable medical history without history of hypothyroidism or hyperthyroidism, cancer, chemotherapy, radiation, or tuberculosis. She denied alcohol, tobacco, or current medication use. Her family history included a sibling with sarcoma in their 50s. On examination, a 4.0-cm mobile, nontender right lower anterior neck mass was palpated in a suprasternal location. No lymphadenopathy was noted. Laboratory results showed normal serum calcium levels and leukocyte counts. Initial ultrasonography showed a 4.2-cm solid nodule adjacent to the lower pole of the right thyroid. Computed tomography results of the neck showed a 3.4-cm circumscribed, heterogenous, hypodense, enhancing mass that was abutting the inferior right thyroid and at the right lateral margin of the trachea. The mass was just medial to the right common carotid, causing left lateral displacement of the trachea (Figure 1). Fine-needle aspiration demonstrated many small round lymphocytes and a few groups of short bland spindle cells on hematoxylin-eosin staining. Immunohistochemical staining showed AE1/AE3–positive spindle cells and CD1a-, CD3-, terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (TdT)–positive lymphocytes. The excised mass was a 4.8 × 4.0 × 3.2 cm yellow-tan, lobulated nodule with a smooth, firm cut surface, thin fibrous strands, and no hemorrhage, degeneration, or transcapsular invasion.
explanation: Thymomas originate from thymic epithelial cells; therefore, most occur in the anterior mediastinum. However, 4% of all thymoma cases occur ectopically outside of the mediastinum. This extramediastinal location is explained by the embryological descent of the thymus, which arises in the neck during fetal development and descends along the cervical pathway to the mediastinum.1Remnant thymic tissue along this path, commonly adjacent to the thyroid gland, has the potential for epithelial hyperplasia and development of thymoma. Middle-aged individuals are most affected by thymomas; however, ectopic thymomas are more common in prepubertal populations due to thymic involution.2 Contrast-enhanced computed tomography is a frequent first diagnostic study of choice.3It provides insight into thymoma location, size, shape, and potential invasion into surrounding structures.4For lesions abutting other mediastinal structures or irregular appearing lesions, magnetic resonance imaging can help to assist with preoperative planning. Diagnosis of a thymoma requires tissue confirmation either from definitive resection specimens or core needle biopsy. The World Health Organization histologic classification system aids in determining the potential behavior pattern of the tumor based on the degree of epithelial cellular atypia, as well as lymphocyte infiltration. The lymphocytic component consists of immature T cells, which are derived predominantly from the thymic cortex and can be targeted by CD3, CD1a, CD99, and TdT antibodies. However, these markers can also be present in T lymphoblastic lymphoma.5Therefore, pancytokeratin (AE1/AE3), which stains the interconnected network of thymic epithelial cells but not T cells, is used to help distinguish thymomas from lymphoblastic lymphoma (Figure 2).2,5The presence of B symptoms, which often accompany lymphoma, can also help distinguish thymoma, which usually has compressive symptoms alone.2 The grading of thymomas is disputed; however, historically, the Masaoka-Koga and more recently the TNM staging systems are used.3,6The stages differ slightly between systems, but because metastatic spread to lymph nodes and other tissues is rare, both systems focus on the local invasive component of thymomas rather than tumor size or nodal involvement.6In early-stage disease, the thymoma is well encapsulated, without invasion into the gland itself, while advancing stages demonstrate greater degrees of invasion beyond the capsule, up to and including direct invasion of adjacent mediastinal structures (aorta, superior vena cava, lung, pericardium).6Additionally, all patients should be screened for the presence of myasthenia gravis, which is associated with approximately a third of thymoma cases. Although not directly a prognostic factor for survival, the presence of myasthenia gravis can potentially alter the conduct of the planned surgical intervention. Preoperative assessment includes review by anesthesia clinicians with respect to possible perioperative respiratory failure and the selective use of neuromuscular blockade.7,8 Although thymomas may have an indolent course, they have malignant potential due to local invasion and the ability to metastasize.2Thus, treatment for thymomas, regardless of size or invasion, should include surgical resection. Resection of the entire thymus and surrounding tissue is typically done to achieve the best prognostic outcome. This can include en-bloc resection and reconstruction of large surrounding vessels and the sacrifice of nerves, such as the phrenic nerve.7In more advanced stages, multimodal approaches to therapy, including induction chemotherapy, adjuvant chemotherapy, and/or postoperative radiotherapy, may be required.3 Following treatment, the slow growth pattern necessitates extended imaging surveillance. The World Health Organization thymoma type is also an independent prognostic marker of recurrence-free survival but not overall survival.9Current guidelines recommend a computed tomography scan every 6 months for the first 2 years followed by annual imaging for 10 years.4,10The biannual screening timeline may be extended to 3 years in cases of advanced thymomas or if complete resection was not achieved.10

caption: A, Magnetic resonance imaging (T2-weighted) shows a hypervascular tumor over left nasal cavity with obstructive rhinosinusitis at frontal and ethmoid sinuses. B, Gross examination reveals a 4.8 × 3.0 × 1.8-cm whitish to pink-tan tumor.
scenario: A 65-year-old man presented to an outpatient department with a 2-year history of left nasal obstruction. He had a history of hypertension and was taking oral medication (amlodipine [5 mg]/valsartan [80 mg] and indapamide [1.5 mg] once daily) but had poorly controlled systolic blood pressure ranging from 130 to 160 mm Hg. No associated trauma or surgical history was reported. Physical examination revealed a large tumor originating from the olfactory groove in the left nasal cavity, with feeding vessels pushing the middle turbinate outward. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a well-defined and strongly enhancing mass in the left nasal cavity, with obstructive rhinosinusitis in the frontal and ethmoid sinuses (Figure 1A). During surgical exploration, the tumor abutted the superior end of the nasal septum near the cribriform plate. Tumor excision was completed with a surgical margin of at least 5 mm, with the perichondrium of the nasal septum as the deep margin. The feeding vessels of the tumors were cauterized during the resection. Gross examination revealed a 4.8 × 3.0 × 1.8-cm whitish to pink-tan mass lesion (Figure 1B). Histopathological examination revealed sheetlike proliferation of monomorphic ovoid to spindle tumor cells containing ectatic vascular spaces. In addition, immunohistochemical staining showed positive staining for smooth-muscle actin, cyclin D1, and nuclear expression of β-catenin and negative staining for epithelial membrane antigen, cytokeratin, and CD34.
explanation: Sinonasal glomangiopericytoma (GPC) is a relatively rare mesenchymal neoplasm located in the nasal cavity and paranasal sinuses.1,2It was first described by Stout and Murray in 1924 and was initially categorized as a hemangiopericytomalike neoplasm with perivascular myoid differentiation with a relatively benign clinical course.3,4It was described as an indolent tumor with low malignancy potential and accounts for less than 0.5% of all sinonasal tumors.5,6There is a slight female predominance reported and it commonly occurs in patients in the sixth and seventh decades of age.2,4The common clinical manifestations include nasal obstruction and epistaxis.2,6GPC is usually large in size when diagnosed due to its indolent characteristic and nonspecific presentations. Grossly, GPC is submucosal in nature with a smooth surface and polypoid appearance and is sometimes difficult to differentiate from inflammatory polyps under endoscopy, leading to a challenging early diagnosis.4However, inflammatory nasal polyps usually present as bilateral nasal disease and seldom contain feeding vessels. For this patient, diagnosis was made through pathologic examination, which revealed a diffuse, subepithelial proliferation of bland, uniform, closely packed spindled cells surrounding capillaries with perivascular hyalinization (Figure 2); thus, it was previously categorized as a hemangiopericytoma.7A positive immunohistochemical stain for smooth-muscle actin, cyclin D1, and nuclear expression of β-catenin can confirm the diagnosis of GPC. Grossly, both GPC and lobular capillary hemangiomas are polypoid submucosal lesions with smooth surfaces.7However, it is still difficult to distinguish between these lesions because they usually present with a solid and soft texture. Histologically, lobular capillary hemangioma reveals lobular vascular proliferation consisting of vessels of capillary caliber.8On the other hand, inverted papilloma is mucosal origin with cerebriform, lobulated, and firm appearance.6,9In contrast to GPC, inverted papilloma shows male predominance with a 2 to 3:1 male:female ratio and usually arises from maxillary sinus and lateral nasal wall.9In histology, inverted papilloma exhibits squamous epithelial cells within the sinonasal tract, a distinguishing histological feature that sets it apart from GPC.10Solitary fibrous tumors resemble GPC under microscopic histology, but in contrast to GPC, solitary fibrous tumors are immunoreactive for CD34. The etiology of GPC is still unknown, but hypervascularity caused by hypertension, trauma, pregnancy, and the use of corticosteroids have been reported as possible causes.6,7We presumed that long-term hypertension without adequate control might be the possible etiology in this patient. Complete surgical resection with adequate margins remains the primary management strategy in patients with GPC. Recurrences were infrequently documented, with the majority of such instances attributed to incomplete resection; notably, these recurrences manifested predominantly within 1 year after surgery.4Further, owing to the bleeding tendency, preoperative angiographic embolization of GPC feeding vessels has been suggested to reduce bleeding volume during surgical resection.1,4Radiotherapy was reported to be used in conjunction with surgery for local control of the disease.4Chemotherapy was additionally administered to patients presenting with metastatic disease, wherein the metastatic incidence was documented to range from 5% to 10%. It is noteworthy that this observation predates the formal classification of GPC as a distinct clinical entity in 2005, thus potentially introducing a risk of diagnostic misclassification.6Because of its rarity, no formal guidelines have been published for sinonasal GPC, to our knowledge. Sinonasal GPC is a rare mesenchymal neoplasm of the sinonasal tract. It is typically indolent and has low malignant potential, with nasal obstruction and epistaxis being the most common clinical manifestations. The diagnosis is made through histology and immunohistochemical staining, and complete surgical resection with adequate margins remains the standard management. The patient was regularly followed up at our outpatient department after surgery, and there was no tumor recurrence or decreased olfaction during the 3-year follow-up period.

caption: Enlarged left level Vb lymph nodes demonstrating central hypodensity in both coronal (A) and axial (B) computed tomography images.
scenario: An 11-year-old boy with a medical history of allergic rhinitis presented to the emergency department of a children’s hospital with 2 weeks of painful left-sided neck swelling and fever. He had accompanying night sweats, fatigue, and decreased appetite. Initial physical examination revealed multiple distinct matted, firm left-sided cervical lymph nodes. Laboratory evaluation was notable for leukopenia with a white blood cell count of 3700/µL (to convert to 109/L, multiply by 0.001), a microcytic anemia with a hemoglobin of 10.7 g/dL (to convert to g/L, multiply by 10), mean corpuscular volume of 58 µm3(to convert to fL, multiply by 1), an elevated lactate dehydrogenase level of 548 U/L (to convert to µkat/L, multiply by 0.0167), and an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 35 mm/h. Purified protein derivative and infectious mononucleosis testing were negative. A contrast-enhanced neck computed tomography (CT) scan revealed multiple lymph nodes with areas of central hypodensity, and a conglomerate of heterogeneous lymph nodes in the left supraclavicular region (level 5B), measuring approximately 3.7 × 1.4 × 3.6 cm (Figure). The otolaryngology service was consulted, and a left level Va and Vb selective neck dissection was performed. Pathologic evaluation of the lymph nodes showed patchy areas of necrosis with an absence of neutrophils and predominantly paracortical apoptotic lesions composed of immature CD123+dendritic cells, histiocytes, and karyorrhectic debris. There was an absence of hematoxylin bodies. Flow cytometry showed a mixture of T-cell predominant lymphocytes (CD4 to CD8 ratio, 1:1) with no abnormal lymphoid population. Results of tissue studies for Epstein Barr virus, fungi, and acid-fast organisms were negative.
explanation: Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease (KFD), also known as Kikuchi disease and Kikuchi histiocytic necrotizing lymphadenitis, is a rare and benign condition of unknown cause characterized by fever and cervical lymphadenopathy. KFD was initially described among Asian populations in the 1970s; however, it can occur in an individual of any racial and/or ethnic group. KFD occurs at a rate of nearly 1:1 among female and male adults, although it may affect boys more frequently than girls.1It can also affect patients of all ages; in the US, the mean age of patients with KFD is 30 years.2KFD is uncommon and can present with varying symptoms, making it challenging for clinicians to diagnose. The clinical presentation and laboratory findings in patients with KFD are nonspecific and must be differentiated from infectious, autoimmune, and malignant causes of lymphadenitis. Classically, patients with KFD present with fever and localized tender lymphadenopathy, and usually cervical and posterior cervical disease, although bilateral cervical adenopathy as well as extracervical disease have been reported.2 The presence of tender lymphadenopathy distinguishes KFD from nontuberculous mycobacterial lymphadenitis and Rosai-Dorfman-Destombes disease (RDD), both of which present with painless nodes.3,4Additionally, most cases of nontuberculous mycobacterial lymphadenitis occur in children younger than 5 years old, making this diagnosis more unlikely.4Although many patients with KFD have a normal complete blood count, leukopenia has been reported in up to 43% of cases.5Other possible findings include chronic anemia, thrombocytopenia or pancytopenia, elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, abnormal liver function tests, and elevated serum lactate dehydrogenase levels.5 Both ultrasonography and computed tomography imaging can be useful in the diagnostic evaluation of patients with suspected KFD before operative management, and typically reveal multiple enlarged lymph nodes. Nodal enlargement in KFD ranges from 0.5 to 3.5 cm in diameter, typically smaller than those in RDD and lymphomas.6Areas of central hypodensity suggestive of necrosis are present in 16% of KFD cases, and perinodal infiltration is common,2further distinguishing it from RDD. While imaging patterns can support diagnosis of KFD, evaluation of an excisional biopsy specimen is required for definitive diagnosis. Histologic characteristics of KFD include paracortical areas of necrosis with abundant karyorrhectic debris and surrounding histiocytes and plasmacytoid dendritic cells.
