Her symptoms persisted despite treatment with penicillin, azithromycin, and steroids from her primary physician and amoxicillin-clavulanate, sinus rinses, fluticasone propionate, and azelastine spray from an otolaryngologist to treat any contributing postnasal drainage and tonsillitis. Flexible transnasal videolaryngoscopy revealed a lesion on the laryngeal surface of the right epiglottis passing midline extending to the right aryepiglottic fold, but not involving the true vocal cords (Figure 1A). Given inconclusive office biopsy results, direct laryngoscopy with biopsy was performed, showing extensively inflamed squamous mucosa with ulceration, granulation tissue, pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia, and atypia (Figure 1B).
explanation: Biopsy results with Grocott methenamine silver and periodic acid–Schiff stains highlighted fungal elements with features ofCoccidioidesspecies, specifically endospores within a spherule and background inflammation. The patient was then referred to an infectious disease specialist for further workup and management of her newly diagnosed coccidioidomycosis as well as for evaluation of potential disseminated disease. Chest radiography showed no evidence of disease, but theCoccidioidescomplement fixation (CF) returned strongly positive at 1:512, indicating disseminated disease. However, the patient did not exhibit any signs of disseminated disease, denying skin lesions, joint pains, headache, neck stiffness, visual or auditory symptoms, or cranial nerve weakness, and her bone scan did not show any evidence of bony dissemination. She was started on 400 mg of fluconazole, which was then decreased to 200 mg after 4 months when her CF was 1:8, with the plan of discontinuation when her CF was less than 1:2. Repeated office laryngoscopy after 8 months of therapy revealed interval improvement of epiglottic lesions, with normal-appearing laryngoscopy (Figure 2). This patient’s presentation and clinical imaging support a few differential diagnoses. Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) of the larynx is the most pressing diagnosis, as early-stage disease is highly curable with rates ranging from 80% to 95%.1Furthermore, the patient presented with odynophagia, referred otalgia, and cervical lymphadenopathy, all of which can be presenting signs and symptoms of SCC. However, this patient did not have the typical risk factors for SCC, such as advanced age, human papillomavirus (HPV) infection, or a history of tobacco use, making this an unlikely diagnosis. The differential diagnosis for an ulcerative, papillomatous laryngeal lesion should also include laryngeal tuberculosis (TB). Although the incidence of laryngeal TB has decreased substantially in the postantibiotic era, it is now often diagnosed when attempting to rule out laryngeal carcinoma. Primary laryngeal TB without pulmonary involvement is rare but must be considered in patients who present with hoarseness, dysphagia, and odynophagia. The patient’s travel history is particularly important in determining risk of exposure. The current patient had a travel history to Pakistan, which is within the top 10 countries with the highest TB burden.2However, the incidence of laryngeal TB is less than 1% of all TB cases, making it a less likely diagnosis.3 Recurrent respiratory papillomatosis (RRP) has a bimodal distribution, affecting children younger than 20 years and adults in the third and fourth decades of life.4Both the pediatric and adult forms of RRP are most commonly attributable to infection with HPV-6 and HPV-11, resulting in papillomatous lesions anywhere in the aerodigestive tract, most commonly the larynx.4Adult RRP most commonly presents with nonspecific symptoms of airway involvement, especially hoarseness. Papillomatous lesions localized to the larynx, trachea, and/or bronchi are commonly seen on laryngoscopy.4While the patient had papillomatous lesions on her larynx, she had no history of HPV infection, making this diagnosis less likely. Recurrent respiratory papillomatosis should remain in the differential diagnosis for any papillomatous lesion because of the risk of airway compromise with disease progression. Clinicians must consider coccidioidomycosis or other fungal infection in addition to malignant neoplasm, particularly in young healthy patient populations to ensure timely diagnosis and treatment, because approximately 50% of patients with laryngeal coccidioidomycosis require immediate airway intervention.5The current guidelines from the Infectious Diseases Society of America recommend that patients with extrapulmonary soft tissue coccidioidomycosis not associated with bone infection begin antifungal therapy. Oral azoles, especially fluconazole and itraconazole, are the recommended first-line therapy, with intravenous amphotericin B used if the azoles fail.6

caption: A, Fite acid-fast stain of cutaneous lesion identifying pink bacilli (original magnification ×100). B, Hematoxylin-eosin stain of the same cutaneous lesion showing poorly formed granulomas (original magnification ×40).
scenario: A 66-year-old African American man presented to the otolaryngology clinic with a several-month history of severe nasal congestion. Five years before this otolaryngology evaluation, the patient developed diffuse skin plaques with erythema and was subsequently diagnosed with hypopigmented cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (CTCL, mycosis fungoides type). The patient was treated with a regimen of narrowband UV-B phototherapy and triamcinolone cream, which he has continued for 4 years. Owing to significant worsening of his symptoms 4 months before his evaluation, a biopsy of his cutaneous lesions was performed to rule out progression of CTCL (Figure 1). Physical examination demonstrated large annular plaques with peripheral hyperpigmentation of the body. There were also confluent, indurated pink plaques with slightly raised edges along the forehead, malar eminence, and scalp. The nasal septum demonstrated an invertedVdeformity with compromise of the keystone junction. Nasal passages were obstructed with thick mucus and synechiae formation, nearly obstructing the entire nasal passage bilaterally.
explanation: Leprosy, also known as Hansen disease, constitutes a bacterial infection by eitherMycobacterium lepraeorM lepromatosis.The bacterium is an acid-fast bacillus that is typically slow growing, with a predilection for growth within macrophages, endothelial cells, and Schwann cells. Humans are primary carriers of the bacterium; however, 9-banded armadillos are a well-known reservoir ofM lepraewithin North and South America. Individuals at risk of contracting the disease include those with close contact with an infected individual, exposure to armadillos, and immunosuppression or immunodeficiencies. TheHLA-DQ1gene has been implicated in persons more likely to develop the lepromatous form.1 Leprosy was considered eradicated by the World Health Organization (WHO) in 2000 by the definition that confirmed that cases fell below the prevalence rate of 1 infection per 10 000 individuals; however, there continues to be approximately 200 000 cases per year worldwide, with approximately 80% of these cases occurring in India, Brazil, and Indonesia.1-3 BecauseM lepraehas a predilection for cooler regions in the range of 27 °C to 30 °C, the nasal mucosa and skin are ideal sites for reproduction. In fact, a high bacterial burden has been found in the nasal mucosa, and the most important mode of transmission is via respiratory droplets.2,4There are 6 clinical manifestations of leprosy, popularly classified by the Ridley-Jopling clinical classification system. The system includes 2 ends of a spectrum determined by immunologic status with lepromatous leprosy (LL) on one end with least immunity and tuberculoid leprosy (TL) on the other with strong immunity. Borderline TL, borderline LL, midborderline, and indeterminate disease types constitute varying mixtures of both poles.5In general, TL tends to have a robust immune response with a few well-defined, anesthetic skin lesions, whereas LL has a poor immune response and presents with numerous lesions that can affect other organ systems. Lesions within the nasal mucosa are some of the first to appear during leprosy, before any skin manifestations.6Barton7in 1974 studied 77 individuals with leprosy of whom 94% had complained of an initial nasal symptom with 66% of them specifically complaining of nasal obstruction, the latter being the formation of granulomatous lesions within the nasal cavity. As the disease progresses, further mucosal invasion occurs with the presence of ulcerations, epistaxis, and septal perforations. Finally, in the later stages, neuronal invasion occurs leading to anesthesia, increasing the risk of saddle-nose deformity and atrophic rhinitis.2,6 The treatment for leprosy, determined by WHO, is based on the clinical classification. Twelve months of rifampicin, dapsone, and clofazimine is prescribed when treating LL, whereas rifampicin and dapsone are used over a 6-month duration for TL. Owing to the possibility of severe adverse effects, challenges in obtaining clofazimine, and intolerance of these medications, an alternative regimen has been described using ofloxacin, minocycline, and clarithromycin.1,2Reconstructive surgery is typically delayed until the infection has quiesced, as in this patient. Although rare within the US, leprosy remains an infectious disease with significant morbidity if left untreated. Regarding the field of otolaryngology, it is imperative that patients presenting with nasal obstruction, recurrent epistaxis, rhinitis, and/or saddle-nose deformity have a proper workup to evaluate for the cause. Nasal symptoms are among the first to appear in a patient with leprosy; therefore, swift responsiveness and initiation of treatment may save the patient from more significant complications. Dyspigmented plaques with cutaneous dysesthesia, a positive Fite stain, and characteristic deformities, such as saddle-nose deformity and leonine facies (Figure 2), directed us toward Hansen disease as the most likely diagnosis.

caption: Contrast-enhanced computed tomography images. A, Axial: the blue arrowhead indicates extension into the tongue musculature, the yellow arrowhead indicates focally thickened capsule posteriorly, and the white arrowhead indicates a displaced sternocleidomastoid muscle. B, Coronal: the black arrowhead indicates an elevated left submandibular gland, and the white arrowhead indicates a normal right submandibular gland. C, Axial T2-weighted magnetic resonance image showing marked interval enlargement of the multiseptated cystic mass. Arrowheads indicate involvement of the tongue musculature.
scenario: A 2-month-old, full-term female presented with a left upper neck mass that was first noted at birth. Her parents reported no fevers, constitutional symptoms, or enlargement of the mass. On physical examination, there was a nontender 4-cm mass in the left submandibular region with no overlying skin changes. Ultrasonography results showed an avascular cystic structure with internal debris and a single thin septation. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) of the neck soft tissue revealed a 3-cm low attenuation, nonenhancing, cystic-appearing mass that elevated the submandibular gland to the level of the parapharyngeal fat space with medial extension of the lesion into the tongue musculature. The walls were thin except for mildly thickened capsule along the posterior aspect of the lesion (Figure, A and B). Fluid that aspirated from the cyst was serous, and cytology showed mature and anucleate squamous cells with acute inflammation. The mass returned after 3 weeks. Further analysis 8 months after the initial CT via contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed a large, multiseptated cystic structure (Figure, C); the capsule of the wall was mildly thickened and was contrast enhancing. At age 12 months, the mass was excised via neck dissection. A lateral component at the level of the sternocleidomastoid muscle was completely excised. An intraoperative rupture of the thin capsule caused some spillage of cystic contents that were milky white in some areas and mucinous in others.
explanation: Foregut duplication cysts are uncommon floor of the mouth masses that result from remnant embryological foregut structures. They often present as neck masses in otherwise healthy neonates and raise concern for swallowing difficulties and airway obstruction.1-3By definition, the cysts must have a smooth muscle layer, contain foregut-derived epithelium, and attach to a portion of the foregut.2-4Histologically, they contain multiple types of epithelium, including squamous, gastric, respiratory, and cuboidal.4Only 0.3% of foregut duplication cysts appear in the head and neck, and 60% of these cases involve the oral cavity.4Treatment includes observation, aspiration, and resection; recurrence is rare after complete resection of the mucosal lining.2-4 Preoperative imaging is recommended for suspected foregut duplication cysts and can aid in diagnosis.2Generally, the cysts are well-circumscribed and nonseptated, although occasional septations are possible, as seen in this patient.5Ultrasonography reveals a double-wall sign with an inner hyperechoic mucosa-submucosa layer and an outer hypoechoic, muscularis propria layer. Computed tomography shows a uniform cystic lesion with occasional septations and fluid-debris levels. On T2-weighted MRI, the cysts have uniformly high signals, whereas T1-weighted MRI shows variable intensity because of protein contents.3,5 Branchial cleft cysts constitute approximately 20% of all excised pediatric cervical masses, following the failure of pharyngobranchial ducts to entirely obliterate during fetal development.6They present as tender, inflammatory masses along the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle much later in childhood than foregut duplication cysts.6,7Younger patients may present with fistulas between the cyst and external surface of the neck. On imaging, branchial cleft cysts are well-defined, thin-walled, and anechoic. Imaging with T2-weighted MRI shows a hyperintense cyst without wall enhancement. A pathognomonic finding on imaging is an extension of the cyst between the internal and external carotid arteries (beak sign), which was not seen in this patient.6Treatment is surgical excision.1 A ranula is a mucocele or pseudocyst that occurs because of ductal obstruction of the sublingual gland. Plunging ranulas invade the submandibular space through a mylohyoid defect.6,7They present as slow-growing, painless, submental masses; however, they rarely present before the second decade.6,7On ultrasonography, plunging ranulas appear anechoic and lobulated. Computed tomography shows unilocular, thin-walled cystic lesions. Similarly, T2-weighted MRI shows thin-walled cystic structures with high signals that are often accompanied by hyperintense tail-like extensions of the ranula from the submandibular into the sublingual space.6The association of the described lesion with the submandibular gland raised suspicion for a ranula; however, the presence of multiple septations proved inconsistent with this diagnosis. Treatment involves excision of the sublingual gland, as the ranula itself is nonsecreting.7 Lymphatic malformations of the submandibular space arise from connection failures of the lymphatic system. They present at birth or before age 2 years as soft, smooth, nontender, compressible masses.6,7The masses are further divided into macrocystic (>2 cm), microcystic (<2 cm), or mixed. Generally, imaging results reveal a multiloculated cyst with extension of the malformation into surrounding neurovascular structures. Ultrasonography shows intracystic debris with multiple septations. On CT, they appear as multicystic lesions of low attenuation. Contrast-enhanced MRI generally shows thin peripheral and septal enhancement.3While this patient did have a multiloculated cyst, the T1 single intensity, which was consistent with proteinaceous fluid, favored diagnosis of a foregut duplication cyst. After the patient’s surgery, pathology reports showed multiple cysts that were lined by squamous, ciliated bronchiolar-type, and flattened cuboidal epithelia that were associated with salivary and pancreatic glandular structures. Nodules containing pancreatic tissues with islets were present, which was consistent with a foregut duplication cyst. The mass was attached to the retromolar trigone mucosa, which also supported the diagnosis. Two months after surgery, the patient appeared well, with no evidence of mass recurrence or neck fullness.

scenario: A 32-year-old Black woman presented with a 1-year history of facial swelling, predominantly in the right preauricular and left submandibular regions. Her symptoms began after relocation to California and occurred more frequently at her home. However, she could not discern any environmental or dietary triggers. She reported pruritus and swelling, which were usually moderate but occasionally severe, prompting several emergency department visits. During an emergency department visit, she was diagnosed with acute parotitis based on clinical and radiographic findings of diffuse gland edema, without salivary stones or masses. Her symptoms responded to oral prednisone bursts and diphenhydramine, but not to second-generation antihistamines or montelukast. Her workup included immune serology and total immunoglobulin (Ig) E measurements, all of which were within normal limits. A differential blood cell count revealed 10% eosinophils (normal, <6%) and an absolute eosinophil count 500/µL (to convert to ×109/L, multiply by 0.001). Titers for antinuclear antibodies, rheumatoid factor, anti-Ro (SS-A), and anti-La (SS-B) were negative. Sialendoscopy of her right parotid and left submandibular glands found no obstructing stones or strictures. Concurrent steroid irrigation did not provide any substantial benefit. An open biopsy of the right parotid tail revealed nonspecific inflammatory changes and otherwise normal parenchyma. Given the frequency and severity of her symptoms along with multiple treatment failures, she opted to undergo a right superficial parotidectomy, which proceeded without complications. Further histologic examination of the surgical specimen revealed substantial periductal inflammatory infiltrate with eosinophils, as seen in theFigure.
explanation: Otolaryngologists routinely evaluate and treat patients with recurrent salivary gland swelling. A large portion of these patients will have chronic obstructive sialadenitis (COS), possibly with salivary calculi as a cause of salivary stasis and obstruction. Less common diagnoses include autoimmune disorders and nonspecific lymphocytic infiltration. Eosinophilic sialodochitis (ES) is a rare pathologic entity; however, it is not new. Reports of the condition date back to 1879 under the namessialoadenitis fibrosa,allergic parotitis, oreosinophilic sialodochitis.1 Patients with ES typically present with relapsing and remitting major salivary gland swelling with parotid and submandibular glands equally and often bilaterally affected.2Patients typically will present with pain and swelling of the affected gland, pruritus to the overlying skin, and stringlike mucous discharge from the salivary duct orifices. These symptoms overlap greatly with those of other types of COS. Recent studies have suggested that serum IgE and peripheral blood eosinophil levels are elevated in up to 91% of patients with ES,3suggesting an allergic pathogenesis. Eosinophilic sialodochitis has also recently been referred to asallergy-related sialodochitis.1It is important to note, however, that despite serologic findings that suggest a robust allergic response, only 62% to 66% of patients with this diagnosis may experience comorbid atopy,2,4such as allergic rhinitis or asthma (88%), atopic dermatitis or urticaria (41%), and drug or food allergies (29%).3Imaging performed during workup will typically show diffusely enlarged glands without identifiable calculi, as were seen in this patient. Diagnosis of ES is most strongly supported by histopathologic findings of dense eosinophil infiltration (50 ± 39/high-power field) around dilated main and interlobular ducts, mucous metaplasia, intraductal mucus plugs rich in eosinophils, and perifollicular hyperplasia.3Sialograms for patients with ES show “snowflake” or flocculent changes of branch ducts accompanied by irregular stenosis and ectasia of the main duct believed to be secondary to mucous plugging.1 The other diagnoses suggested are less likely in this scenario. Given that there was no evidence of salivary calculi on radiographic imaging or sialendoscopy, sialolithiasis was effectively ruled out for this patient. Additionally, Sjogren syndrome was presumed to be unlikely given the negative serologic antibody findings and no other clinical findings aside from salivary gland swelling. Lastly, Mikulicz syndrome is an IgG-4–related disease that is characterized by swelling of submandibular, parotid, and lacrimal glands, with all 3 components required for diagnosis, and the patient did not report lacrimal gland swelling. The importance of differentiating ES from other forms of COS is particularly relevant to its treatment, although no standard options exist. Sialendoscopy has been shown to relieve recalcitrant symptoms in 80% to 90% of patients with COS.2,4Patients with ES may also benefit from treatment with antihistamines, antileukotrienes, and systemic glucocorticoids, with gland excision as a final option. Immunohistochemical studies on excised glandular tissue of patients with ES have shown infiltration of interleukin (IL)-4, IL-13, IL-5, and exotoxin-positive cells,3which are key cytokines in atopic disease; as such, biologic therapies may have a potential role in treatment. The current patient, for example, experienced a partial clinical response to benralizumab, an anti–IL-5 receptor antibody, after her diagnosis was made. To date, there are no agreed-upon diagnostic criteria for ES, and its clinical presentation can be nonspecific. We present a case of a 32-year-old woman with recalcitrant bilateral salivary gland swelling and pain, found to have ES on gland excision after exhausting other treatment options. Recurrent salivary swelling is a common complaint among otolaryngology patients, and ES—although rare—should be part of the differential diagnosis.

scenario: A White man in his 70s with a medical history notable only for mitral valve repair was incidentally found to have cervical lymphadenopathy on magnetic resonance imaging while undergoing workup for shoulder pain. A fine-needle biopsy of an enlarged left-sided cervical lymph node yielded benign results. One month later, he presented to a local emergency department with diffuse abdominal pain. Symptoms began 6 weeks earlier and had been intermittent in nature. He had also experienced fatigue, night sweats, decreased appetite, and weight loss for 6 weeks. He otherwise denied having fevers, myalgias, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, or easy bruising. Physical examination revealed bilateral cervical, axillary, and inguinal lymphadenopathy in addition to mild diffuse abdominal pain. Laboratory results revealed a hemoglobin level of 13.1 g/dL (to convert to g/L, multiply by 10), a white blood cell count of 6.4 × 103/μL, and a platelet count of 404 × 103/μL  (to convert to × 109/L, multiply by 1) in addition to negative results for HIV, hepatitis B virus, and hepatitis C assays. Additional workup results were notable for elevated levels of interleukin (IL) 10 (1091 pg/mL), IL-6 (3.1 pg/mL), C-reactive protein (4.9 mg/dL [to convert to mg/L, multiply by 10]), and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (79 mm/h). A computed tomography scan of the neck, chest, abdomen, and pelvis further revealed extensive cervical, supraclavicular, retroperitoneal, pelvic, and inguinal lymphadenopathy, with extensive inflammation and fat stranding adjacent to these enlarged nodes. Positron emission tomography–computed tomography further demonstrated fluorodeoxyglucose-avid lymph nodes above and below the diaphragm. The patient then underwent excisional biopsy of an enlarged right cervical lymph node (Figure).
explanation: A microscopic analysis of the biopsy revealed focal concentric mantle cell zone architecture (or onion-skin morphology;Figure). Further, the capsule was noted to be focally thickened, with the presence of vascular proliferation in addition to substantial intermedullary plasmacytosis. Immunohistochemical staining demonstrated human herpes virus–8 (HHV8) positivity in the spindle cells in areas of vascular proliferation (diagnostic of Kaposi sarcoma;Figure) and the round large lymphoid cells in the follicles (diagnostic of coexisting multicentric Castleman disease [MCD]).1A peripheral blood sample also demonstrated HHV8 positivity, and a diagnosis of MCD was made. There were no granulomas or necrosis seen, making granulomatous diseases, including tuberculosis and sarcoidosis, unlikely. Moreover, the preserved nodal architecture was not consistent with lymphoma. Castleman disease (CD) was first described in the mid-1950s and is currently regarded as a group of at least 4 disorders with a wide range of presentations and overlapping histopathologic patterns.2Multicentric CD represents a subcategory of CD that involves lymphadenopathy across multiple lymph node stations in which a morphological triad has been described that comprises (1) diffuse marked plasmacytosis, (2) prominent germinal centers that often have hyaline vascular changes, and (3) preserved nodal architecture.3In particular, HHV8-associated MCD (HHV8-MCD) comprises most MCD cases.1Its pathogenesis is associated with uncontrolled HHV8 infection and thought to involve viral infection of B cells and plasmablasts with dysregulation of cytokines and a resultant increase in IL-6 that then is followed by the symptoms, signs, and lymph node pathology associated with this condition.4Human herpes virus 8 MCD is most commonly seen in HIV-positive patients, although HHV8-MCD has also been reported in HIV-negative patients.3Human herpes virus 8 MCD tends to present during the seventh decade of life in HIV-negative patients (as opposed to the fifth decade in HIV-positive patients), and includes systemic signs and symptoms, including fevers, night sweats, fatigue, hepatosplenomegaly, and liver and kidney dysfunction.2Diagnosis is established by testing for HHV8 in the biopsied lymph node tissue or circulation in a patient with multicentric lymphadenopathy with the previously noted CD histopathological features.2Notably, HHV8-MCD not only confers an elevated risk of Kaposi sarcoma (in up to 50% of cases) but also large B-cell and primary effusion lymphomas (about 15%).1 Unlike unicentric CD, which involves lymphadenopathy in a single nodal station and for which complete surgical excision is usually curative, MCD has a poorer prognosis and requires systemic treatment.1The mainstay of systemic therapy for HHV8-MCD involves rituximab-based (an anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody) approaches, which have improved overall survival for this patient population from 33% to 90%, with many achieving clinical remission.2Although most of the case series have examined HHV8-MCD in HIV-positive patients,5rituximab-based therapies with or without treatment with etoposide have also demonstrated success in HIV-negative patients.2,6,7While to our knowledge there are currently no consensus guidelines on HHV8-MCD treatment in HIV-negative patients, many experts recommend an individualized approach and treatment based on duration of symptoms and trends in the relevant inflammatory markers. This patient ultimately received a diagnosis of HHV8-MCD and was connected with a hematology-oncology specialist for further treatment. Rituximab-based therapy was offered as a treatment option in addition to referral to the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Disease for further assessment. This case illustrates the importance of maintaining a broad differential diagnosis, including Castleman disease, in the workup of cervical lymphadenopathy in elderly patients. In particular, cervical lymphadenopathy is a common presenting problem for which referrals are commonly made to otolaryngologists for further evaluation and possible surgical excision. It also underscores the importance of prompt referral to a hematology-oncology expert given the potentially treatable nature of this disease, in addition to the elevated risk for secondary cancer.

scenario: A 53-year-old woman presented to the emergency department after awakening with right preauricular and right upper neck swelling. She had a history of coronary artery disease and prior myocardial infarction that was treated with warfarin. She denied any personal or family history of cancer. She was previously briefly a smoker. A physical examination revealed no erythema or tenderness of the parotid. Her cranial nerves were intact, specifically the right facial nerve and its branches. The oral mucosa was intact with no epithelial lesions. Urinalysis results revealed slight hematuria. Her international normalized ratio (INR) was 4.4. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) revealed an ill-defined infiltrative mass centered in the deep lobe of the right parotid with extension into surrounding soft tissue spaces (Figure, A). A follow-up CT was performed 6 weeks later (Figure, B).
explanation: Swelling of the parotid gland has a broad differential diagnosis, but enlargement from spontaneous bleeding is rare. Etiologies that frequently cause enlargement of the parotid region can be divided into either neoplasms or inflammation. In adult patients, a neoplastic process is generally more likely. Children and young adults have a propensity for infection or other inflammatory pathology.1Differentiating between benign and malignant parotid gland lesions with imaging can be challenging, as they are often visually indistinguishable. In the early stages of cancer, clinical features, such as pain, fixation, or paralysis, may be absent, especially in low-grade tumors.2When clinical symptoms do arise, a high-grade infiltrative lesion should be considered.2 The most common benign tumors of the parotid gland are pleomorphic adenoma and Warthin tumor.3Warthin tumor is known for having nonenhancing central regions, but this is not a specific finding. Pleomorphic adenomas have varied imaging appearances, as their name suggests. Both tumors display a low T1 signal and high T2 signal compared with the surrounding gland. Pleomorphic adenomas often have a rim of decreased signal intensity that represents their fibrous capsule.3,4Warthin tumor can be identified with Tc-99m pertechnetate scintigraphy; Warthin tumor and oncocytoma are the only salivary gland tumors known to concentrate pertechnetate.5 Mucoepidermoid carcinoma and adenoid cystic carcinoma are the most frequent parotid cancers.6The imaging appearance depends on the grade of the tumor, with low-grade cancers mimicking benign lesions. Magnetic resonance imaging results are nonspecific in early stages, as cancers can appear similar to benign neoplasms.7Aggressive cancers, such as salivary ductal carcinoma, have low T2 signal, and perineural spread is also a strong indicator of cancer.8 Primary parotid gland lymphoma should be considered in patients with preauricular enlargement. Multifocal disease is suggestive of lymphoma, but can also be seen with metastatic disease and Warthin tumors. Diffusion-weighted magnetic resonance imaging can be advantageous, as lymphomas classically restrict diffusion.9Ultimately, biopsy of parotid lesions is often necessary, as imaging alone is usually insufficient for a specific diagnosis. The therapeutic INR level for individuals taking warfarin ranges from 2 to 3.5 depending on the reason for administration.10A supratherapeutic INR, as was present in this patient, increases the risk of intracranial hemorrhage, gastrointestinal hemorrhage, hematuria, and bleeding from any other site.10The most likely mechanism for bleeding within the parotid region is trauma. This patient denied any antecedent trauma, but minor trauma is often overlooked by patients. It is possible that a strong Valsalva maneuver could lead to a vessel rupture with subsequent hematoma formation. With conservative treatment, the patient’s parotid swelling slowly resolved during the course of 6 weeks. Follow-up blood work results demonstrated an INR level of 2.5, and CT imaging showed complete resolution of the abnormality (Figure, B). Although hemorrhage in the setting of supratherapeutic anticoagulation most commonly affects the brain, genitourinary system, or gastrointestinal tract, it may occur in essentially any tissue. Primary hemorrhage of the parotid gland should be considered in patients with excessive anticoagulation and sudden-onset parotid swelling. Radiologic resolution with conservative management confirms the diagnosis.

caption: A, A neck CT scan showing an intrathyroidal mass causing tracheal compression and is in close proximity to the right common carotid artery and right internal jugular vein. B, A NIRAF image of the surgical field showing right thyroid lobe, a right parathyroid gland, and a homogenously dim capsulated lesion of interest.
scenario: An 18-year-old male presented to the primary care physician with a 4-month history of a slowly progressive painless lateral neck mass on the right side. The patient denied any history of dysphagia, dysphonia, drainage, previous neck surgery, trauma, or recent fever. There was no significant medical or family history of thyroid disease. On examination, the mass moved with swallowing. The patient had normal thyroid stimulating hormone and calcium levels and a parathyroid hormone (PTH) level of 63 pg/mL. Neck ultrasonography revealed a well-circumscribed anechoic lesion with a diameter of 5.9 cm in the right thyroid lobe without any internal solid nodularity or septation. A neck computed tomography (CT) scan revealed an intrathyroidal lesion extending inferiorly to 3 cm above the angle of Louis causing tracheal compression and displacement (Figure, A). The patient underwent right hemithyroidectomy to relieve tracheal compression. A near-infrared autofluorescence (NIRAF) camera yielded a homogenously dim lesion (Figure, B). Pathologic examination confirmed a normal right thyroid lobe, a normal right parathyroid gland, and a cystic lesion at the inferior pole with no evidence of malignant disease in the specimen. The tissue inside the lesion stained positive for PTH.
explanation: The positive PTH staining of tissues inside the cyst combined with the homogenously dim image yielded by the NIRAF camera are clues for the parathyroid cyst diagnosis. Benign thyroid nodules may be the first diagnosis that comes to mind in the differential diagnosis of a solitary neck mass given their high incidence compared with other possibilities. Thyroid nodules do not stain positive for PTH. In addition, imaging the thyroid with the autofluorescence camera, the thyroid nodules are more likely to look heterogeneous with both bright and dim spots, especially in multinodular goiter. The absence of recent fever or infection coupled with the 4-month history of the mass excludes most causes of reactive viral lymphadenopathy. Reactive lymphadenopathy typically lasts for up to 2 weeks. If caused by EBV, lymphadenopathy may persist for up to 6 weeks. Thyroglossal duct cysts are typically midline lesions occurring anywhere between the foramen cecum to the suprasternal notch, but most commonly are diagnosed at or just below the hyoid bone. They are frequently diagnosed during childhood in association with infection or a history of infection. However, physicians should not exclude thyroglossal duct cysts based by age alone because some patients may present for the first time during adulthood. The differential diagnosis of a neck mass is broad. Accurate diagnosis depends on anatomy (midline/lateral) and patient age (pediatric, young adult, or adult) among other factors. Most neck masses in children and young adults are inflammatory or congenital. There is a 5% to 10% chance of detecting malignant disease in adults, which increases with age, hence the need for comprehensive assessment of neck masses.1,2 The patient’s medical history, lack of fever, or systemic symptoms can help exclude inflammatory causes. The differential diagnosis of congenital causes includes laryngocele (often presents with cough, hoarseness, and globus sensation), ranula (a slowly growing mass arising in the floor of mouth owing to obstruction in the sublingual glands), and dermoid cyst (midline submental neck masses), in addition to thyroglossal duct cyst (discussed earlier) section.3None of these masses stain positive for PTH. Parathyroid cysts are a less common clinical finding with a similar presentation to that of a solitary thyroid nodule, representing a diagnostic challenge. A recent systematic review4of 359 published parathyroid cysts cases reported a mean age of 49.24 years with a mean (SD) diameter of 4.81 (2.88) cm. Nonfunctioning parathyroid cysts were more common than functioning (61.6%). Most common presenting symptoms included neck mass (41.7%) and compressive symptoms (20.6%). Parathyroid dysfunctions were reported in 17.5%. Pathologically, parathyroid cysts are lined by a single layer of cuboidal or low columnar epithelium.5Management of parathyroid cysts is usually observation. Surgery is recommended with compressive symptoms, as in this case. Other treatment options include sclerotherapy or ethanol injection.6,7 Intraoperatively, the cyst was visualized using a NIRAF camera, a near-infrared detection technology that has shown promise in differentiating parathyroid from thyroid tissues. Tissue fluorescence occurs when a substance is excited by the energy of shorter wavelength light and subsequently emits longer wavelength light.8Some tissues contain intrinsic fluorophores that exhibit a native fluorescence without a dye, a characteristic known as autofluorescence. Parathyroid autofluorescence offers a simple and sensitive method to interrogate tissue suspicious for parathyroid origin. TheFigureshows a bright parathyroid gland (panel B, inside the circle highlight) in contrast to the homogenously dim parathyroid cyst. Over the recent years, probe- and camera-based near-infrared imaging technology systems were tested to detect parathyroid autofluorescence without the need for contrast agents. This technology is a rapidly emerging topic of research with important implications to prevent incidental parathyroidectomy.9,10More research is ongoing to quantify autofluorescence in correlation with the underlying thyroid and parathyroid pathology. Parathyroid cysts may be misdiagnosed and are difficult to characterize during surgery. Yielding a homogenously dim intraoperative image of a cyst under a NIRAF camera coupled with PTH positive staining of intracystic fluid or tissues are indicative of parathyroid cyst.

caption: Preoperative audiogram reveals a right-sided low- to mid-frequency moderate conductive hearing loss and a bilateral high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss. dB denotes decibels; HTL, hearing threshold level; SL, sensation level; SRT, speech reception threshold; and TDH, telephonic dynamic headphones.
scenario: A 51-year-old woman presented with a 24-hour history of severe dizziness that she described as “room spinning,” right aural fullness, and a subjective right-sided hearing loss. She denied any medical history of vertigo, recent upper respiratory infection, head trauma, or prior otologic surgery. A physical examination revealed no abnormalities on otoscopic evaluation; however, a strongly positive right-sided Dix−Hallpike test was elicited with rotary nystagmus; a subsequent Epley maneuver was performed. The patient’s symptoms subjectively worsened during the following several days. Therefore, an audiogram test (Figure 1) and computed tomography (CT) of the temporal bone were performed.
explanation: The patient’s audiogram findings revealed a right-sided low- to mid-frequency moderate conductive hearing loss, as well as a bilateral high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss (Figure 1). Findings of the CT of the temporal bone were important for air within the vestibule and the semicircular canals, as well as in the basal turn of the cochlea, consistent with a pneumolabyrinth (Figure 2). All 4 of the possible diagnoses may be responsible for causing symptomatic dizziness. However, the presence of air in the bony labyrinth is specific for a pneumolabyrinth, and therefore, the remaining options would be incorrect. Pneumolabyrinth was first described in 1984 by Mafee and colleagues1who observed air in the vestibule and cochlea on postoperative imaging of a patient who had undergone a mastoidectomy for cholesteatoma for an iatrogenic stapes footplate fracture. Since then, multiple cases of pneumolabyrinth have been reported in the literature and most were associated with trauma with or without temporal bone fracture2,3or with a prior otologic surgery.4,5A systematic review published in 2021 by Botti and colleagues6reviewed 78 articles involving pneumolabyrinth, most cases of which were associated with temporal bone fracture (31.8%), stapes surgery (18.2%), head trauma without temporal bone fracture (14.4%), penetrating trauma (15.9%), and barotrauma (11.4%). This patient presented with a spontaneous idiopathic cause of pneumolabyrinth; she had no history of traumatic head injury nor any prior otologic surgery. Given the focus of the air bubbles around the oval window in the labyrinth, it was presumed that either a spontaneous tear or disruption of the annular ligament of the stapes was involved. We began a right middle ear exploration with tissue graft repair of the presumed spontaneous oval window fistula; however, the middle ear appeared normal, and palpation of the ossicular chain revealed normal mobility of all the ossicles. Mucosal flaps were elevated around the oval window, and a fat graft harvested from the postauricular subcutaneous tissue was placed medial to this in an attempt to repair the presumed oval window fistula. Given the rarity of the condition, most of the current data on pneumolabyrinth is from case reports and small case series, and there is no definitive treatment algorithm. Most cases are managed by either conservative approaches (eg, bed rest, steroids) or surgical repair of the presumed structural defect via an exploratory tympanotomy. Schied and colleagues recommend that patients with progressive hearing loss or vertigo be treated with middle ear exploration.7Conservative management failed in this patient, and after 1 week of persistently severe symptoms with audiogram evidence of substantial hearing loss, it was decided to perform surgical treatment via an exploratory tympanotomy. Tissue graft repair of the presumed oval window fistula proved to be effective. At a postoperative follow-up visit, the patient noted a subjective improvement of all preoperative symptoms. Two months postoperatively, results of a repeat audiogram test indicated complete improvement of the conductive component of the hearing loss, and a CT of the temporal bone showed resolution of air in the labyrinth. This patient initially presented with sudden-onset routine otologic complaints—eg, vertigo and aural fullness—as well as positionally triggered vertigo with nystagmus and mixed hearing loss. After symptoms worsened, further testing revealed a spontaneous pneumolabyrinth. This case report illustrates the importance of considering a wide range of differential diagnoses when evaluating patients with routine otologic concerns whose symptoms fail to improve after conservative management.

scenario: A 51-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of headache, right-side jaw pain, paresthesia, and trismus. The patient reported that the facial and jaw symptoms had evolved gradually over the past 5 years and that multiple medical therapies had provided only minimal relief of pain. The patient’s medical history included anxiety, depression, emphysema, hyperlipidemia, migraines, and pseudoseizures. She denied prior head trauma and had no pertinent surgical history. On physical examination, the patient had normal body habitus and reported bilateral tenderness of the temporomandibular joints and paresthesia of the right trigeminal nerve in the V2 and V3 distribution with intact masseteric nerve and symmetric facial nerve. Audiometric evaluation showed normal hearing bilaterally. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed a cystic mass in the right side of infratemporal fossa (ITF) that was nonenhancing on T1 sequencing with contrast and hyperintense on T2 (Figure 1A).
explanation: The ITF is a difficult-to-access space between the skull base, lateral pharyngeal wall, and ramus of the mandible. It is bounded anteriorly by the posterolateral wall of the maxillary sinus; posteriorly, by the carotid sheath; laterally, by the ramus of the mandible; medially, by the lateral pterygoid plate, tensor veli palatini, and levator veli palatini; superiorly, by the greater wing of the sphenoid; and inferiorly, by the medial pterygoid muscle. The medial border of the infratemporal fossa is continuous with the pterygopalatine fossa.1 The differential diagnosis of an ITF mass typically includes various tumors, such as juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma, parotid tumors, and schwannoma.2In rare cases, encephaloceles can present in the ITF. Diagnosis of ITF lesions can often be delayed because symptoms are vague, and there are few examination findings that suggest this specific diagnosis. Computed tomography (CT) and MRI with contrast are complementary investigations in the evaluation of ITF lesions, providing details about the relationship between the lesion and adjacent bony and soft tissue structures. In this case, initial MRI findings revealed the clue to the diagnosis. A smooth lobulated mass demonstrated homogenous high signal intensity on T2, low signal intensity on T1, and was nonenhancing with gadolinium, which ruled out solid tumors (eg, schwannomas) that typically enhance with contrast. Vascular lesions and tumors also would have characteristically different findings on MRI, with flow voids to suggest increased vascularity.3To verify, a CT angiography was performed, and its results did not show substantial vascularity. Ultimately, based on the results of the imaging and given the defect noted along the foramen ovale (Figure 1B), encephalocele was suspected. To confirm that the lesion represented an encephalocele with cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and rule out other diagnoses, a CT-guided aspiration was performed; results were positive for β-2 transferrin (Figure 2). Encephaloceles occur at the skull base when the dura and CSF herniate through a bone defect in the skull.4Acquired encephaloceles may arise from trauma, tumors, iatrogenic injury, or increased intracranial pressure. Sacs containing meninges and CSF are meningoceles, whereas those containing brain tissue are encephaloceles. In the present case, where an obvious cause was absent, a diagnosis of spontaneous encephalocele was made. Most skull base encephaloceles occur in the anterior skull base and present as a sinonasal obstruction or along the tegmen of the middle fossa accompanied by otologic concerns. Encephaloceles cases arising from Meckel cave, such as the present case, are uncommon and only a small handful are reported in the literature.5Options for management typically include repair because of the small increased risk of meningitis from a CSF leak.6 Because this patient had progressive symptoms despite maximal medical management of migraines and temporomandibular joint dysfunction, she elected to have surgical repair. Surgical repair of the encephalocele was performed via a middle cranial fossa craniotomy to divide the base of the encephalocele to prevent further communication with the infratemporal component. Facial pain improved postoperatively, but the trigeminal nerve (V2 and V3) paresthesia persisted. We will continue to monitor with internal MRIs to survey persistent or residual disease.

caption: Intraoperative photograph of the left lateral neck and the excised specimen. The black arrowhead indicates left neck lesion, the white arrowhead the external jugular vein.
scenario: A 63-year-old man presented with a history of previous left superficial parotidectomy 10 years before for a Warthin tumor. His histology results showed a 5-cm Warthin tumor, with a focus of nodular oncocytic hyperplasia in the adjacent parenchyma and reactive intraparotid lymph nodes. He presented to the ear, nose, and throat clinic and complained of pain in the operative site of 6 months duration. This occurred intermittently once a week and lasted for a few minutes each time. It was associated with a small lump over the left neck, and the pain was worse on touch and head turning. On examination, there was a 3-mm nodularity palpated deep to the neck wound along the mid sternocleidomastoid muscle. It was associated with focal tenderness. His facial nerve function was otherwise normal, and sensation in the ear lobe was intact. A magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan was performed, and the results showed no focal lesion in either parotid glands or at the area of interest over the left sternocleidomastoid muscle. The patient was counseled for an excisional biopsy of the left neck nodule. The intraoperative photograph of the neck and the excised specimen is shown inFigure 1.
explanation: B. Greater auricular nerve neuroma With the history of a parotidectomy, the presence of a painful nodule at the surgical site brings concern of tumor recurrence. This could be in the form of a recurrence of the primary tumor, lymph node metastasis from an occult head and neck primary, or a low-grade lymphoma arising in the background of a Warthin tumor. Specific features elicited in the clinical history and physical examination pointed toward the uncommon but notable postoperative complication of a greater auricular nerve (GAN) neuroma. The GAN arises from the cervical plexus (C2 to C3), emerges from under the posterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle (SCM) in the upper half of the neck, and runs across the lateral surface of the SCM toward the auricle.1The GAN has anterior and posterior branches. Anterior branches that enter the parotid gland parenchyma have to be routinely sacrificed in parotid surgery, while the bigger posterior branch can be preserved in cases when complete tumor excision allows for it.2,3 The GAN transection results in anesthesia and paraesthesia of the auricle and surrounding skin. These patients report functional difficulties with using the telephone, shaving, combing their hair, and wearing earrings. The anesthesia resolves for 50% of patients at 12 months, and this percentage continues to increase with time.4However, with time, another rarer complication can occur: the formation of a traumatic GAN neuroma. The incidence of traumatic neuroma after removal of the GAN during parotid surgery has been previously reported to be 6%, occurring anywhere from 2 to 10 years after surgery.5It can also occur after rhytidectomy and radical neck dissections.6,7 The GAN neuromas present as small and painful nodules at the site of division of the GAN. They are often associated with pain or paraesthesia on direct pressure, with a shooting and radiating character.5Imaging in the form of computed tomography or MRI may not identify a small GAN neuroma, while an attempt at fine-needle aspiration cytology can be tender, but these are helpful to exclude other differentials, such as tumor recurrence and lymphadenopathy. For this patient, clinical features, as well as the unremarkable MRI scan results, made the other differential diagnoses less likely. Histopathology is required to confirm the diagnosis, as is seen with this patient.Figure 2shows a thick native nerve with 1 end showing haphazardly distributed small nerve bundles within collagenized stroma, which is consistent with traumatic GAN neuroma. This is a nonneoplastic lesion that occurs in response to injury, including previous surgery.8To prevent the complication of a GAN neuroma, a clear understanding of the course of the GAN is important. This will help prevent inadvertent injury and achieve preservation of the GAN during parotidectomy. Ozturk et al3described a method using a 30° angle inferior to the lobule to consistently identify the GAN, and Hui et al9showed that preservation of the GAN was achievable in 69% of cases with an average additional time taken of 10 minutes. To reduce the risk of GAN neuroma, posterior branches should be preserved if tumor clearance is not compromised. The parotid gland fascia flap is another modification of the usual parotidectomy approach to allow for preservation of the GAN.10When GAN removal is necessary, various authors have recommended transection of the GAN with either cautery or cold steel and allowing it to retract into the SCM. When managing a GAN neuroma, treatment options include observation, medical treatment for neuropathic pain, and surgical excision. Medication options include carbamazepine, pregabalin, amitriptyline, and various other analgesics. Excision of the GAN neuroma has been described to successfully treat the painful condition, provide definitive histological diagnosis, and exclude more severe differentials, such as tumor recurrence or metastasis.5In this case, the patient reported complete resolution of symptoms immediately postoperatively.

scenario: A 64-year-old man presented to the otolaryngology clinic with hoarseness of voice for 3 weeks associated with intermittent dry cough. He had no medical history or family history of cancer and was not a smoker. In the absence of other suggestive symptoms, as well as a normal physical examination that did not reveal any enlarged cervical lymph nodes or oropharyngeal or neck mass and an unremarkable nasoendoscopic examination, a diagnosis of laryngopharyngeal reflux was made. The patient was advised to try conservative management with dietary advice and proton pump inhibitors, and a clinical review was scheduled in 6 weeks. The patient only returned 3 months later when his hoarseness became worse. Repeat nasoendoscopy now showed left vocal cord palsy in the paramedian position. In the absence of a history of trauma and associated neurological or systemic symptoms, the main concern was an underlying tumor that impinged on the vagus nerve at various points or its recurrent branch. Results of a computed tomographic (CT) scan showed an ill-defined soft tissue mass, which was likely nodal disease, at the left supraclavicular (Figure 1), as well as the prevertebral and paravertebral region, which partially encased the left common carotid, left subclavian, and left vertebral arteries. This was along the expected course of the left recurrent laryngeal nerve and likely accounted for the left vocal cord palsy. However, the primary site of disease remained unclear. A fused positron emission tomography with CT (PET/CT) scan with fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) tracer was then performed.
explanation: The PET/CT scan showed an intensely FDG-avid sigmoid lesion (Figure 2A) with associated intensely FDG-avid superior rectal and left common iliac adenopathy (Figure 2B) and FDG-avid soft tissue in the left supraclavicular fossa and aortopulmonary window (Figure 2C). Because metastasis of sigmoid colon cancer to the prevertebral and paravertebral lymph nodes resulting in recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy is highly unusual, a radiologically guided core biopsy of the left supraclavicular mass was performed. Histology as well as immunophenotype analysis confirmed that the tumor originated from the lower gastrointestinal tract. Flexible sigmoidoscopy showed a large stenosing sigmoid tumor, and histologic findings from biopsies were concordant with adenocarcinoma. In view of the imminently obstructing tumor, the patient underwent laparoscopic Hartmann surgery to avert a clinical crisis of intestinal obstruction during chemotherapy. The existing literature has reported cases of colon cancers with metastatic disease to the larynx1or thyroid2,3that presented with hoarseness of voice. However, unlike this patient with normal examination findings, these patients either had obvious neck masses or abnormal larynx on nasoendoscopy. In the absence of physical findings or other localizing symptoms, the attending physician may easily dismiss the symptom of hoarseness, which is a common presentation encountered by otolaryngologists and family physicians. Most dysphonia is self-limited and related to upper respiratory tract infection, especially in the absence of red flags and physical findings.4,5Persistent dysphonia warrants a more extensive evaluation, with the key consideration to rule out head and neck cancers.4,5Common tumors associated with such presentation include skull base tumors, mediastinal lymphadenopathy, as well as lung, thyroid, laryngeal, and esophageal cancers. If repeat nasoendoscopic findings were normal, laryngeal visualization would then be mandatory with videolaryngoscopy, stroboscopy, or direct laryngoscopy.4,5A CT scan or magnetic resonance imaging of the path of the vagus/recurrent laryngeal nerve should be performed to evaluate unilateral vocal cord palsy of unknown cause.4,5In the present patient, no obvious primary site of head and neck cancer was identified to account for the substantial lymphadenopathy encasing the left common carotid artery. A subsequent PET/CT scan identifying a sigmoid cancer and an image-guided core biopsy of the left paravertebral mass, which was congruous with a lower gastrointestinal tract origin, eventually solved the diagnostic conundrum. Several important points are raised by the present case. First, in evaluating patients with a seemingly benign symptom of hoarseness, physicians need to be alert for red flags that indicate rare and serious causes. Second, a clinical review should be arranged for all patients to ensure resolution of hoarseness, and a thorough repeat examination, including visualization of the larynx, should be performed if hoarseness is persistent. Finally, the choice of diagnostic test must reflect clinical thinking. In this case, a PET/CT scan was appropriately and expediently arranged to hunt for the primary site of cancer, and a core biopsy of the left paravertebral mass eventually led to a unifying diagnosis. This underscores the importance of individualizing investigations to patients’ specific clinical presentations.

B, Intraoral examination shows linear vestibular ulcerations with buccolabial aphthous ulcers. C, Hematoxylin-eosin stain of biopsy specimen of the vestibular ulcerated tissue shows noncaseating granulomatous inflammation (original magnification, ×100). Acid-fast bacilli staining was negative.
scenario: A 32-year-old woman was referred by her dentist to an oral surgeon for evaluation of persistent bilateral cheek swelling and mouth pain. Two months prior to presentation, the patient had awoken with bilateral linear “gashes” in her mandibular vestibule that were accompanied by bilateral buccal facial swellings. Since that day, the facial swelling remained unchanged, and although the mucosal lesions healed, the oral pain persisted. The patient’s medical history was noteworthy for depression, for which she was taking bupropion and fluoxetine, and prior alcohol use disorder, for which she was 3 years sober. She denied any smokeless tobacco use but endorsed daily electronic cigarette use. The extraoral examination detected bilateral buccal facial swelling of the lower facial third without associated trismus or lymphadenopathy (Figure, A). Intraorally, bilateral scarring of the mandibular buccal vestibule was noted with focal areas of ulceration. Small aphthous ulcerations were also present on the right buccal mucosa (Figure, B). An incisional biopsy of the right vestibular lesion was performed, and the specimen showed diffuse plasmalymphocytic infiltrates within the lamina propria. On higher magnification, noncaseating granulomatous inflammation was observed (Figure, C). Staining for acid-fast bacilli was negative.
explanation: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) encompasses a group of 2 chronic inflammatory autoimmune diseases that primarily involve the intestines. The cause of IBD is multifactorial and thought to have both genetic and environmental contributions that result in a dysregulated immune response to certain gut flora. While ulcerative colitis (UC) predominantly affects the large intestines, Crohn disease (CD) has a propensity to involve all other parts of the gastrointestinal tract. The most common CD symptoms are weight loss, low-grade fever, fatigue, lower abdominal pain, and nonbloody diarrhea. Extraintestinal manifestations may be observed with both UC and CD but are seen more routinely with CD.1 Oral manifestations are the presenting sign of CD in as many as one-third of children and young adults with the disease and may be either synchronous or metachronous with abdominal symptoms.2Similar to that of the small intestine, the oral cavity can exhibit areas of deep linear ulcerations separated by islands of normal uninvolved mucosa that form a cobblestone appearance. The additional finding of mucosal tags is also fairly specific for CD.3Noncaseating granulomatous inflammation of the lips or facial soft tissues is highly suggestive of CD in the setting of linear oral ulcerations. However, alternate causes of orofacial granulomatosis, such as sarcoidosis, tuberculosis, and Melkersson-Rosenthal syndrome, should be acknowledged and considered on the differential diagnosis. Nonspecific oral lesions that may manifest in both CD and UC are shallow aphthous ulcers, mucogingivitis, stomatitis, angular cheilitis, and glossitis.3,4Although there is poor correlation between oral and intestinal disease activity in CD, the oral cavity has a very high rate of granuloma detection in biopsy specimens, and thus, are a useful source of diagnostic material.5 The workup of suspected CD includes serologic testing for inflammatory markers, testing of stool samples for fecal calprotectin, and endoscopic examination with mucosal biopsy. The CD diagnosis generally requires proof of segmental and transmural inflammation of the luminal gastrointestinal tract; however, during periods of remission or in the absence of intestinal manifestations, isolated oral CD can be diagnosed based on the aforementioned clinical and histologic findings, after ruling out active tubercular infection and sarcoidosis.6 In conclusion, without a medical history of CD, its oral manifestations may be challenging to diagnose clinically. In children and young adults, clinicians should acknowledge that oral ulcerations and swellings may be the first signs of underlying CD. Incisional biopsy should be considered when multiple oral findings are present on examination. Oral disease activity does not parallel intestinal disease activity, and patients with resolved oral CD and subclinical intestinal symptoms may still develop intestinal CD.5

caption: The T1-weighted, contrast-enhanced, and fat-suppressed axial (A) and coronal (B) magnetic resonance imaging scans demonstrate the enhancing right-sided lesions overlying the distal aspect of the parotid and extending deep into the parotid parenchyma.
scenario: A previously healthy 8-year-old boy presented to an outpatient clinic for further evaluation of a fluctuating right parotid mass that had been present for 3 years. The patient was not immunocompromised and denied any trauma to the area. In the 2 months prior, he had received multiple rounds of antibiotics from other health care professionals. Outside computed tomography of the face showed a 3-cm cystic structure in the superficial aspect of the right parotid gland with associated lymphadenopathy. An outside health care professional had attempted incision and drainage of the area with negative cultures. The patient presented to our clinic with an isolated right 2-cm fluctuant and tender mass overlying the parotid gland. There was no accompanying cervical lymphadenopathy, and facial nerve function remained fully intact. The patient denied fevers or systemic symptoms. Results of laboratory evaluation revealed normal complete blood cell count and erythrocyte sedimentation rate levels with negative infectious workup results for Epstein-Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, HIV, and tuberculosis (TB). Magnetic resonance imaging showed a 1.9-cm peripherally enhancing, centrally necrotic lesion overlying the superficial right parotid gland with multiple subcentimeter necrotic lymph nodes within the right parotid gland (Figure 1).
explanation: Shortly after his presentation to our clinic, the patient developed violaceous skin changes with purulent drainage, which appeared consistent with atypical mycobacterial or nontuberculous mycobacterial (NTM) infection (Figure 2). He subsequently underwent drainage and curettage. Histopathologic examination revealed acute chronic inflammation with negative cultures. The infectious disease service started antibiotics for NTM, but they were stopped owing to an adverse reaction. The patient remained asymptomatic for 10 months but had a recurrence in the same area with extension into the parotid gland without involvement of the masseter. He subsequently underwent wide local excision. Cultures returned positive forMycobacterium abscessus. The differential diagnosis of this condition should include mycobacterium TB adenitis, viral lymphadenitis, hematologic cancer, aerobic abscess, and bartonella henselae.1While a branchial cleft cyst and chronic sialadenitis with abscess could present similarly, the skin changes and indolent course without systemic symptoms are more suggestive of an NTM. Magnetic resonance imaging showing a necrotic lesion with associated lymphadenopathy is not suggestive of a lymphovascular malformation. An NTM infection can prove to be a diagnostic challenge, especially when the characteristic skin changes are absent and cultures are negative. The typical age of presentation is 1 to 5 years old, with an incidence of 0.77 to 1.3 in 100 000 children.2-5Hundreds of species exist, butMycobacterium aviumcomplex is most commonly implicated in lymphadenitis.5These bacteria are believed to have primarily environmental (soil or water) origins.6In children, this most commonly involves submandibular or cervical nodes and, less frequently, the preauricular, sublingual, and parotid lymph nodes.1-3,7 When suspecting NTM, it is important to rule out TB adenitis because it has a considerably different treatment paradigm.5Tuberculosis typically has more systemic symptoms, whereas NTM lymphadenitis commonly presents as local erythema and fluctuance without substantial tenderness, which can progress to violaceous skin changes with fistula formation.6Staining methods include fluorochrome, Ziehl-Neelsen, and Kinyoun, although NTM is visualized in only 30% to 60% of cases.5Recommendations support performing both solid and broth culture medias, and different species of bacteria require different intubation times (7 days to 12 weeks).5Polymerase chain reaction testing, when available, tends to have the greatest sensitivity.6Definitive diagnosis of NTM is with a positive culture, although cultures are only positive in 50% to 82% of specimens, which further adds to the diagnostic difficultly.5 Treatment options include observation, antimicrobial agents, surgical procedures, or a combination of any of these.6,7Antimicrobial therapy alone is associated with a prolonged treatment course with potential adverse effects and a higher rate of recurrence.7A meta-analysis showed no difference for recurrence rates between antimicrobials vs observation.7Total surgical excision has demonstrated a cure rate greater than 90% in multiple studies, and as such, current literature supports total surgical excision with or without adjuvant macrolide antimicrobials as the treatment of choice.5-8 Special considerations for surgical management of parotid NTM infections include risk of injury to the facial nerve and the psychosocial effect of having a scar on the face.7In the present case, the patient had fistula formation before surgery; thus, he was already at risk of cosmetic disfiguration from the infected wound even before operating. Of 16 published studies documenting surgical treatment of pediatric parotid NTM infections, in which 59% were total or near total excision, no cases of permanent facial weakness were reported.9Another study showed a permanent nerve weakness in only 2% of patients undergoing surgery for head and neck NTM.7 The present patient was doing well at last follow-up, with full facial function and a well-healing incision. Although NTM of the parotid is an infrequent presentation of a relatively common pediatric infection, it should remain on the differential diagnosis.

B, Histopathologic image of biopsy specimen (original magnification ×100) shows aggregates of multinucleated giant cells (arrowhead) associated with intima fibroplasia (hematoxylin-eosin).
scenario: An otherwise healthy White man in his 60s presented with right jaw pain, trismus, and facial swelling. Symptoms started a year before, after receiving dental implants for new lower dentures. The patient noted right upper and lower eyelid swelling most notable in the morning but denied associated fevers, chills, vision changes, dysphagia, headaches, urinary symptoms, or rashes. Physical examination revealed a 3-cm round fluctuant area lateral to the right lateral canthus, mildly tender to palpation. No overlying warmth or erythema and no lymphadenopathy. The patient’s dentures appeared to be well fitting, but mouth opening was at approximately 50% of expected. Laboratory results included an erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 20 mm/h, and normal complete blood cell count, comprehensive metabolic panel results,  and lactate levels. Findings on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) (Figure, A) were most consistent with osteomyelitis of the mandible with inflammation of surrounding soft tissues. Right temporalis muscle biopsy results for Gram stain and culture, fungal stain and culture, and acid-fast bacillus stain were unremarkable. The patient’s symptoms did not improve after 7 weeks of empirical intravenous ertapenem followed by 8 weeks of oral cefuroxime and minocycline. Additional laboratory test results, including serum IgG4, SPEP, brucella AB, Q fever AB, RF, urinalysis, and microalbumin/creatinine levels, were all unremarkable. Results for p-ANCA and c-ANCA were negative. Repeated MRI findings showed progression of the inflammation and new involvement of the temporal lobe dura. Findings on positron emission tomographic computed tomography (PET-CT) scan showed nonspecific inflammatory changes to the bone, muscle, and brain meninges. A biopsy of the temporalis muscle, sphenoid wing, and dura was performed (Figure, B).

options.C: Synovitis, acne, pustulosis, hyperostosis, and osteitis syndrome

distractors: Synovitis, acne, pustulosis, hyperostosis, and osteitis syndrome
explanation: The lack of response to a full course of antibiotics and negative culture results made actinomycosis unlikely. The final biopsy results showed aggregates of multinucleated giant cell and histiocytes in association with internal elastic lamina, and several arteries with considerable mural changes and thickening of the intima resulting in complete luminal obliteration, all consistent with vasculitis.1The patient was prescribed prednisone at 60 mg once daily and his symptoms improved within 1 week. Prednisone was reduced to 50 mg once daily. Complete symptomatic resolution was noted at follow-up after 1 month of prednisone. When discussing head and neck pathologic disease, a couple of vasculitides are usually considered as primary causes; namely, giant cell arteritis (GCA) and granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA).2Giant cell arteritis is a systemic granulomatous vasculitis of the medium- and large-sized arteries with a predilection for the extracranial branches of the carotid and vertebral arteries.1The classification criteria for GCA by American College of Rheumatology (ACR) requires the patient to have at least 3 of the following: (1) age of 50 years or older, (2) localized headache of new onset, (3) temporal artery tenderness or diminished pulse, (4) ESR of 50 mm/h or greater, and (5) temporal artery biopsy findings showing granulomatous inflammation or mononuclear infiltration.1 Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is a small-vessel systemic vasculitis that is immunologically mediated (ANCA-associated vasculitis).3Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is more common in older individuals and in men.3According to the classification criteria set by the ACR in 1990, the diagnosis of GPA is given when at least 2 of the following are met: (1) abnormal urinary sediment (red cell casts or more than 5 red blood cells per higher power field), (2) abnormal findings on chest radiographs (nodules, cavities, or chest infiltrates), (3) oral ulcers or nasal discharge, and/or (4) granulomatous inflammation on biopsy.3Therefore, this patient’s presentation is not typical for GCA or GPA. Osteomyelitis of the mandible can be separated into acute or chronic with acute being less than 1-month duration. Chronic osteomyelitis can be secondary chronic type (SCO), which follows an acute presentation or primary chronic type (PCO) that is inflammatory and nonsuppurative. Primary chronic osteomyelitis represents a disease of insidious onset without a clear acute phase. This disease manifests with recurrent bouts of pain, swelling, trismus, and regional lymphadenopathy. This patient had all of those except for lymphadenopathy. Importantly, PCO presents with absence of pus, fistulas, or sequestration, differentiating this disease from SCO.4 Nine cases of PCO have been reported in patients with Takayasu arteritis (TAK).5One of those cases was PCO of the mandible in a 27-year-old woman who presented with jaw pain during pregnancy and had an ESR of 107 mm/h.5Takayasu arteritis is another large vessel vasculitis and primarily affects the aorta and its main branches. Takayasu arteritis shares histopathologic and clinical features with GCA. The main distinctions between TAK and GCA are patient age and location of the lesions.5 Primary chronic osteomyelitis has been associated with synovitis, acne, pustulosis, hyperostosis, and osteitis syndrome (SAPHO) and chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis (CRMO), but isolated occurrences of PCO are more common. Chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis is a rare disease of children that is characterized by prolonged and recurrent episodes of pain and swelling and has been associated with a number of dermatologic conditions like psoriasis and acne, and a number of inflammatory conditions including ANCA-associated vasculitis.6,7Synovitis, acne, pustulosis, hyperostosis, and osteitis syndrome is described as multifocal osteoarticular disease along with acne and palmoplantar pustulosis manifesting as insidious pain and swelling of the affected bone.8,9Given the age of the patient and lack of skin manifestation, we do not have enough data to link this case to either CRMO or SAPHO.

caption: Evaluation of the larynx from awake flexible laryngoscopy (A) including posterior commissure (A, inset) and operative microlaryngoscopy (B) with biopsy (C; original magnification ×40).
scenario: A 59-year-old man presented with progressive hoarseness and dyspnea over a 2-month period. Fifteen months previously, he had undergone allogeneic stem cell transplant (allo-SCT) with a matched related donor for treatment of fms-like tyrosine kinase (FLT3) internal tandem duplication–mutated acute myeloid leukemia (AML). The patient had been diagnosed with chronic gastrointestinal graft-vs-host disease after a workup for diarrhea. Results of a restaging bone marrow biopsy 2 weeks prior to presentation showed no evidence of leukemia. Physical examination findings revealed no neck masses or abnormalities, but the patient was noted to be severely dysphonic and stridulous. Flexible laryngoscopy findings demonstrated a right vocal fold neoplasm crossing the posterior commissure with associated bilateral vocal fold motion impairment and obstruction of the glottic airway (Figure, A). Awake tracheostomy was performed for airway protection, and biopsy of the neoplasm was obtained via operative microlaryngoscopy (Figure, B). Histologic findings demonstrated diffuse infiltrate of large cells with irregular nuclear contours, vesicular chromatin, and prominent nucleoli (Figure, C). Immunohistochemical stains showed CD33, CD43, and CD117 positivity, with a subset positive for CD7 and myeloperoxidase. Stains were negative for CD3, CD20, and cytokeratin expression.

options.A: Squamous cell carcinoma of the larynx
options.C: Extramedullary myeloid sarcoma of the larynx
options.D: Marginal zone lymphoma of the larynx

answer: Extramedullary myeloid sarcoma of the larynx
distractors: Squamous cell carcinoma of the larynx
Marginal zone lymphoma of the larynx
explanation: C. Extramedullary myeloid sarcoma of the larynx Diagnostic endoscopy results demonstrated a neoplasm of the larynx, excluding graft-vs-host disease, which most often manifests as mucositis in the upper aerodigestive tract. The lack of cytokeratin expression excluded malignant neoplasm of epithelial origin. Immunohistochemical staining for CD43 was positive, confirming that the neoplasm was of hematolymphoid origin. Negative staining for CD3 and CD20 excluded T-cell and B-cell lymphomas, while positive staining for CD7 is commonly seen with AML. A myeloid next-generation sequencing panel of the laryngeal tissue redemonstrated the known mutation inFLT3internal tandem duplication in the leukemia and laryngeal neoplasm. Subsequent bone marrow biopsy demonstrated no evidence of leukemia. Positron emission tomographic imaging only showed a hypermetabolic laryngeal mass. Thus, AML relapse manifesting as isolated myeloid sarcoma of the larynx was diagnosed. Primary conformational radiation treatment was initiated with 24 Gy administered over 5 standard fractions. Follow-up positron emission tomographic imaging showed complete metabolic response of the laryngeal mass. Posttreatment laryngoscopy findings demonstrated complete tumor response with only residual motion impairment of the right vocal fold. His tracheostomy was decannulated, and he demonstrated no evidence of recurrent disease 9 months following treatment. Myeloid sarcoma is a unique clinical presentation of AML that is defined as an extramedullary tumor composed of blasts from 1 or more myeloid lineages.1-3Myeloid sarcoma can be the de novo presentation of AML and may or may not be associated with peripheral blood or bone marrow involvement.
