It may present as a single lesion or involve multiple organ systems and may represent progression from an antecedent myeloid neoplasm.2,3Patients are considered to have isolated myeloid sarcoma if bone marrow aspiration and biopsy results reveal no evidence of hematologic disease.3Myeloid sarcoma can occur anywhere in the body but most commonly is found in soft tissues, bone, peritoneum, lymph nodes, and the gastrointestinal tract.3Involvement of the head and neck is less common, with a recent report implicating this region in 5.4% of cases of myeloid sarcoma.4,5 A high level of suspicion for myeloid sarcoma is needed upon the development of any persistent new mass in a patient with established leukemia. National guidelines recommend expedited laryngeal assessment for any patient experiencing dysphonia who is at risk of cancer.6Ultimately, laryngoscopy was the evaluation most essential to establishing the patient’s diagnosis and allowing safe airway management throughout treatment. An analysis of patients who received an allo-SCT for AML showed a 5-year cumulative incidence of isolated extramedullary relapse of nearly 10%.7Risk factors for extramedullary relapse include younger age, high-risk disease cytogenetics such as theFLT3mutation, a myelomonocytic immunophenotype, and extramedullary disease prior to transplant.3,7-9 There are limited data to guide therapy for isolated myeloid sarcoma relapse after allo-SCT, and treatments are tailored to specific patient and disease characteristics. Options for treatment include tapering immunosuppression, systemic chemotherapy plus or minus donor lymphocyte infusion or second allo-SCT, local radiation therapy, and surgical resection.3In the present patient’s circumstance, surgical excision was not possible without total laryngectomy, so radiation therapy was pursued to preserve laryngeal function along with systemic targeted therapy with gilteritinib. The present case illustrates an unusual presentation of an isolated myeloid sarcoma involving the larynx manifesting with the primary complaint of dysphonia treated with radiation therapy. Acute myeloid leukemia can infiltrate almost any tissue, necessitating consideration of myeloid sarcoma upon the development of a new head and neck complaint in a patient with prior acute leukemia.

caption: A, Postcontrast coronal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrated a bulky, cystic left neck mass at levels 3, 4, and 5. B, Axial computed tomography (CT) scan with contrast highlighted extensive septations and modularity within the mass.
scenario: A 40-year-old man presented with a large left neck mass in the setting of recently treated mixed nonseminomatous germ cell tumor (NSGCT) of the right testicle with metastasis to the retroperitoneal and mediastinal lymph nodes. He was treated with a right radical orchiectomy and 4 cycles of etoposide, ifosfamide, and cisplatin (VIP) chemotherapy with resulting reduction in metastatic tumor burden and normalization of α-fetoprotein and β-human chorionic gonadotropin. The patient’s neck swelling, which initially decreased in size while undergoing chemotherapy, progressively enlarged shortly after concluding treatment. He underwent magnetic resonance imaging and computed tomography of the neck that showed a clearly defined, bulky supraclavicular mass confined to left neck levels 3, 4, and 5 (Figure).
explanation: Despite an excellent retroperitoneal and mediastinal tumor response to 4 cycles of VIP chemotherapy, this patient’s left supraclavicular mass continued to enlarge. While chemorefractory metastasis was in the differential diagnosis, normalization of tumor markers and radiographic appearance on magnetic resonance imaging indicated the diagnosis of growing teratoma syndrome (GTS). Surgical resection was performed given the high risk of mechanical compression of surrounding neck vasculature owing to unchecked teratoma growth. Final pathology results demonstrated mature teratoma tissue, confirming the diagnosis of GTS. Growing teratoma syndrome was first described in 1982 by Logothetis et al,1in which 6 patients with metastatic germ cell tumors were described to have enlarging abdominal and pulmonary masses despite successful chemotherapy regimens. The criteria by Logothetis et al1for diagnosing GTS included (1) a normalization of β-human chorionic gonadotropin and α-fetoprotein values, (2) presence of a mass on examination that exhibited continual growth despite chemotherapy treatments, and (3) absence of any NSGCT malignant histologic characteristics on pathological examination. On imaging, GTS may demonstrate a well-circumscribed mass with increased cystic changes and curvilinear calcifications, resembling a mature teratoma.2,3TheFiguredemonstrates the present patient’s large, nodular neck mass; calcifications were not present on computed tomography in this case. While this may radiographically appear similar to persistent malignant disease or a benign teratoma, the normalization of serum tumor markers and the rapid, chemotherapy-resistant growth suggests a diagnosis of GTS.1A lymphocele would appear as a unilocular, hypodense, nonenhancing mass without soft tissue nodularity. Approximately one-third of patients treated with chemotherapy for NSGCT tumors will have residual retroperitoneal disease; less than 10% of these patients will demonstrate chemotherapy-resistant disease with persistent tumor growth.4While completion of the intended chemotherapy course is recommended, GTS is chemotherapy resistant and therefore will likely demonstrate persistent growth, most commonly in the retroperitoneum or thorax.4Growth rate may vary; however, it is generally quite rapid: the estimated volume growth rate is 9.2 cm3/mo.4This enlargement can progress to compression of vital organs or vasculature, and thus, prompt surgical resection is recommended.4 Owing to the nature of the criteria described by Logothetis et al,1diagnosis of GTS is usually made after completion of the chemotherapy regimen.5An intervention during chemotherapy is only recommended if clinically significant symptoms are experienced owing to proximal organ compression; this recommendation is echoed by the 2021 updated European Association of Urology testicular cancer guidelines.5,6In the mediastinum and supraclavicular region, GTS may result in cough, dyspnea, chest pain, and superior vena cava syndrome, among other symptoms.7Complete surgical resection of GTS is often curative, with only 4% of patients demonstrating recurrence, whereas recurrence rates may be as high as 83% in those who undergo incomplete resection.4,8Growing teratoma syndrome is capable of undergoing malignant transformation into recurrent NSGCT or sarcoma in 3% of cases.9 While the cause of GTS is largely unknown, several hypotheses have been proposed to explain the persistent chemorefractory growth. The most widely accepted hypothesis, posited by André et al,8suggests that the chemotherapy treatment regimen may destroy chemosensitive tumor cells, leaving chemoresistant cells that result in GTS. Cytogenic analysis shows that growing teratoma tissue differentiates to favor more stable karyotypes, allowing for stable growth.8Growing teratoma tissue has also been found to have a genetic concordance with other metastatic malignant germ cell tumors and could be derived from a commonly transformed precursor cell.10 Growing teratoma syndrome is a rare complication of NSGCT and is particularly uncommon in the head and neck. When encountered, complete surgical extirpation of the teratoma is necessary to prevent further tumor growth and impingement on local structures.

caption: Contrast-enhanced computed tomography scan of the neck with coronal (A) and axial (B) views demonstrating the right cystic neck mass.
scenario: A 44-year-old woman presented to the otolaryngology clinic with a 6-month history of a right neck mass with compressive symptoms. She first noticed swelling that progressed to pressure and dyspnea while supine. She reported fatigue but denied pain, voice change, weight loss, hemoptysis, and dysphagia. A physical examination revealed a visible and palpable fullness to the right neck without overlying cutaneous or sinus tract changes. Results of a complete blood cell count, a thyroid stimulating hormone test, triiodothyronine and levorotatory thyroxine testing, and a complete metabolic panel were normal. Ultrasonography showed a 7.9 × 6.3-cm septate cystic mass lateral to the right thyroid gland. A contrast-enhanced computed tomography scan of the neck demonstrated a large, nonenhancing cystic-appearing lesion abutting the lateral and posterior margins of the right thyroid lobe and extending from the level of the piriform sinus to the thoracic inlet (Figure). Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration revealed clear fluid with a parathyroid hormone (PTH) level of 67 pg/mL (reference range, <100 pg/mL; to convert to ng/L multiply by 1.00). A barium swallow study showed no communication between the cyst and the piriform sinus. Excision in the operating room was performed, and right thyroid lobectomy was necessary because of the intimate association of the lesion to the thyroid lobe.
explanation: Given the size of the cystic lesion and the compressive symptoms, the patient was taken to the operating room for excision. The mass was intimately associated with the right thyroid lobe as well as the recurrent laryngeal nerve, necessitating right thyroid lobectomy for complete excision of the lesion. Use of an intraoperative nerve monitoring system proved helpful in the removal of this lesion by aiding in identification and confirming integrity of the recurrent laryngeal nerve throughout the dissection. Histologically, the cyst was lined by a single layer of cuboidal cells and surrounded by islands of normal parathyroid parenchyma. These findings were consistent with a parathyroid cyst. Parathyroid cysts are uncommon lesions representing 1% to 5% of cystic neck masses.1These cysts usually present as an asymptomatic mass or are found incidentally with imaging. Rarely, a large cyst can cause compressive symptoms.2Parathyroid cysts are more common in women and arise in the fourth or fifth decade of life. Most parathyroid cysts involve the inferior parathyroid glands, but they have been reported from the mandible to the mediastinum.1Functional cysts are associated with elevated calcium and PTH but are less common than nonfunctional cysts.1This patient did not have a preoperative PTH level, but her serum calcium levels were normal. Therefore, we presume that this was a nonfunctional cyst. Parathyroid cysts are often mistaken for more common lesions such as thyroid cysts. Radiographically, these cysts can be difficult to distinguish and require fine-needle aspiration for diagnosis. Aspiration of parathyroid cysts classically reveals clear fluid.2Straw-colored fluid would be expected in a thyroid cyst, and bloody fluid may suggest a prior hemorrhage within a thyroid nodule. Elevated PTH in cystic fluid is considered diagnostic.3The normal PTH of the aspirate in this patient made the diagnosis a challenge. Branchial cleft cysts, like parathyroid cysts, often present as an asymptomatic neck mass. Second branchial cleft cysts are most common and are located anterior and medial to the sternocleidomastoid. Fourth branchial cleft cysts, which are very rare, are associated with the thyroid gland but are usually on the left. Most branchial cleft cysts present in the first decade of life,4and needle aspiration typically does not yield clear fluid. Thyroglossal duct cysts are relatively common neck masses that most often present in childhood or early adulthood. Theses masses are midline and are intimately associated with the hyoid bone. These cysts classically move with swallowing or tongue protrusion because of attachment to the foramen cecum of the tongue.5The characteristics of this patient’s nonmobile lateral neck mass make this diagnosis unlikely.

caption: A, The right-sided nodule showed an organoid zellballen pattern, with sharp demarcation from thyroid tissue (hematoxylin-eosin). B, At higher magnification, the tumor cells exhibited amphophilic granular cytoplasm, round to oval nuclei, and salt-and-pepper chromatin (hematoxylin-eosin).
scenario: A 50-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of a neck mass that was associated with hoarseness of voice and globus sensation. Physical examination showed thyromegaly (right greater than left) with an approximately 5-cm palpable nodule in the right lobe. There was no tenderness or cervical lymphadenopathy. There was no prior radiation exposure to the head and neck area. Thyroid function test results were normal, and she did not take thyroid medications. A relative had received a diagnosis of papillary thyroid cancer at age 50 years. There was no other pertinent family history, including a history of multiple endocrine neoplasia. Ultrasonography results showed a multinodular goiter with a dominant 4.6-cm right thyroid nodule, 1.6-cm left-sided thyroid nodule, and suspect left level IV lymph node. Ultrasonography-guided fine-needle aspiration biopsy results showed papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) (Bethesda VI) with aBRAFV600Evariation in the left nodule and lymph node, and atypia of undetermined significance (Bethesda III) with a suspicious Afirma genomic sequence classifier in the right nodule. She underwent total thyroidectomy with modified left lateral neck dissection. Gross examination of the specimen showed a 2.9-cm pale-tan, partially circumscribed, soft nodule in the right thyroid lobe; a 1.4-cm pale-tan, fibrotic, centrally brown nodule in the left lobe; and a 1.8-cm pale-tan, rubbery, partially circumscribed nodule in the isthmus. Histologic examination of the right thyroid lesion was performed (Figure), with ancillary testing.
explanation: Because of their rarity and overlapping features with other common thyroid entities, thyroid paragangliomas (TPGLs) are rarely suspected on fine-needle aspiration cytology. Although histopathologic assessment can render a definite diagnosis in most cases, immunohistochemistry may be helpful, especially in cytology specimens. In this patient, distinct from the PTCs in the left lobe, isthmus, and lymph node, the right-sided nodule showed an organoid zellballen pattern. The tumor cells showed amphophilic granular cytoplasm, round to oval nuclei, and salt-and-pepper chromatin and were positive for synaptophysin but negative for AE1/AE3, thyroid transcription factor–1 (TTF-1), thyroglobulin, paired-box gene 8, monoclonal carcinoembryonic antigen, and calcitonin. Intact succinate dehydrogenase (SDH) B expression was detected by immunohistochemistry. Focal sustentacular cells were highlighted by an S100 immunostain. These findings confirmed the diagnosis of TPGL. Because of morphologic and immunophenotypic similarities, TPGL is frequently misdiagnosed as medullary thyroid carcinoma. In contrast to TPGL, medullary thyroid carcinoma usually contains amyloid material in the stroma and is characterized by immunoreactivity for calcitonin. Immunophenotypically, it shows the immunopositivity of epithelial markers and lacks S100-positive sustentacular cells. Thorough evaluation of histopathologic features, particularly cytologic features, is usually sufficient to distinguish TPGL from PTC, as the latter has distinctive nuclear features, with crowded enlarged, glassy nuclei, and irregular nuclear contour, grooves, and pseudoinclusions, and is immunoreactive with thyroglobulin and TTF-1 and largely negative for neuroendocrine markers. Hyalinizing trabecular tumor is a thyroid tumor of follicular cell origin with a trabecular pattern that consists of cells arranged around delicate vessels with marked intratrabecular hyalinization. By immunohistochemistry, hyalinizing trabecular tumor is positive for thyroglobulin and TTF-1. Paragangliomas are rare neuroendocrine tumors that originate from neural crest-derived paraganglion cells situated in the region of autonomic nervous system and accompanying nerves. They are more common in the head and neck, superior mediastinum, and retroperitoneum.1Thyroid paraganglioma represents fewer than 0.10% of thyroid neoplasms2and only approximately 0.012% of all head and neck tumors. It was first described in 1964,3and more than 50 cases have been reported,1with a malignancy rate of 4% to 16%.4Thyroid paragangliomas arise from paraganglia within the thyroid capsule, thus eventually developing intrathyroidally.5The literature suggests that they usually present as asymptomatic, nonfunctioning thyroid nodules. They are more common in women and occur over a wide age range (24-73 years), with a mean age of 48 years.5Approximately 14% of patients with thyroid paragangliomas are reported to have concurrent diseases in either the carotid body or vagal paraganglia.5Therefore, follow-up imaging should be performed relatively soon after initial surgery. To date, to our knowledge, no reliable histopathologic features or molecular markers are available to distinguish malignant paragangliomas from benign ones. Evidence of metastasis is currently considered as the only reliable criterion to diagnose malignancy.6The TPGLs that are reported in the literature have mostly followed an indolent course, but there is no way of determining which have metastatic potential, so periodic serial imaging would need to be continued in the rare event of recurrence or malignancy. Surgical extirpation is required to make the diagnosis of TPGL and is concurrently a standard treatment.7 Approximately 30% to 40% of pheochromocytomas and paragangliomas are associated with hereditary genetic abnormalities that involve more than 20 genes, includingSDHx, MEN1, RET, VHL, NF1, TMEM127, HIF2A,andMAX,8,9while up to 30% of all head and neck paragangliomas are familial,8most of which are associated withSDHxvariations.10Genetic testing for familiar syndromes using an 86-gene panel failed to detect any relevant variations, and testing results for plasma catecholamines and urine metanephrines were negative in this patient. This aligns with TPGLs reported in the literature5that are typically nonfamilial and nonsecretory, similar to other head and neck paragangliomas.

caption: Clinical image showing left soft palate defect.
scenario: A 71-year-old man with a history of rheumatoid arthritis and type 2 diabetes presented to the otolaryngology team with 6 weeks’ history of pain and ulcers in the pharynx. He also complained of nasal regurgitation. He denied having any systemic symptoms. He took linagliptin, valsartan, and 15 mg of methotrexate weekly. He was a nonsmoker and consumed very little alcohol. Clinical examination including flexible nasendoscopy revealed multiple shallow ulcers on the posterior wall of the nasopharynx. There was a large defect involving the entire soft palate on the left. There was no obvious mass or any exophytic lesion. The edges of the soft palate defect were smooth and clean (Figure 1). There were no cranial nerve palsies. There was no cervical, axillary, or inguinal lymphadenopathy. Findings of the remaining head and neck examinations were normal. Results of laboratory investigations, including lactate dehydrogenase level and autoimmune antibody tests, such as antinuclear antibody and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody, were negative. Screening test results for HIV andTreponema pallidumwere also negative. The only positive result was immunoglobulin (Ig) G for Epstein-Barr virus (EBV). The IgM for EBV was not detected. Magnetic resonance imaging of the head and neck on short tau inversion recovery sequence confirmed the soft palate defect but also showed some thickening and hyperenhancement around the edges of the defect. There was no demonstrable nasopharyngeal mass. The hard palate was intact, and there were no significant cervical lymph nodes. The patient had biopsies taken from the ulcers and edges of the soft palate defect.
explanation: Histologic findings from the biopsy showed stratified squamous mucosa and respiratory-type mucosa with large areas of surface ulceration. There were dense underlying lymphoid infiltrates composed of lymphocytes, transformed lymphoid cells, and plasma cells. The transformed cells resembled atypical immunoblastic or Hodgkin and Reed-Sternberg–like cells (Figure 2A) dispersed between lymphocytes with no evidence of palisaded lymphocytes around those. These cells showed strong positivity for CD20, Pax5, MUM1, CD30, and CD15 on immunohistochemical staining (Figure 2B). More than 90% of the cells’ nuclear expression also showed EBV positivity on EBV-encoded RNA testing, but the results of B-cell clonality analysis using polymerase chain reaction were negative for any monoclonal B-cell population. No lymphoepithelial lesion, dysplasia, or epithelial malignant neoplasm was seen. The differential diagnoses include diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) and Hodgkin lymphoma. However, Hodgkin lymphoma is unlikely to occur extranodally, and CD20 positivity stands against this. There is also no sufficient morphological or immunohistochemistry evidence to support a diagnosis of DLBCL. In addition, DLBCL clinically tends to be more diffused than localized, as in this case. The clinical history, examination findings, and histologic findings would therefore be consistent with a diagnosis of EBV-positive mucocutaneous ulcer (EBVMCU), a new lymphoproliferative disease (LPD) entity established by the World Health Organization in 2017.1Characterized by shallow, sharply circumscribed mucosal or cutaneous ulcers, EBVMCU predominantly occurs in the oropharynx but also commonly affects the skin and gastrointestinal tract. It is not associated with any lymphadenopathy and systemic or B symptoms, such as fever, night sweats, or weight loss, which could be important discriminators for other differential diagnoses, including other LPDs or malignant neoplasms.2,3 Individuals who are immunosuppressed or immunocompromised develop EBVMCU, ie, when the virus overwhelms the host’s immune response. The majority of patients have iatrogenic immunodeficiency owing to drugs such as methotrexate, azathioprine, cyclophosphamide, or a tumor necrosis factor-α inhibitor.2-4Other groups of patients who are prone to EBVMCU are those with age-associated immunodeficiency (>60 years) owing to T-cell hypofunction and those with primary immunodeficiency, such as T-cell deficiency and hypogammaglobunemia.2-4It has also been reported in patients with HIV/AIDS.5 In terms of management, EBVMCU can be managed expectantly, as some cases can regress spontaneously or following the cessation or reduction of the iatrogenic immunosuppressants. This was the case with the present patient. The progression of disease stopped when methotrexate therapy was stopped, and the patient currently is in remission 6 months later. Patients with progressive disease or recurrence very rarely require systemic therapy such as rituximab or radiotherapy and often go into remission following their treatment. In a long-term study of 186 patients, only 8 patients had recurrence, and 4 had progressive disease. The rest of the cohort had either complete or partial remission.2,3 In conclusion, EBVMCU is a new LPD with excellent prognosis. However, distinguishing EBVMCU from other LPDs can be challenging. Hence, it is vital that clinicians are able to recognize the disease entity based on clinical and histopathological findings to provide the patients with appropriate management plans.

caption: Computed tomography of the neck with intravenous contrast with axial soft tissue window (A) and sagittal reconstruction in bone window demonstrating linear hyperdense focus in the floor of mouth and submental triangle (B).
scenario: A 64-year-old woman with a history of hyperlipidemia, hypertension, HIV infection, coronary artery disease, and squamous cell carcinoma of the left mandible treated with composite resection, left neck dissection, and fibula free flap (FFF) reconstruction followed by postoperative radiotherapy presented with sharp, shooting left neck pain. Beginning 5 months after her reconstruction, the patient reported point tenderness on the left jaw, facial swelling, and electric pain with severity of 7 out of 10 in the left neck that occurred with talking or eating. Her postoperative course was complicated by osteoradionecrosis post-tracheostomy, plate removal, and left segmental mandibulectomy. She received regular physical therapy and lymphedema therapy and was seen by Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation, who treated her with onabotulinum toxin A injections; neither provided significant resolution of her symptoms. Review of a computed tomography scan of the head and neck (Figure 1) performed on follow-up 5 years after initial reconstruction demonstrated a long, hyperdense structure in the left submental, submandibular region with accompanying soft-tissue thickening. On further review of prior imaging, this calcification appeared as a new finding in various scans dating back to 5 months after FFF reconstruction compared with preoperative imaging. There was no fluorodeoxyglucose avidity in the area of question on multiple positron emission tomography scans done during this follow-up window.

options.D: Ossification of the free flap pedicle

answer: Ossification of the free flap pedicle
explanation: D. Ossification of the free flap pedicle A painful neck mass is most worrisome for recurrence during surveillance of head and neck cancer.1,2Though traumatic neuroma or chronic postoperative pain is possible,3ossification of the FFF pedicle is the correct diagnosis for the following reasons. First, the lesion was stable over 5 years, with lack of fluorodeoxyglucose avidity on positron emission tomography, making recurrence less likely. Second, despite standard-of-care palliation techniques, her symptoms were recalcitrant. Third, the linear radiopacity located in the submental triangle, where the pedicle often courses, makes ossification more likely than a neuroma. The FFF is the standard for oromandibular reconstruction because of its high success rate and low donor-site morbidity.2A rare complication is pedicle ossification. Often asymptomatic, it may present as a firm, tender neck mass with trismus and pain with mastication and ipsilateral neck rotation.4,5Diagnostic imaging including computed tomography or panoramic radiographs can confirm this finding. Most commonly, pedicle ossification is detected incidentally on surveillance imaging.4The true incidence is unknown, with reports ranging from 4% to 65%; surprisingly, only 2.5% present symptomatically.4,6Ossification is more common in younger patients and those not receiving high-dose adjuvant radiotherapy.4 The pathogenesis remains unclear, but multiple theories describe pedicle ossification. The predominant theory implicates osteogenic proliferation of the periosteum along the vasculature.7During harvest, a cuff of muscle remains attached to the fibula alongside the peroneal vessels to preserve periosteal blood supply. Osteotomies are made to match the ablative geometry, leaving the periosteum and muscle along the pedicle, which atrophies and disappears over time.2However, under the stimulus of osteoinductive molecules, bone formation can occur from the periosteum and travel along the pedicle.2The osteogenic potential depends on local factors, including mechanical stress and proliferative stimuli.8Stretching of the periosteum during speech and mastication may be a key stimulus for osteogenesis.5In a rabbit model, costal periosteum has been shown to regenerate bony defects in the tibia within 6 weeks.9 Other theories include fracture repair, blood flow, local mechanics, and hormonal influence. The fracture repair theory describes osteoprogenitor recruitment in areas between recipient and donor osteotomy sites, which behave like a fracture. Blood flow theory, which relies on the interaction of stem cells and bone morphogenetic protein, asserts that higher perfusion in the leg compared with cervicofacial areas causes enhanced perfusion surrounding the pedicle after inset, leading to osteogenic stimulus and bone formation.2The local mechanical theory likens ossification to callus formation from masticatory stress, inducing bone morphogenetic protein signaling.2Some studies describe that the hormonal microenvironment (eg, high concentrations of estrogen and doses of dexamethasone) has been shown to increase osteogenic capacity.5However, this is disputed by some reports demonstrating a higher incidence of ossification in men or no statistical difference among sexes.6,8 Conservative therapy includes oral physiotherapy for 6 months after surgery.5Surgical excision (Figure 2) is recommended for functional or debilitating deficits and is considered safe given the natural history of pathogenesis. By the time of symptom manifestation, the flap has fully incorporated with adequate collateral circulation, permitting low-risk, outpatient surgery.4,5,7In the present patient’s case, her symptoms were refractory to nonsurgical therapy; therefore, excision of the ossified pedicle was undertaken. Though her neck discomfort resolved, her postoperative course was complicated by orocutaneous fistula, worsening osteoradionecrosis, and superinfection requiring hospitalization and tracheostomy. To minimize ossification, multiple studies advocate for a modified FFF harvest with additional dissection of periosteum along the pedicle and awareness of inset approaches to reduce mechanical stress from mastication.2,5Contradictory reports claim that there is no increased risk of flap loss with modified harvests, while others assert that the risk of vessel injury and flap compromise outweigh the low percentage of symptomatic cases.2,5,7

caption: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and computed tomographic (CT) scans.
scenario: An 80-year-old woman presented with a 1-year history of right pulsatile tinnitus and aural fullness. Her symptoms were more prominent at night and in the quiet and improved when upright. Physical examination demonstrated an intact tympanic membrane with no middle ear mass; there was no neck mass palpated or bruit auscultated. The patient had further workup with magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and a computed tomographic scan (Figure 1). The patient was taken to the operating room for a right transtemporal biopsy. Operative findings demonstrated extensive tumor extending along the posterior fossa dura and deep to the jugular foramen that filled the area of the skull base. The tumor was debulked and sent for pathologic evaluation.
explanation: Results of testing showed that the patient had a plasmacytoma of the skull base involving the jugular foramen. The MRI demonstrated a 2.7 × 2.2 × 1.7-cm mass involving the posterior skull base, which was hyperintense on T2 fluid-attenuated inversion recovery and isointense with brain on T2. The precontrast T1 images demonstrated a slight hyperintensity with intense enhancement on T1 postcontrast. A subsequent computed tomographic scan of the temporal bone demonstrated a destructive lesion of the right occipital temporal skull base adjacent to the jugular foramen. Pathological findings identified kappa monotypic plasma cells, which coexpressed CD56 and CD117 (Figure 2). Morphologically, there were sheets of plasma cells with round nuclear borders and course chromatin, consistent with plasmacytoma. A plasmacytoma is a plasma cell neoplasm in which there is a single mass of clonal plasma cells with minimal bone marrow involvement and no symptoms other than those derived from the primary lesion. Two types of plasmacytoma exist: extramedullary plasmacytoma (EMP), primarily seen within the soft tissues of the head and neck, and solitary bone plasmacytoma (SBP), most commonly seen within the vertebrae. Skull base plasmacytoma is an uncommon presentation of EMP, with a plasmacytoma of the jugular foramen being even more rare. Symptom manifestations of plasmacytomas are dependent on the location of the tumor. The present patient had involvement of the temporal bone near the jugular foramen and pulsatile tinnitus on the affected side without any cranial nerve deficits. Sweeney et al1evaluated cases of temporal bone plasmacytoma and found that 71% of patients present with a vascular-appearing middle ear mass; separately, 71% present with conductive hearing loss while 29% present with a sensorineural hearing loss. The authors noted that 44% of patients were diagnosed with multiple myeloma and 56% of patients had a cranial nerve deficit, with the most common being cranial nerve VIII, followed by VII. Only 32% of temporal bone cases involved the jugular foramen, with the most common location being the mastoid. Plasmacytoma of the temporal bone can have an extremely variable presentation and findings on further workup. Chen et al2report a patient with results of MRI, octreotide scan, and preoperative angiography that were all consistent with jugular paraganglioma, with biopsy revealing plasmacytoma in the patient, who was subsequently diagnosed with multiple myeloma. Plasmacytoma is a radiosensitive tumor with much of the treatment being focused around this modality. Radiotherapy alone as treatment for a plasmacytoma has shown good long-term local control between 79% and 91%.3Plasmacytoma can progress to multiple myeloma in some cases, with rates ranging from 65% to 84% for SBP and 50% to 60% for EMP.4In these patients, chemotherapy is needed in addition to radiation to treat the systemic disease.3Bindal et al5evaluated patients with a skull base plasmacytoma and suggested that patients without multiple myeloma or myelomatous changes at the time of diagnosis are unlikely to progress to systemic disease. Na’ara et al6performed a meta-analysis of skull base plasmacytomas that included 47 patients. The majority of these patients’ tumors (59.5%) involved the sphenoclival region with nasopharynx, petrous apex, and orbit being the other areas involved. The 5-year overall survival for patients with SBPs was noted to be 59%, which is lower than the rate of 80.8% for other EMPs of the head and neck.6,7The location of the tumor, age of the patient, degree of resection, and administration of chemotherapy were not found to have any prognostic value on the outcome of a skull base plasmacytoma.6 Presented here is a rare case of a patient with a skull base plasmacytoma involving the jugular foramen. The treatment plan for this patient includes presentation at a multidisciplinary tumor board with likely adjuvant radiotherapy.

caption: A, Clinical image of the right earlobe. B, Histopathologic image (hematoxylin-eosin staining) showing basaloid cells with a nucleus in the periphery (upper) and ghost cells without a nucleus in the center (lower).
scenario: An 18-month-old girl presented with a 1-year history of a slow-growing mass in the right earlobe. There were no symptoms, such as tenderness or discharge, associated with the mass. She had no history of underlying medical disease or trauma. On physical examination, a 1.5 × 1.0–cm, firm, nodular, angulated, pinkish, nontender mass was observed in the posterior aspect of the right earlobe (Figure, A). The skin over the mass was semitransparent, and the mass moved freely beneath the skin. Under suspicion of a tumorous lesion, complete excision was performed after the patient received general anesthesia. Histopathologic findings were characteristic for 2 cell types; basaloid cells with a nucleus were present in the periphery, and ghost cells without a nucleus were present in the center (Figure, B). Six months after surgery, the wound had healed well, and there has been no recurrence.
explanation: Pilomatricoma is a benign tumor that originates from hair follicle matrix cells.1-7It occurs frequently during the first 2 decades of life, especially in children 10 years or younger, and appears more in females than in males.1,3,6-8The head and neck are the most commonly involved regions, particularly the neck and preauricular regions.1,3,6,8Pilomatricoma is rare in the auricle.3,6 Pilomatricoma was first described by Malherbe and Chenantais as a benign neoplasm of the sebaceous gland in 1880 and was named calcifying epithelioma of Malherbe.1,3,5,8In 1942, the tumor was thought to originate from hair cortex cells, and, in 1961, the termpilomatrixomawas proposed to describe its origin in the hair follicle matrix by Forbis and Helwig. The term was modified topilomatricomain 1977.3 Pilomatricoma is typically observed as a firm, superficial, nontender, mobile, well-demarcated single nodule with bluish red discoloration of the skin.1,3,5-8It usually grows slowly over several months or years and is asymptomatic.1,6It appears as an irregular and angulated mass when stretched, which is calledtent sign.3,5,8Multiple pilomatricoma is associated with Gardner syndrome, myotonic dystrophy, Steinert disease, Turner syndrome, and Rubinstein-Taybi syndrome.1,3-5,7,8 Radiologic evaluation has limited usefulness in diagnosing pilomatricoma, although it can help to differentiate pilomatricoma in the preauricular area from parotid tumor.1,3,5Pilomatricoma appears as a sharply demarcated, calcified, subcutaneous nodule on computed tomography and as high-signal intensity bands on T2-weighted magnetic resonance imaging.1,3 Fine-needle aspiration cytology could lead to misdiagnosis if there are no ghost cells in the aspirate.1,3,5On histopathology, sharply demarcated dermal nodules surrounded by a capsule of fibrous tissue are observed. Basaloid cells with a nucleus are observed in the periphery and ghost cells, which are also calledshadow cells, without a nucleus are observed in the center. Calcification is observed mostly in ghost cell regions, and foreign body reaction is identified in areas of keratinized debris.1-5 The preferred treatment is surgical excision.1,3-5,8Recurrence after complete excision is rare.1,3-5,7,8Few cases of malignant transformation of pilomatricoma have been reported.1,2To our knowledge, malignant transformation has not been reported in children. If the mass recurs or has histologic malignant features, such as increased atypical mitoses and infiltration, pilomatrix carcinoma should be suspected.1,3,8Thus, histopathological diagnosis is mandatory after excision. Pilomatricoma of the auricle should be differentiated from epidermoid cyst, dermoid cyst, sebaceous adenoma, hemangioma, and basal cell carcinoma.4,7Compared with these masses, pilomatricoma appears as an irregular nodule that moves freely under the overlying skin.4,6 Epidermoid cysts are common benign masses in the earlobe. Epidermoid cysts appear as soft, nontender, and cystic masses.9Pilomatricomas may appear similar to epidermoid cysts clinically. However, epidermoid cysts have a keratinized and stratified squamous epithelium and keratin material within the cyst histopathologically. Hemangioma is a benign vascular soft tissue tumor that occurs most commonly in the heads and necks of children.10The bluish red discoloration that is associated with pilomatricoma because of dilation of blood vessels could lead to confusion with hemagioma.5However, half of hemangiomas regress spontaneously within age 5 years.10 Basal cell carcinoma usually appears as a nodular and nontender mass with an ulcer in the center. It shows a benign progression and rarely metastasizes. It commonly occurs in elderly individuals.9Histologically, shadow cells are absent, and there is clefting around basaloid cells.2Pilomatricoma might also present with ulceration.3,4However, in this case, the patient was age 18 months and there was no ulcerative lesion. Although pilomatricoma of the auricle is rare, it should be included in the differential diagnosis of nodular masses in the auricle, especially in the case of a superficial irregular sliding mass with semitransparent overlying skin in children.

caption: Nasal endoscopy (A) and computed tomography (B) showing a pedunculated mass on the posterior wall of the nasopharynx. C, Histopathology of the nasopharyngeal mass. A lymphoid follicle with an atretic germinal center is seen that is penetrated by hyalinized blood vessels (arrowheads) (original magnification ×400).
scenario: A 19-year-old man presented with a chief complaint of left nasal obstruction. He had been experiencing nasal stuffiness for 2 years, which was aggravated 6 months before his initial visit. Endoscopic examination showed mild septal deviation to the left side and a well-demarcated, pedunculated mass on the posterior wall of the nasopharynx (Figure, A). His medical, surgical, and family histories were unremarkable. In addition, biochemical test and chest radiography results showed no abnormal findings. Paranasal sinus computed tomography results revealed a 2.1 × 1.7 × 2.2–cm mass protruding from the posterior wall of the nasopharynx into the lumen (Figure, B). The mass was completely excised using an endoscopic approach. Pathologic examination showed that the mass comprised lymphoid tissue that was associated with prominent vascular structures with hyalinized walls. Some lymphoid follicles had atretic germinal centers that were traversed by hyalinized blood vessels, forming a lollipop-shaped structure (Figure, C). Immunohistochemical staining showed CD20-positive B lymphocytes in the follicular areas and CD3-positive T lymphocytes in the interfollicular areas; CD21-positive follicular dendritic cells were also found in the germinal centers.
explanation: Castleman disease (CD) is characterized by atypical lymph node hyperplasia; it is also known as angiofollicular mediastinal lymph node hyperplasia, follicular hyperplasia of lymph nodes, and angiomatous lymphoid hamartoma.1Castleman disease most frequently occurs in the lymph nodes of the mediastinum, followed by those in the stomach and the head and neck. Castleman disease is histologically classified as either hyaline vascular type, plasma cell type, or, rarely, mixed type.1It is clinically classified into unicentric (localized or isolated) and multicentric (systemic) types. The pathogenesis of CD remains unclear. However, human herpesvirus 8 (HHV8) infection has been associated with the occurrence of about 50% to 60% cases of multicentric-type CD.2The unicentric type is mainly the hyaline vascular type. Unicentric CD occurs in the lymph nodes and is usually asymptomatic, but can present with local compression symptoms following lymph node enlargement. In contrast, multicentric CD can present with symptoms, such as fever, fatigue, hepatosplenomegaly, systemic lymphadenopathy, and peripheral neuropathy. Laboratory test results show anemia, hypoalbuminemia, gammaglobulinemia, and thrombocytopenia.3The hyaline vascular type occurs more frequently in younger age groups, without any sex differences; however, most of the plasma cell–type CD cases show multicentric lymph node involvement and occur in older adults (age >50 years), with a higher prevalence in men than in women. Castleman disease has no specific characteristics on radiological imaging. Sonography findings show a hypoechoic mass that resembles a lymphoma. Computed tomography results usually reveal a well-demarcated mass with low density or enhancement. In addition, magnetic resonance imaging results usually show isosignal intensity or mild high-signal intensity in T1-weighted images and high-signal intensity in T2-weighted images.4Therefore, pathological examination is needed for confirmatory diagnosis of CD. The hyaline vascular type shows abundant hyalinized blood vessels within and between the increased follicles. Lymphocyte cell counts in the germinal centers are decreased, and the mantle zone is widened. The lymphocytes of the mantle zones are concentrically arranged around the germinal center (onion-skinning), and the follicles may be radially penetrated by a blood vessel (lollipop feature).5Plasma cell—type CD shows relatively normal nodal architecture with hyperplastic follicles. The interfollicular region might be mildly hypervascular and characteristically contains sheets of mature-appearing plasma cells.5 Nasopharyngeal masses in adolescents are rare, and most cases are benign. Differential diagnoses should include angiofibroma, choanal polyp, respiratory epithelial adenomatous hamartoma, and malignant tumor. Angiofibroma is the most likely diagnosis in adolescent males with nasopharyngeal masses. Nasopharyngeal angiofibroma commonly exhibits epistaxis, and imaging studies usually show a highly enhanced soft tissue mass with a clear margin. Respiratory epithelial adenomatous hamartoma shows proliferation of glands that originate from the surface epithelium and are surrounded by a thickened basement membrane in an edematous stroma.6Malignant conditions, such as nasopharyngeal lymphoma and nasopharyngeal carcinoma, should be considered despite their rarity. For localized masses, surgical resection is mainly performed as a standard treatment and shows high cure rates.7In contrast, multicentric CD cases are treated using chemotherapy with vinblastine, etoposide, and chlorambucil; steroid therapy; and radiotherapy. The prognosis of multicentric CD is variable, including relapse and remission, rapidly progressing fatal disease, development of malignancy, or stable and persistent disease.8The median survival of patients with multicentric CD is 30 months.8Poor prognosis is associated with polyneuropathy, organomegaly, endocrinopathy, presence of monoclonal immunoglobulin in serum, and skin changes.2Malignant neoplasms can occur in one-third of patients with multicentric CD. In patients with hyaline vascular–type CD, follicular dendritic cell sarcoma can develop. Kaposi sarcoma is associated with multicentric CD with HHV8 infection, whereas lymphoma commonly occurs in multicentric CD cases without HHV8 infection.2 Another study reported the case of a 23-year-old man with follicular dendritic cell sarcoma that developed 11 years after the initial diagnosis of nasopharyngeal CD.9Cases of localized CD in the nasopharynx are extremely rare.3,9However, the characteristics of CD should be known so that complete surgical excision can be performed for treatment.

caption: A, Complete opacification of the left paranasal sinus. The black arrowhead indicates fat obliteration in the left pterygopalatine fossa compared with the right (yellow arrowhead). B, Erythematous left nasal soft-tissue mass. C, Plasmacytoma with aggregates of plasmablastic forms (arrowheads, original magnification ×2).
scenario: A woman in her 50s was admitted to the hospital with new left-sided nasal congestion, facial pain, and cheek numbness. Her medical history included kappa light chain multiple myeloma refractory to multiple chemotherapeutic regimens. She had been admitted 4 months earlier with similar symptoms of facial pain and sinus pressure. At that time, she was found to have persistent sinus mucormycosis, which required multiple rounds of surgical debridement. On this admission, her vital signs were stable, and she was afebrile. Laboratory test results showed a white blood cell count of 0.97 × 109per liter with absolute neutrophil count of 650 × 106per liter and platelet level of 17 × 109per liter. A computed tomography scan showed complete opacification of the left paranasal sinuses (Figure, A). The patient underwent surgical debridement, and a prominent erythematous soft-tissue mass was seen in her left nasal vestibule (Figure, B). The nasal mass was resected for pathologic analysis (Figure, C).
explanation: The patient’s presenting symptoms were similar to the previous presentation of mucormycosis and, given her immunocompromised state, were initially thought to be caused by recurrent invasive fungal sinusitis. However, the computed tomography scan showed evidence of a left maxillary soft-tissue abnormality concerning for plasmacytoma. In addition, the erythematous mass seen in the nasal vestibule had an appearance inconsistent with fungal sinusitis. Surgical pathologic results of the resected mass showed aggregates of plasmablastic forms with immunohistochemical staining for the plasma cell marker CD138, confirming the diagnosis of plasmacytoma. Plasmacytomas are tumors composed of monoclonal immunoglobulin–producing plasma cells and most commonly present in bone (medullary plasmacytoma). However, they can also occur in soft tissue, as in this case (extramedullary plasmacytoma [EMP]).1,2Medullary plasmacytomas occur in the axial skeleton (calvarium, spine, and rib cage) in 83% of cases.1Most EMPs arise in the upper respiratory tract; specifically, 80% of solitary EMPs arise from the head and neck region.3 The plasma cells seen in both plasmacytomas and multiple myeloma are histologically indistinct. Plasmacytomas are discrete aggregates of these cancerous cells, whereas multiple myeloma is a systemic hematologic disease.1Co-occurrence of multiple myeloma with plasmacytoma is relatively common. In particular, some studies estimate that the incidence of EMPs in patients with multiple myeloma ranges from 7% to 18%.4These soft-tissue plasmacytomas have a variety of causes, including local growth from medullary plasmacytomas or hematogenous spread of multiple myeloma to lymph nodes, skin, or sites of previous surgical procedures.4,5 This patient’s history of repeated surgical debridement for fungal sinusitis likely contributed to the development of nasal plasmacytoma. Trauma, including surgical scars or catheter insertions, can serve as niduses for plasmacytoma formation.4,5Aside from her surgical history, the chronic inflammation of her previous persistent fungal sinusitis also might have contributed to her presentation because inflammatory states have been suggested to promote plasmacytoma development in patients with multiple myeloma.4 On imaging, medullary plasmacytomas may present as lytic lesions, whereas EMPs can present as aberrations in soft tissue.3Radiographic signs from this patient’s case included the complete opacification of the left paranasal sinus caused by the tumor obstructing the sinus outflow tract. In addition, soft-tissue changes seen on a computed tomography scan, such as obliteration of the normal fat within the pterygopalatine fossa, were suggestive of EMP (Figure, A). However, radiographic findings are usually nonspecific for initial diagnosis, and patients require biopsy or resection with pathologic review.3 Most cases of plasmacytoma are managed with radiotherapy or wide surgical excision. This patient’s symptoms were presumed to be caused by fungal sinusitis; thus, the subtotal surgical excision performed for diagnosis of the mass doubled as symptom management for the plasmacytoma. Further treatment for this patient included the continued medical management of multiple myeloma. Radiotherapy could have been considered if the plasmacytoma recurred. Patients with plasmacytoma tend to do well, with survival greater than 70% at 5 years.5However, for plasmacytomas associated with multiple myeloma, the aggressiveness of the underlying malignant tumor ultimately dictates the clinical course.1Although this patient experienced no recurrence of the plasmacytoma, she ultimately died as a result of complications of multiple myeloma shortly after tumor resection. This case underscores the importance of including plasmacytoma in the differential diagnosis for head and neck masses, particularly for patients with risk factors, such as multiple myeloma or prior surgeries. Ultimately, management of EMP is straightforward and includes radiotherapy or excision. However, the discovery of such a tumor could serve as a sentinel event to prompt workup for multiple myeloma.6

caption: Reconstructed lateral view images of swallowing dynamic computed tomography at rest (A) and on swallowing (B). The hyoid bone and the ossified part of the cartilage are shown in white. The cartilaginous part of the thyroid cartilage is reconstructed in yellow, the air space in light blue, and the contrast-medium swallowing in pink. The superior thyroid notch (blue arrowhead) and right superior border (white arrowheads) of the thyroid cartilage rubbed with the hyoid bone from the inside at the time of maximum laryngeal elevation on swallowing.
scenario: A 42-year-old woman (height, 160 cm; weight, 50 kg) presented with a 3-month history of a clicking sensation and painful swallowing, mainly on the right side, with a sudden onset. She had consulted other physicians, but the cause could not be identified. The symptoms gradually exacerbated, seriously deteriorating her quality of life and causing a 5-kg weight loss. She also experienced insomnia and depression. Antidepressants and psychotherapy, prescribed under the suspicion of a psychogenic cause, did not alleviate her symptoms. She had no relevant medical history and no smoking or drinking history. Cardiovascular, respiratory, and neurological findings were unremarkable. A careful physical examination, with palpation of the hyoid bone and thyroid cartilage region on swallowing, revealed a clear clicking movement and right-sided friction with accompanying pain. However, results of laryngoscopy and other common imaging studies showed no pathology. Hence, to assess the dynamic structural changes during swallowing, we performed swallowing dynamic computed tomography (SD-CT), which can reveal moving structures by creating a dynamic-volume data set during swallowing.1,2Comparison of the reconstructed SD-CT images at rest (Figure 1A) and on swallowing (Figure 1B) revealed that the superior thyroid notch and the right superior border of the thyroid cartilage contacted the hyoid bone internally during maximum laryngeal elevation on swallowing.
explanation: Normally, a space is present between the thyroid cartilage and the hyoid bone during swallowing. The severe rubbing between the hyoid bone and the thyroid cartilage during swallowing caused the clicking sensation and cervical pain; thus, we diagnosed her with a clicking larynx. Because conservative therapy, including physiotherapy, analgesic injections, and medications, was ineffective, surgery was performed under local anesthesia to identify sites in contact on swallowing. On visualization of the structures during swallowing, the right superior part and the superior notch of the thyroid cartilage were found to contact the hyoid bone. The thyroid cartilage was partially excised (Figure 2A). The operation conferred immediate improvement, and complete symptom relief was noted at the 3-month follow-up. The 3-month postoperative SD-CT revealed no contact between the hyoid bone and the thyroid cartilage (Figure 2B). A clicking larynx is a clicking sensation in the neck on swallowing or when moving the head and is often associated with pain in the neck.3The most common cause is neck trauma; however, half of the cases are idiopathic.4,5Alteration of the thyroid cartilage, ossification of the cartilage, or abnormal bone formation in the thyrohyoid ligament may be underlying causes. A thorough physical examination may provide diagnostic clues because the clicking location can be identified by palpation of the neck on swallowing.5The major clicking locations are the superior cornu or the top edge of the thyroid cartilage, and the contact of these structures with the cervical spine occasionally causes laryngeal clicking sounds.4,6 A decisive method to confirm the diagnosis of a clicking larynx has not been established because a clicking larynx often shows no abnormality on laryngoscopy, blood examinations, and radiography.3-6Although computed tomography can demonstrate that the distance between the hyoid bone and the thyroid cartilage is actually shortened or that they are in contact with each other,6it is difficult to detect the defining moment by a nondynamic test. In contrast, SD-CT provides precise, 3-dimensional dynamic images, enabling treatment-oriented evaluation of swallowing-related problems. Sequential structural assessment during swallowing using SD-CT can help determine the exact location of the clicking larynx. To our knowledge, this is the first report on the use of SD-CT for the diagnosis of a clicking larynx. The differential diagnosis includes Eagle syndrome, triticeous cartilage, and hyoid bone syndrome; a clicking sound/sensation can occur in those diseases but is most common with a clicking larynx. Neck pain in Eagle syndrome is associated with an elongated styloid process or stylohyoid ligament calcification and is treated by surgical excision.7Triticeous cartilage is a small cartilaginous component located in the posterior end of the thyrohyoid ligament. This condition may sometimes cause dysphagia and neck pain.8In hyoid bone syndrome, throat pain occurs at the greater cornu of the hyoid bone and is treated by surgical excision or intralesional triamcinolone injection.9These conditions differ somewhat from a clicking larynx in the site of origin and symptoms. Thus, SD-CT is useful for detecting the clicking location and making the diagnosis. Surgery is the most effective treatment option for a clicking larynx.5,6It is usually performed under general anesthesia6; however, we used local anesthesia because it allows for contact site identification during swallowing and helps confirm improvement in the physical contact by cartilage resection. Generally, symptoms improve immediately after surgery. To our knowledge, no recurrence of symptoms has been reported in previous cases.3-6In conclusion, a clicking sensation on swallowing is suggestive of a clicking larynx, and a careful examination and SD-CT should be performed.

caption: Evaluation of the ear canal hemangioma from a clinical (A), axial computed tomography (CT) (B), coronal CT (C), and sagittal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) (D) perspective. The arrowead indicates the malleus and the asterisk indicates the tumor.
scenario: A 54-year-old woman with a medical history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and migraines presented to a tertiary care otolaryngology clinic reporting 3 months of worsening right ear pain and 1 month of pulsatile tinnitus and hearing loss. She denied a history of fever, otorrhea, prior ear infections, vertigo, or otologic surgery. The patient first saw her primary care physician, who visualized a mass in the right ear canal and attempted needle aspiration, which led to self-resolved bleeding. She was given ciprofloxacin ear drops and trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole, which did not improve her symptoms. On examination, her right external auditory canal (EAC) was completely obstructed by a fleshy, pulsatile mass with a red hue (Figure 1A). Results of Weber tuning fork examination lateralized to the right ear and a Rinne examination suggested a conductive hearing loss. Formal audiogram results confirmed conductive hearing loss in the right ear and type B tympanometry, which was indicative of poor eardrum mobility. Computed tomography (CT) of the temporal bone without contrast showed a well-circumscribed 9-mm lesion in the EAC with bony erosion along the junction of the anterior wall and floor (Figure 1, B and C). Magnetic resonance imaging results showed a well-circumscribed, contrast-enhancing mass that was confined to the EAC (Figure 1D).

options.A: Lobular capillary hemangioma of the EAC

answer: Lobular capillary hemangioma of the EAC
explanation: A. Lobular capillary hemangioma of the EAC An ear canal cholesteatomas develops spontaneously or after infection, trauma, or surgery. It is not as common as middle ear cholesteatoma and is not a vascular tumor.1Imaging results would likely reveal bonier canal erosion than seen in this case. Tympanic paraganglioma/glomus tympanicum is a primarily vascular tumor that also presents with conductive hearing loss and bloody otorrhea. However, these tumors arise from the tympanic plexus in the middle ear, not the EAC. High-riding jugular bulbs present with an inferiorly based blue mass behind an intact eardrum. Pulsatile tinnitus and conductive hearing loss are commonly present. The mass may enlarge during a Valsalva maneuver. Imaging results would be diagnostic for this finding. The presentation of a patient with a capillary hemangioma in the ear canal can be variable. Symptomatic patients can report subjective hearing loss, ear fullness, otorrhagia, pain, pulsatile tinnitus, and purulent otorrhea. In some cases, these lesions are incidentally found on examination.2On examination, capillary hemangiomas in this location commonly present as a red, soft, exophytic mass. Conductive hearing occurs because of occlusion of the EAC, which can be identified through tuning fork examination and formal audiometry. When this type of vascular mass abuts the tympanic membrane, as was noted in this case, pulsatile tinnitus is common. Hemangiomas are benign vascular tumors that are seen mostly in the pediatric population. Capillary hemangiomas are the most common type of hemangioma and typically develop in the liver, spleen, and kidneys.3Most of these lesions spontaneously regress and do not require intervention unless they cause symptoms. While hemangiomas are relatively common in the general population, it is rare for these vascular tumors to involve the ear canal. To our knowledge, there are 26 reports of EAC hemangiomas, most of which are capillary or cavernous.4 Diagnostic workup for a vascular-appearing tumor of the EAC should include otoscopic examination, audiogram, and diagnostic imaging. Capillary hemangiomas appear as nodular, circumscribed, enhancing soft tissue masses on CT with possible focal bone erosion. Magnetic resonance imaging may be appropriate if the tumor is not adequately visualized on CT or if the proximity to overlying brain tissue is not clear. Angiography is useful if the mass has an unclear association with vasculature within the temporal bone. The differential diagnosis for EAC lesions is broad, including vascular tumors (eg, glomus tumors, arteriovenous malformations, or fistulas), cancers (eg, squamous cell carcinoma, basal cell carcinoma, rhabdomyosarcoma, and adenoid cystic carcinoma), infectious causes that present with an aural polyp, congenital etiologies (such as a first branchial cleft cyst), and acquired etiologies, such as an encephalocele. Management of an EAC capillary hemangioma in a symptomatic patient typically includes surgical excision of the mass, which should provide resolution of symptoms. Biopsy can be pursued before complete excision, although discretion should be used given the anatomy of the external and middle ear relative to the middle cranial fossa, jugular vein, carotid artery, facial nerve, ossicles, cochlea, parotid gland, and temporal mandibular joint. Specifically, in the setting of a vascular-appearing mass located medially in the EAC, as seen in this case, a biopsy in the operating room may be most prudent, given the potential for bleeding and patient discomfort. Expectant management may be appropriate in smaller lesions that do not cause significant symptoms. In most reported cases, there is rarely local recurrence of a tumor after a gross total resection.4This case highlights the importance of approaching EAC lesions cautiously, given the broad differential diagnosis for a solid tumor in this location. The patient underwent gross total resection in the operating room, and her symptoms have resolved (Figure 2).

caption: A, Epiglottic mass on direct laryngoscopy. B, Hematoxylin-eosin stain of the lesion. The lesion is characterized by a proliferation of small, somewhat irregular vessels with plump endothelial cells and relatively high proliferation. C, Glucose transporter 1 staining reveals immunopositivity.
scenario: A 5-month-old boy presented to the emergency department with acute oropharyngeal bleeding that self-resolved. Prior to presentation, he had a several-month history of slow feeding and intermittent noisy breathing. Physical examination revealed inspiratory stridor that was worse when supine. Bedside flexible endoscopy findings revealed a fleshy supraglottic mass obscuring a view of the glottis. The patient’s airway was secured in the operating room with an endotracheal tube over a 0° Hopkins rod. The mass was pedunculated on the lingual surface of the epiglottis and had areas of high vascularity and other areas of thrombosis (Figure, A). The vallecula, aryepiglottic folds, arytenoids, glottis, and subglottis were otherwise uninvolved. A biopsy was obtained, and pathology results revealed relatively high proliferation of small, irregular vessels with plump endothelial cells staining positive for glucose transporter 1 (GLUT1) (Figure, B and C).
explanation: Infantile hemangiomas are benign vascular tumors that affect up to 5% of children.1Studies report a higher incidence in White, female, and low-birth-weight infants. They are not present at birth but typically present by 1 month of age and rapidly proliferate in the first few months of life. This is then followed by slow involution over the course of years. Histologically, they are characterized by proliferation of endothelial cells that are GLUT1 positive. Early samples may appear somewhat solid. Perineurial invasion is relatively common and should not be regarded as evidence of malignant neoplasm. Mast cells may be numerous. Infantile hemangiomas should be differentiated from congenital hemangiomas, which are present at birth, do not proliferate, and do not express GLUT1.1 Treatment of infantile hemangioma is recommended if it causes pain, bleeding, disfigurement, or functional impairment. Propranolol is often the first-line medical therapy, followed by corticosteroids. Intralesional steroid injection, topical timolol, and laser therapy may also be considered. Early surgical treatment is usually used if pharmacotherapy has failed or if the lesion is focal and favorable for resection.2 Airway hemangiomas require prompt treatment because of the risk of airway obstruction. They are most often located in the subglottis, and infants usually present with stridor.3There should be a high index of suspicion for airway hemangioma in a patient with airway symptoms and segmental hemangioma in a beard distribution4or PHACE syndrome (posterior fossa malformations, hemangioma, arterial anomalies, coarctation of the aorta/cardiac defects, and eye abnormalities).5A case of bleeding as the presenting symptom of epiglottic hemangioma was previously reported 30 years ago.6Systemic propranolol is an effective treatment of most airway hemangiomas and is recommended as the first-line treatment.7-9However, multimodality therapy may be necessary in cases refractory to propranolol. In this case, the patient was kept intubated, and attempts were made to initiate systemic propranolol therapy. However, the patient was unable to tolerate it owing to hypotension and bradycardia. As such, the patient returned to the operating room for excision of the mass, which was achieved under suspension microlaryngoscopy. The patient was reexamined under anesthesia 8 weeks later with no recurrence of the lesion and slight scarring of the aryepiglottic folds.

caption: A, Nasal endoscopy showing bilateral and symmetric inferior turbinate hypertrophy without erythema, exudate, or ulceration; without mucoid rhinorrhea; and no intranasal masses, lesions, or polyps. B, Computed tomography of the sinuses showing a 9-mm spherical structure in the left inferior nasal cavity with surrounding spiculated calcifications and chronic dystrophic calcification.
scenario: A healthy 15-year-old male patient presented with several years of bilateral congestion and hyposmia. He and his family denied facial trauma, recent or recurrent sinusitis, rhinorrhea, difficulty breathing, pain, change in vision, and constitutional symptoms. He had never had allergy testing but did have occasional allergic symptoms, including sneezing and itchy eyes and nose. He did not report any drug, alcohol, or tobacco use. He was developmentally normal. On physical examination, the patient appeared healthy and had a normal-sounding voice. The tonsils were small, without crypts or tonsilloliths, and there were no neck masses. A flexible fiberoptic nasal endoscopy was performed, and its findings showed bilateral and symmetric inferior turbinate hypertrophy without erythema, exudate, or ulceration, and without mucoid rhinorrhea (Figure 1A). There were no intranasal masses, lesions, or polyps. The patient was prescribed intranasal steroid spray, oral antihistamines, and sinonasal saline rinses, and was instructed to return to our clinic in 4 to 6 weeks, but was subsequently lost to follow-up. One year later, the patient returned to our clinic with the same concern. Examination findings, including those of a second nasal endoscopy, were the same. However, when he blew his nose, a pungent, foul odor filled the room. The patient reported that he did not feel he had bad breath, but he was embarrassed that every time he blew his nose there was a foul odor. A computed tomography fusion scan of the sinuses without intravenous contrast was performed (Figure 1B).
explanation: The results of the computed tomography scan showed clear sinuses, but a 9-mm spherical structure was noted in the left inferior nasal cavity with surrounding spiculated calcifications and chronic dystrophic calcification, suggestive of an intranasal foreign body. The patient was taken to the operating room for a bilateral nasal endoscopy, turbinate reduction, and removal of a foreign body from the left nasal cavity. The inferior turbinate was medialized, and there was friable granulation tissue inferomedial to the inferior turbinate. This tissue was gently suctioned, and bleeding was encountered. After continued suctioning and application of a topical decongestant with an oxymetazoline-soaked pledget, a metallic foreign body was visualized (Figure 2). This body was removed and epistaxis was controlled. During postoperative discussion with the patient and his family, the patient reported having been shot in the nose with a pellet gun when he was approximately 8 or 9 years old. The parents recalled this event, but because there had been no significant symptoms at the time, they had not sought further evaluation. At the first postoperative visit, nasal endoscopy showed normal mucosa and turbinates bilaterally, and the patient reported resolution of the foul odor. Foreign bodies are a common cause of urgent care and otolaryngology office visits in children. Typically, this occurrence peaks in early childhood because older children are usually more reliable historians and are less likely to intentionally place intranasal foreign bodies. Common symptoms of an intranasal foreign body include epistaxis, rhinorrhea, foul odor, snoring, and, when long-term as in this case, purulence. Most often, the foreign bodies found in children are organic objects, such as pebbles, beads, and nuts.1 Pellet guns fire small metal or plastic pellets at speeds of up to 1000 feet per second.2Injuries from the use of pellet guns are common in adolescents, with more than 90% occurring in those younger than 19 years.2There are numerous examples of traumatic injury to the eyes, mouth, and sinuses owing to accidental or intentional firing of pellet guns1-4; however, this case was unique given its remote history and lack of symptoms of traumatic injury. Delayed onset of presentation with nasal foreign body is more common in young children and less frequent in older children and adults.5 Nontraumatic nasal pellet inhalation appears to be extremely rare in adolescents with no history of trauma. Patients with a history of recurrent rhinorrhea, congestion, and putrid nasal discharge or odor warrant careful examination for foreign bodies, regardless of age or history. With long-term nasal foreign bodies, there may be complete mucosalization over the foreign body, making diagnosis more difficult, as in this case. Cases of sinonasal injury with a pellet gun may result in the foreign body being lodged in an area of the nasal cavity or sinus that is not visible on nasal endoscopy (ie, within the maxillary or sphenoid sinus, the inferior or middle meatus, or high intranasally). Therefore, imaging may be required to further evaluate. Although a rare cause and presentation, the late onset of symptoms and the metallic properties of the pellet could have resulted in toxic effects and spread of infection in this patient.

caption: Gross and histologic findings. A, Serial sections of the intraparotid mass demonstrate a well-demarcated solid nodule with tan-white, glistening cut surfaces. B, Microscopic examination shows a multilobulated, complex lesion with prominent stromal fibrosis and collections of ductal structures with varying degrees of cystic change (hematoxylin-eosin). C, Acinar cells with brightly eosinophilic intracytoplasmic granules (hematoxylin-eosin).
scenario: A 9-year-old boy was referred to the pediatric otolaryngology clinic with a 3-month history of a left-sided neck mass. The mass had been slowly enlarging and he had been experiencing mild intermittent pain, but no additional symptoms were reported. His medical history was significant for several episodes of upper respiratory infection during the previous winter season, and he previously had an adenotonsillectomy several years prior and bilateral ear tubes placed 1 year before presentation. Physical examination showed a mildly tender, nonmobile, left parotid mass near the angle of the mandible with no overlying skin changes or drainage around the mass. There was no lymphadenopathy or other lesions noted in the neck area, and cranial nerve VII was fully intact. Ultrasonography results of the neck showed a left 1.5-cm preauricular nodular mass with internal and marginal vascularity. A neck magnetic resonance imaging study without contrast performed at an outside institution revealed the 1.5-cm heterogeneous intraparotid nodule that was predominantly isotense to glandular tissue on T1 images with vague hypointensity of a small irregular central region, as well as vague hyperintensity on T2 images. He subsequently underwent fine needle aspiration biopsy to assess the lesion, which demonstrated benign-appearing salivary gland tissue and clusters of myoepithelial cells. The mass was continuing to enlarge, and the patient’s pain was increasing in that area, so the decision was made to perform left superficial parotidectomy with preservation of the facial nerve. Intraoperatively, the left parotid mass was noted to be just below the lower branches of the facial nerve. The excised parotid mass was sent to the pathology department for analysis. Gross examination of the specimen demonstrated a 1.6 × 1.5 × 1.1–cm tan-white, well-circumscribed lesion that was partially surrounded by salivary gland parenchyma (Figure, A). Histologic examination of the nodule was performed (Figure, B and C).
explanation: Microscopically, hematoxylin-eosin–stained sections demonstrated a well-circumscribed solid mass with a lobular architecture. Within the lesion, there was variably abundant, hyalinized collagen surrounding closely packed ductal structures with varying sizes, some of which were cystically dilated. The lining epithelial cells were bland, and mitotic figures were absent. There were frequent clusters of acinar structures with brightly eosinophilic, intracytoplasmic granules. These characteristic histologic features confirmed the diagnosis of sclerosing polycystic adenoma (SPA). Sclerosing polycystic adenoma is an uncommon salivary gland tumor first described by Smith et al1in a series of 9 cases using the termsclerosing polycystic adenosis. Since then, this entity has been increasingly recognized, with more than 100 cases reported so far.2,3Recently, SPA has been included in the latest edition of the World Health Organization classification of head and neck tumors.4Sclerosing polycystic adenoma was initially considered to be reactive or inflammatory in nature; however, emerging evidence suggests a clonal process,5a propensity to recur, and rare instances of malignant transformation.2-4Therefore, based on the newly recognized findings, the termsclerosing polycystic adenomahas been proposed to reflect a true neoplastic process.2,3This notion is further supported by the recent discovery of recurrent gene variations in thePI3Kpathway of cell cycle regulation in SPA that are analyzed through targeted next-generation sequencing, withPTENvariations identified in all cases (n = 4).6 While data on the incidence of SPA in the literature are limited, accumulating evidence shows that SPA occurs over a wide age range from children to elderly individuals (7-84 years), with a mean age at presentation of 41 years.7Sclerosing polycystic adenoma occurs slightly more often in female patients, with a male to female ratio of approximately 2:3.7Patients with SPA typically present with a painless, slow-growing mass, although few patients reported various degrees of pain.7The parotid gland is the most common site (more than 80% of cases), followed by the submandibular gland.2,3Rare cases have been reported in the minor salivary glands of the oral cavity as well.8,9Sclerosing polycystic adenoma most commonly occurs as an isolated tumorous condition in the salivary gland and only rarely associates with other lesions, including pleomorphic adenoma, oncocytoma, and Warthin tumor.8Sclerosing polycystic adenoma in a familial setting has been reported; 2 sisters received a diagnosis of this lesion.10While most often identified as a single nodule, rare cases exhibited multifocal lesions.8To our knowledge, this patient represents the youngest male in the literature to have this diagnosis.6-10 Conservative surgical excision is the preferred treatment for SPA.2,4,7In a review by Espinosa et al,7approximately 60% of patients received superficial parotidectomy with preservation of the facial nerve, 22% received total parotidectomy, and 17% received tumor enucleation. The recurrence rate is low (approximately 17%) and appears to be associated with tumor enucleation and multinodular or nonencapsulated lesions.7Long-term clinical follow-up is recommended for patients with SPA.2,7

caption: Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the neck in the coronal (A) and axial (B) views demonstrating a large, predominantly left-sided, obstructive, submucosal, upper airway lesion extending from the nasopharynx to the glottis.
scenario: A 71-year-old man presented to the emergency department with dyspnea, dysphonia, dysphagia, and neck swelling. He denied chills, fever, neck stiffness, new medications, otalgia, sick contacts, trismus, and use of an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor. His complex medical history included factor V Leiden deficiency requiring therapeutic anticoagulation, heart failure with atrial fibrillation, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease associated with 110-pack-year smoking history. Laboratory studies demonstrated an international normalized ratio of 16.4, a prothrombin time of 118.1 seconds, and a partial thromboplastin time of 81.4 seconds. On examination, the patient had substantial dysphonia, fullness in the left submandibular region, and ecchymosis of the lateral left neck extending toward the midline. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography performed in the emergency department revealed a large, intermediate-density, modestly enhancing, left-sided submucosal lesion extending from the nasopharynx inferiorly to the glottis with encroachment on the airway (Figure).
