Flexible fiberoptic laryngoscopy demonstrated a large submucosal mass extending from the left posteroinferior nasopharyngeal wall to the left lateral and posterior pharyngeal walls, obstructing the view of the left supraglottis, glottis, and piriform sinus. The right side of the epiglottis was ecchymotic and edematous. The mass extended farther along the aryepiglottic fold to involve the arytenoid and interarytenoid space, as well as the false vocal fold on the left. The vocal cords were only partially visualized. Given the important laryngoscopy findings, the decision was made to proceed with awake fiberoptic nasotracheal intubation in the operating room to secure the patient’s airway.

options.D: Spontaneous airway hemorrhage with obstructive hematoma

answer: Spontaneous airway hemorrhage with obstructive hematoma
explanation: D. Spontaneous airway hemorrhage with obstructive hematoma Warfarin sodium was first approved for inhibiting coagulation in the 1950s. Warfarin inhibits the vitamin K-dependent clotting factors in the coagulation cascade, factors II, VII, IX, and X, as well as proteins C and S, leading to systemic anticoagulation.1Indications for its use include prophylaxis and treatment of venous thrombosis and pulmonary embolism, prevention of thromboembolic events associated with atrial fibrillation or cardiac valve replacement, and reduction of the risk of death or recurrent cardiovascular events after myocardial infarction.1The most frequent adverse reaction to warfarin is hemorrhage.1The most common sites of bleeding are the gastrointestinal, genitourinary, cutaneous, and intracranial locations.2,3 Spontaneous hemorrhage into the soft tissues of the head and neck poses a potentially lethal complication owing to airway compromise. Hemorrhage locations that could compromise the airway include the lingual, sublingual, retropharyngeal, supraglottic, glottic, and submandibular spaces.4In a systematic review,4the most common site was a sublingual hematoma (67%), followed by retropharyngeal hematoma (27%). Laryngeal bleeding is extremely rare. Although the cause of airway bleeding could be coughing, sneezing, or straining, it may also occur spontaneously without an inciting event.5,6Local infection in the upper respiratory tract could also lead to vasodilation and subsequent hemorrhage.7The present patient reported no such antecedent events, similar to 2 previous case reports.2,8 The differential diagnosis for airway lesions presenting with a similar combination of fiberoptic and imaging findings include an abscess, angioedema, and potentially, a malignant neoplasm. In this case report, key features consistent with a hematoma include cutaneous changes of ecchymosis and fiberoptic identification of ecchymosis and edema of the upper airway. The patient's airway was secured by fiberoptic intubation, and he was transferred to the intensive care unit. The patient died a few weeks later due to causes unrelated to this case. Management of upper airway hematomas has been debated. Rosenbaum and colleagues9suggest that emergency instrumentation via intubation or tracheostomy may prove fatal in patients with severe coagulopathy, and therefore, they recommend observation as the first step. However, Cohen and Warman6recommend early tracheostomy in these patients. Karmacharya and colleagues4state that the outcomes do not differ based on the management strategy. However, it is important to note that airway edema and recurrent bleeding are unpredictable and may lead to worsening of symptoms and a possible change in clinical status. Spontaneous upper airway hemorrhage is a rare, but serious and potentially lethal complication of anticoagulation therapy. Patients presenting with head and neck symptoms, such as dysphagia, dysphonia, dyspnea, odynophagia, and/or stridor, and a history of warfarin use—especially with supratherapeutic levels—must have a prompt airway endoscopy to assess the airway. When symptoms or examination findings are concerning, it is crucial to secure the airway quickly to avoid worsening or recurrence of bleeding. Patients with milder symptoms, such as small nonobstructive hematomas, can be placed under close observation in an intensive care unit where prompt reversal of the supratherapeutic coagulation status is possible if necessary.

caption: Cervical computed tomography scan of the sagittal (A) and axial (B) planes. In the sagittal plane, there is retropharyngeal fluid accumulation, and in the axial plane, there is fluid accumulation in the retropharyngeal and vascular spaces with fat infiltration.
scenario: A 56-year-old patient with no medical history presented spontaneously to the emergency department of our university hospital (Assistance Publique Hôpitaux de Paris) for bilateral neck swelling that had developed over 24 hours. The patient had no traumatic or iatrogenic triggers. He reported an edema of the lower lip that resolved spontaneously the day before. He had no dyspnea nor dysphagia, but did have a discrete dysphonia. He had no fever. Neck swelling was global, bilateral, and painless, and was most severe on the left side. There was a rash, the border of which was marked with a felt pen. Nasofibroscopy results showed a normal airway with a posterior pharyngeal wall bulging. Oropharyngeal and oral cavity examination results were normal, with no trismus. A contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) scan showed a large retropharyngeal fluid accumulation of 2 × 10 × 6 cm that extended laterally to the vascular spaces, especially on the left side (Figure, A and B). This was associated with infiltration of the mediastinal fat and a thin left pleural effusion. There was no vascular thrombosis or dental abnormality. Hyperleukocytosis levels were 12 000/mL. We did not have the result of the C reactive protein assay.
explanation: Because of the rash, acute neck swelling, large cervical fluid accumulation with mediastinal infiltration, and hyperleukocytosis, we treated the patient as if he had cervical necrotizing fasciitis. He immediately underwent an operation. Orotracheal intubation was easily performed. The left cervicectomy and opening of the superficial fascia revealed a milky fluid that was coming from all the soft tissues. The introduction of the surgeon’s finger allowed an easy and large retropharyngeal and retroesophageal dissection from the skull base to the posterior mediastinum. Samples were sent to bacteriology, mycobacteriology, anatomopathology, and biochemistry laboratories. Two lavage modules were fixed, and the cervicectomy was not closed. Another incision to wash and drain the anterior mediastinum and a tracheostomy were performed. Amoxicillin and clavulanic acid, 3 grams per day, were administered. A first dressing change was performed under general anesthesia on the first day. Bilateral pleural effusions led to bilateral pleural drainage, bringing back a milky fluid. At day 2, the cervical liquid was sterile, but lipids were found (cholesterol levels, 73.4 mg/dL; triglyceride levels, 377.9 mg/dL [to convert to millimoles per liter, multiply by 0.0259 and 0.0113, respectively). We corrected our initial diagnosis and focused on a spontaneous cervical lymphorrhea. Consequently, the cervicectomy was closed. The patient was fed with parenteral nutrition during the first week, and then had an oral fat-free diet. The pleural effusion did not reappear, and there was neither scar inflammation nor fever. Two nonproductive aspirating drains were removed 48 hours later. An etiological assessment was performed later, and thoracoabdominopelvic CT scan, positron emission tomography scan, and lympho–magnetic resonance imaging results were normal. Approximately 2 liters of chyle drains each day into the venous system via the thoracic duct, which includes 14 mL per hour during youth and  100 mL per hour after a meal.1,2This canal crosses the diaphragm and goes through the thorax, crossing the esophagus from right to left, runs along the left pleural dome, and flows into the confluence of the subclavian and left internal jugular veins.3,4Thus, depending on the location of a wound on its thin wall, lymphorrhea may lead to ascites, right or left chylothorax, or left cervical lymphorrhea.2 Cervical lymphorrhea are mainly due to iatrogenic trauma, complicating 1% to 3% of cervical surgeries.5To our knowledge, in the scientific literature, only 1 article reported idiopathic spontaneous cervical lymphorrhea.6The patient was a 50-year-old woman with progressive and apyretic left cervical swelling without dyspnea or dysphagia. The CT findings in that patient were similar to those in the patient in this article. Lymphangiography results revealed a dilation of lymphatic vessels. Surgeons performed a ligation of the thoracic duct, and a fat-free diet was given. There was no recurrence. The management of traumatic cervical lymphorrhea has been reviewed by Lisan et al.5If levels are less than 500 mL per day, an oral fat-free diet is indicated.7,8In case of failure at day 5 or if the output is between 500 and 1000 mL per day, parenteral nutrition with intravenous somatostatin is used. In case of failure at day 10 or if the output is greater than 1000 mL per day, an invasive procedure on the thoracic duct is indicated (eg, embolization by lymphangiography, ligation by thoracoscopy, or revision by cervicectomy).2,5 Spontaneous cervical lymphorrhea being extremely rare, we looked for the etiologies of nontraumatic chylothoraxes, which include lymphoma, autoimmune, tuberculosis, lymphangioleiomyomatosis, and idiopathic.2Retrospectively, the indication of surgical drainage and tracheotomy is debatable, particularly in a patient without apyrexia and dyspnea. However, we were able to protect his respiratory tract and ascertain the chylous and aseptic nature of the fluid. After reexamination of the CT scan, the fluid accumulation was centered in the lower left cervical space, had 0 Hounsfield units of density, and had blurred boundaries, whereas an abscess usually shows rim enhancement. There was no pharyngeal, dental, or skin infection. The C-reactive protein assay results were normal, but were received after the first surgery. There is no fluid collection in angioneurotic and Quincke edema. Spontaneous cervical lymphorrhea is extremely rare and should be a diagnosis of exclusion after other conditions, including infection, are formally ruled out with clinical, biochemical, microbiological, and radiological findings.
